inherited_lead: Literally, to strike or plant (卓) the staff (拄杖): "to strike the staff on the floor." The phrase occurs 5,243 times in 287 allowlisted texts. In the Chan record it is a teaching-seat action, not merely a description of walking with a stick. A master strikes once and says, "all at once, smashed to pieces" (卓拄杖一下，云：一時粉碎), or strikes and supplies the demanded phrase. The action can punctuate a public exchange, accompany a shout, or close a formal address immediately before "stepped down" (下座). The corpus counts the blows explicitly: "once" occurs 777 times and "three times" 32 times. These observable placements are the Chan deviation; the entry assigns no unstated meaning to the blow. | The omitted instrument varies: texts explicitly supply 'with a staff' (以拄杖), 'with a whisk' (以拂子), or no instrument. These are grammatical specifications of one action, not separate things. The Chan graph (禪) names Chan here, so the object is the Chan seat. No corpus warrant was found for assigning the blow a single symbolic message. | ” (如何是大用現前). Dahui Zonggao likewise raises the whisk and says that the old man has arrived, then asks whether the assembly sees him. In another record, a master says that even if old man Śākyamuni came there, he would receive thirty blows; Dahui comments on a story of Śākyamuni disputing the buddha-teaching with Indra by saying, “This old fellow deserves thirty staff-blows” (這老漢好與三十拄杖). The form also remains a quotation label: Yunmen says, “Old man Śākyamuni has already spoken; Maitreya still does not know” (釋迦老子道了也，彌勒猶自不知). A later master says, “Speak a sentence where old man Śākyamuni could not speak; take a step where the great teacher Bodhidharma could not go” (釋迦老子說不到處，說取一句；達磨大師行不到處，行取一步). The strongest coarse appraisal is textual and explicit: “Śākyamuni is a dry shit-stick” (釋迦老子是乾屎橛), paired with “Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are shit-carrying fellows” (文殊普賢是擔屎漢). The deviation lies in the form’s repeated Chan use: a revered name becomes an immediately addressable “old man” whom masters quote, enact, out-say, rebuke, and strike in public discourse.

In a title or section heading, a preface (序) is introductory prose placed before a recorded-sayings collection, anthology, or edition. The graph commonly follows the work title, as in 'Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Monk Foyan' (佛眼和尚語錄序), 'Preface to the Extensive Record of the Monk Yongjue' (永覺和尚廣錄序), and 'Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Monk Sanfeng Cang' (三峰藏和尚語錄序).

The isolated four graphs say, 'stop (歇)—that is (即) awakening (菩提),' but the corpus's recurring full quotation supplies the omitted subject: 'the crazed mind does not stop; when it stops, that is awakening' (狂心不歇，歇即菩提). A historical compendium follows the phrase with its own explicit explanation, beginning 'as for “when it stops, that is awakening”' and describing what it calls awakening. Chan masters repeatedly take up the quoted line in hall discourse. One says that when dust-labor suddenly stops, 'when it stops, that is awakening,' then immediately asks the assembly, 'from where is it obtained? | Allowlist count: 38 hits in 26 texts. One fixed-proposition sense. Family checked against stop/rest (歇), rest and cease (休歇), let it rest and cease (休去歇去), crazed mind (狂心), and awakening (菩提). Literally “lay down a word,” this means to offer a response phrase when a master raises a case, an encounter (因緣), or a question and calls for an answer. It occurs 889 times across 205 allowlisted texts and names a standard public testing routine. A master orders the assembly to offer responses; participants put forward words or manage a turning phrase; the recurrent recorded verdict is that the responses “do not accord” (不契). In Nanquan's door case, many people offer responses but none accords with Nanquan's meaning. Another senior monk offers ninety-six turns without satisfying the master. When the assembly's responses fail, the master may supply his own final phrase or speak in their place. Dahui likewise reports successive responders failing to accord in Dongshan's saying and an assembly failing in the bamboo-slat case. Verbal “offer a phrase,” agent “one who offered a phrase,” and nominal “the phrase offered” constructions all denote the same response event and product. The Chan deviation is the institutional demand for an on-the-spot phrase to be publicly measured against a raised case; the entry does not infer what makes any response accord.

Literally “verdant green bamboo.” In the Chan corpus these four ordinary landscape words are overwhelmingly the first half of a disputed stock proposition: “verdant green bamboo is entirely the true-as-is” or “entirely the body of reality,” paired with “luxuriant yellow flowers are none other than complete discernment” (青青翠竹，盡是真如／法身；鬱鬱黃花，無非般若). The proposition is not a settled glossary equation. The Ancestral Hall Collection explicitly records that some call it a wrong saying while others accept it; elsewhere in the same text one teacher answers “it does not pervade form” (不遍色), and Dazhu Huihai rejects identifying the bamboo itself with the body of reality. Dahui preserves both sides and describes Nanyang Huizhong as maintaining “verdant green bamboo is entirely the body of reality” while Dazhu breaks it as “verdant green bamboo is not the body of reality” (國師主張青青翠竹盡是法身；大珠破青青翠竹不是法身). The phrase also enters interviews: asked “verdant green bamboo is entirely the true-as-is; what is the true-as-is? | Literally, flourishing or luxuriant (鬱鬱) yellow flowers (黃花): "flourishing yellow flowers." The phrase occurs 57 times in 41 allowlisted texts. Its distinctively Chan deployment is the frequently quoted proposition, "the green bamboo is entirely the body of the teaching; the flourishing yellow flowers are nothing other than wisdom" (青青翠竹，盡是法身；鬱鬱黃花，無非般若). The fuller exact yellow-flower formula occurs 18 times in 17 texts, while "green bamboo" (青青翠竹) occurs 116 times in 68. The records preserve disagreement rather than a single unopposed gloss. A question to National Teacher Huizhong says that some call the proposition an erroneous saying while others trust it as inconceivable; his recorded answer accepts it by placing bamboo and flowers within the range of the teaching body and wisdom. The same transmitted passage then has a Huayan lecturer ask Dazhu Huihai why he does not permit the formula; Dazhu distinguishes appearing in response to bamboo and flowers from wisdom or the teaching body being located in those objects. Later, Shending Yikui rebukes people who hear the formula, hold rigidly to it, and never shift at all, calling a fitting phrase "a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand ages" (一句合頭語，萬劫繫驢橛). In another exchange he asks how wisdom is understood when the yellow flowers are right here, and tells the respondent that he has let the yellow flowers down. Chan thus bends a scene of colored plants into a portable, disputed proposition and a live examination question; this entry reports the acceptance, distinction, and correction recorded by the texts without deciding among them.

To address or instruct the assembled community publicly. The term occurs 12,002 times in 399 allowlisted texts and is a standard discourse heading beside the formal hall address (上堂) and small convocation (小參): a master “addresses the assembly, saying” (示眾云/曰), sometimes after ascending the seat. The corpus groups the formal hall address (上堂) and address to the assembly (示眾) as public formats and compares a small convocation with an address to the assembly. It can be delivered in writing as a verse after the assembly answers a question. The format also includes final instructions (臨終示眾), as when Luopu begins by asking the assembly about one matter. Chan turns “show to the assembly” into a recurring name for the master’s public verbal address; it is not a private exchange.

Asked the great meaning of the buddha-teaching, he again puts it down and stands with folded hands; asked whether there is an upward matter, he shoulders it and goes. In the street he says he is waiting for a person and rejects the monk who claims to have arrived. Later records quote his verse, "Maitreya, true Maitreya, divides into hundreds of thousands of bodies, constantly showing himself to people, while people do not recognize him" (彌勒真彌勒，分身千百億，時時示時人，時人自不識), then comment on it. The Zen Budai is thus the bag-bearing street monk whose putting down, shouldering, waiting, and Maitreya verse are repeatedly raised and judged.

The graph “speech” (語) is translated here as the actual response, not left as an unexplained “word.” The recurring sequence “had no response” (無對) → “ordered the assembly to respond in his place” (命眾代語) → “submitted responses did not accord” (下語不契) → “the master supplied one” (師代) establishes the institutional sense directly.

proposing_entries: 上堂、下座、世尊、便下座、喝一喝、德山托鉢、釋迦
inherited_lead: Literally, "then descended from the seat" (便下座). In Chan records this is a formal scene-closing action tied to the high teaching seat, not merely someone sitting down or leaving ordinary furniture. The Buddha cases make the institutional structure explicit: the Buddha mounts the seat (陞座), the assembly settles, Manjusri or Kasyapa strikes the sounding block and announces the king of teachings' teaching or that the talk is finished, and the Buddha then descends. The phrase can close a spoken address after a final question, as when Linji tells the assembly to ask the two hall leaders about host and guest and descends. It also closes action without a final speech: after Magu exits during the exchange of seats, Linji descends. In the Mazu-Baizhang encounter, Baizhang rolls up the mat as soon as Mazu mounts the hall, and Mazu descends and continues the exchange in his quarters. The distinctive Chan deployment is the visible termination of the formal teaching-seat event; sometimes the descent itself is the entire recorded close. | Cross-checked 'ascend the seat' (陞座), 'ascend the hall' (上堂), 'then stepped down' (便下座), 'planted the staff' (卓拄杖), and the Buddha seat narratives. The formal closure and physically being pulled from a seat share one concrete action, so item 8 does not warrant a split. | The formula occurs 7,091 times in 320 allowlisted texts. Family comparison: “shout” (喝) can be a noun or verb, “one shout” (一喝) counts it, and “gave a shout” (喝一喝) is the finite narrative action. Speaker, addressee, and sequence position are different deployments of the same action, not different things. Compare leaving the seat (下座), ascending the seat (陞座), planting the staff (卓拄杖), and the abbot's quarters (方丈).

Literally, "an idle or at-ease person of the Way" (閑道人). Chan usage bends ordinary idleness into a named epithet, most often in the full line "an at-ease person of the Way who has ended study and does nothing contrived" (絕學無為閑道人). Huangbo explains that people of old heard one statement and thereby "ended study" (絕學), and so received this name; he contrasts them with people seeking much knowledge and many explanations. Tianru explicitly lists "the great sea of extinction" (大寂滅海), "the ground of actual principle" (實際理地), and this full epithet as different names for "great rest" (大休). The Mirror Record distinguishes accumulating study, ending study, and then passing beyond both, saying that only on reaching the end of study does one first draw near the Way. Other records deploy the shortened term in verse: the whole world is full of people seeking buddha, but an at-ease person of the Way is hard to find (茫茫盡是覓佛漢，舉世難尋閑道人). The epithet therefore names a Chan roster type through explicit ending-study and great-rest definitions, not a generic loafer.

inherited_lead: ' (如何是祖師西來意: 如何是, 'what is'; 祖師, 'the Patriarch'; 西來, 'coming from the West'; 意, 'meaning or intent'). The Patriarch is Bodhidharma, and the west is India in relation to China. This is the most frequently repeated set question put to masters in the lamp records and recorded sayings: the full eight-graph form occurs 1,858 times in 231 allowlist texts, while the shorter phrase 'the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West' (祖師西來意) occurs about 2,081 times. The records preserve different replies by named people. Zhaozhou answers 'the cypress tree in the garden' (庭前柏樹子); Linji, asked while washing his feet, answers 'just now this old monk is washing his feet' (恰值老僧洗脚); National Teacher Huian answers 'why not ask about your own meaning? | A stock question spoken between two people, not one master's private idiom. MasterName is null on these narrated or raised exchanges; each AttributionNote identifies the questioner and answerer. Compare the shorter noun phrase 'the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West' (祖師西來意). | A fixed liturgical question, almost always in the frame (如何是祖師西來意) — 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?

The “thousand hands and eyes,” attested 242 times in 108 allowlisted texts, is the invoked form of Great Compassion, or Guanyin. Chushi Fanqi’s image record identifies it directly: “Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes are Guanyin’s responsive transformation-body” (大悲千手眼者，觀音大士應化之身也). In the Chan record the figure is repeatedly placed inside public interviews asking which is the “true eye.” Daowu asks, “Among Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes, which is the true eye?

Literally, “one act” or “single conduct” (一行) plus “complete command” (三昧). In the Chan corpus Huineng's Platform Record supplies the governing definitions and the Zen-specific correction. It defines the term as “at all times, while walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, constantly carrying a straightforward mind” (於一切時中，行住坐臥，常行直心), and again as carrying a straightforward mind without attachment to anything (於一切法上，無有執著). The Record of the Patriarchal Hall gives the parallel: “in every place, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, all is one straightforward mind; this is the site of the way, this is the pure land” (於一切處行住坐臥，皆一直心，即是道場，即是淨土). The Platform Record then identifies and rejects a contrary deployment: people attached to the term say that sitting without moving and suppressing thoughts is “complete command in one act”; the text says that if so, this is the same as insentient things and an obstructing condition (同無情，却是障道因緣). This explicit correction is the entry's central Zen bend: the named “one act” is defined across all four postures and straightforward mind, not reduced to unmoving sitting. A preface to another Platform edition also defines it as “the single aspect of the realm of things” (法界一相) and says that although the many good acts differ, all are made correct in one act (萬善雖殊，皆正於一行).

Literally to issue into brightness: to bring something to light or make it clear. The term occurs 1,304 times in 250 allowlisted texts. Chan biographies repeatedly say that someone brings “the great matter,” “the mind-ground,” or “the essentials of mind” to light. One record lists bringing the great matter to light alongside having one's mind-ground opened through mountains and waters and recognizing one's original face through things encountered; the text supplies these neighboring predicates without making them synonyms. A later address states its aim as having each person “directly bring to light one's own fundamental great matter” (直下發明自己本分大事), anchoring direct instruction rather than retrospective biography. Other biographies say “there will certainly be clarification” (必有發明) or that someone was “not greatly clarified” (不大發明). Those result and degree constructions name the outcome of the same bringing-to-light event, not another lexical referent. | Translate the corpus term rather than importing modern “invention” or automatically making it “enlightenment.” Named-object verbs and result-noun grammar remain one sense. Compare the great matter (大事), fundamental great matter (本分大事), mind-ground (心地), essentials of mind (心要), awakening to the Way (悟道), awakening (悟), and realization (證).

Allowlist counts recorded in the audit: the headword “staff/blow” (棒), 18,109 hits in 415 texts; “one blow” (一棒), 2,954; “thirty blows” (三十棒), 2,766; “twenty blows” (二十棒), 407; “one bout of blows” (一頓棒), 63; “receive a blow” (喫棒), 1,191; and “painful blows” (痛棒), 752. The object-versus-blow split is preserved and strengthened: six object witnesses and seven act witnesses, with every sense independently anchored. Attribution remains cautious because several formulas circulate in raised cases and later compilations, and witnesses differ over which Deshan bears the thirty-blows formula.

Family check: “clap the hands” (撫掌), “hand-clapping” (拍手撫掌), “clap and laugh loudly” (撫掌大笑), “clap once” (撫掌一下), and “clap three times” (撫掌三下) all denote the same physical action. They differ in accompanying speech and count, not referent, so they remain one sense.

Literally, "swap out the eyes" (換卻眼睛). In ordinary wording this would name a bodily exchange; Chan records use it as an accusation that a saying, written formulation, sight, sound, or teacher has displaced a person's own seeing. A commentary says a monk asking Xuansha about his own self had his eyes swapped out by Xuansha's reply. Shiyu says altered wording and changed characters (改文易字) swap out people's eyes, and elsewhere says waterbirds, groves, bells, and gongs do it. Sanyi warns against letting the writing brush exchange black beans for one's eyes (毛錐子將黑荳換卻眼睛), then identifies bird-script, dragon-writing, paper, ink, and written characters as fit for ordinary circulation rather than Chan discussion. A case comment even judges the words "Where is the eminent monk?

inherited_lead: Literally, “at / meet the trigger or occasion.” In Chan records the occasion is repeatedly public and interpersonal: one account says that in all his questions and answers he “did not yield when meeting the occasion” (問答，當機不讓); a verse pairs a clear question and a direct answer with “meeting face-to-face on the occasion” (當機覿面). The phrase can introduce a request—“with one phrase meeting the occasion, please speak the teaching” (一句當機請師說法)—or appraise an immediate response. A master strikes the staff and says, “freed through on the occasion; it is no other thing” (當機透脫，更非別物). Yuanwu's verse says that buddhas and patriarchs “value what is ready-made when meeting the occasion” (佛祖當機貴見成) and immediately calls for someone to come before the assembly and settle doubt. Thus the corpus bends a general word for apt timing toward the live occasion of encounter, question, answer, and response.

' (迴光返照看身心是何物). Shitou's Grass Hut Song says, 'turn the light around and shine back, then return' (迴光返照便歸來). Linji tells his listeners that at the words they should 'themselves turn the light around and shine back, seeking nothing else' (便自迴光返照，更不別求). Chengtian Cique says, 'only turn the light around and shine back; carefully search beneath your own heels and look what it is' (但自迴光返照，向自己脚根下子細推尋，看是箇什麼). Gongchen Jueke closes an address with 'each of you, please turn the light around and shine back; do not hesitate further' (各請迴光返照，休更踟躕). Fenyang's verse supplies a result-clause: 'turn the light around and shine back, illuminating present and past' (迴光返照明今古). The corpus thus records an imperative verb phrase, a poetic return, a prohibition on seeking elsewhere, and direct objects or complements such as body and mind, beneath one's heels, and present and past.

Literally "one" (一) "move, placement, or stroke" (著): "one move," attested 3,121 times in 351 allowlisted texts. The game-like noun appears in recurring Chan compounds: "let one move pass" (放過一著, 617 occurrences), "the final move" (末後一著, 104), "the upward move" (向上一著, 279), "one move ahead" (先一著, 38), and the suffixed "one move" (一著子, 601). A case-comment collection appraises an earlier response as "precisely letting one move pass," then adds "danger" (正是放過一著；險). A lamp address pairs "Linji's vanguard—let one move pass" with "Deshan's later command—set it aside" (臨濟先鋒，放過一著；德山後令，且在一邊). Questions ask, "before living beings and buddhas arose, where did one move fall?
" (凡聖本來不二，迷悟豈有殊途). Zhe'an says, "confusion and awakening are not different; motion and stillness have one source" (迷悟不異，動靜一源).

The graphs join 'one's own portion, allotment, or lot' (本分) to 'matter or affair' (事): the matter that belongs to one's own basic lot. The corpus sets it against 'outside one's lot' or 'extra' (分外) and records about 840 occurrences across 184 allowlisted texts. It is repeatedly asked as 'what is one's own fundamental matter? | ' (如何是本分事), 'what is the student's own fundamental matter? | Zen-allowlist count: 672 hits in 176 texts. Allowlist count for the unsplit string: 2,214 hits in 311 texts. Primary family check: 'visible form/color' (色), 'sound' (聲), 'seeing and hearing' (見聞), 'sound, form, and language' (聲色言語), and 'sound, form, and names' (聲色名字). The ordinary 'sensual attractions' and the idiom 'without changing voice or expression' refer to different things and are split below under depth-gate item 8.

To divide (分) and to distinguish or separate (別): 'to distinguish' or 'tell apart,' and as a noun, distinguishing. The Chan corpus most often places it in negative constructions: 'do not arouse distinguishing' (不起分別), 'do not distinguish' (莫分別), and 'apart from distinguishing' (離分別). It is paired with 'thinking' (思量)—'thinking and distinguishing' (思量分別, 165 occurrences)—and with 'deluded thought' (妄想), as 'deluded-thought distinguishing' (妄想分別). Dahui says, 'this matter is not what thinking and distinguishing can grasp; now say—when you neither distinguish nor think, what is it? | 且道不分別不思量時是箇甚麼). The allowlisted concordance has 418 matches in 147 texts. Family revalidation against “straw sandals” (草鞋), “travel on foot” (行脚), and “wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) confirms one object sense. ‘Wear out sandals’ is a verb phrase involving that object, not a second thing. | Footwear woven from grass or straw. In Chan records the sandals belong especially to going on foot between teachers: “to wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) and “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years” (更買草鞋行脚三十年) make the ordinary shoe part of the institutional life of itinerant inquiry. Literally ‘a mass of doubt.’ The Chan record makes doubt materially mass-like: a discourse says that inside and outside ‘roll into one mass of doubt’ (滾作一箇疑團), and other records speak of making the whole body, sitting, walking, dressing, eating, and even the encountered world into that mass. The same physical grammar governs its end: it is ‘broken through’ (打破疑團), or remains ‘unbroken’ (疑團不破). In an autobiographical public account, repeated blows make the speaker's mass of doubt more acute (疑團愈切). Thus the phrase is not merely ordinary uncertainty; these later Chan records deploy it as the consolidated, bodily condition named around sustained investigation and its reported breaking. The corpus does not make the mass a separate object from the doubt or state a further gloss for the breaking.

The Zen deviation is institutional and textual: ‘subjective understanding’ (情解) is a recurrent negative label in public-case commentary for understandings generated around quoted sayings. (參禪) is the recorded activity of investigating Chan, which the corpus binds to the one great matter of life and death. Gaofeng Yuanmiao states its temper: (參禪須是鐵漢) — to investigate Chan one must be an iron man — (著手心頭便判) (the moment you set to it the mind is decided). Literally, one knows (自知) cold and warmth (冷暖) for oneself, usually in the comparison “like a person drinking water, knowing hot and cold for himself” (如人飲水冷暖自知). Huiming uses it after Huineng's instruction to report that he now has an entry; Huangbo joins it to conduct in each movement, dwelling, and instant; and other teachers pair it with looking for oneself rather than seeking from another. The phrase also becomes an object of interrogation: Longmen Foyan grants that hot and cold can be known, then asks what the one who knows for himself is. Daodu pairs “knowing hot and cold for oneself” with “handling slow and urgent matters for oneself” and says the matter cannot be spoken out even when both parties exert themselves. The Chan bend is this sensory commonplace's use as a first-person report, an answer about the Way, and a question about the knower; the texts preserve the water comparison and these recorded deployments.

Literally, "the clay ox enters the sea." In the Chan record this impossible animal is repeatedly followed by an explicit report of lost trace or news: Lingyan Yuannri says, "the three-legged donkey leaps into the sky; the clay ox enters the sea without a trace" (三脚驢兒跳上天，泥牛入海無蹤跡), and another verse has "the clay ox enters the sea with no news; the wooden horse neighs into the wind and cannot be pursued back" (泥牛入海無消息，木馬嘶風趁不回). It also appears as an answer: when Baiyun Zhizuo is asked, "what is the eye inside a skull? | 泥牛入海). Later records call this a public case (泥牛入海公案, "the public case of the clay ox entering the sea") and pair it productively with the wooden horse. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore not ordinary husbandry: it is a stock spoken and versified image whose own recurrent predicates are "without trace," "without news," and "unseen."

Literally, 'release' or 'let pass': to permit free movement rather than hold fast. The allowlisted record has 1,034 occurrences in 224 texts. Its recurrent formal counterpart is 'hold fast' (把定) or 'hold in place' (把住): one address says, 'holding fast: dripping water freezes and the rivers stop; releasing: the sun is warm, the wind mild, and the mountains and streams compete in beauty' (把定也，滴水滴凍，江河絕流；放行也，日暖風和，山川競秀), then asks which is good. Other records pair 'release' with 'draw back in' (收來) and use the compact binome 'drawing in and releasing' (收放). The term occurs as a finite verb, in the question 'what is a saying of release?

Literally “inside the room” or “in the chamber.” In Chan records the recurrent institutional chamber is a place of direct examination: masters “question a monk in the chamber” (室中問僧), present an old saying there, or arrange an object and test each person who enters. One biography says a head monk was assigned to share the chamber seat and “grasp the bamboo switch to test students” (令分座室中，握竹篦以驗學者); another records the no-buddha-nature saying being presented repeatedly in the chamber, followed by a strike when the student began to speak. Recorded-sayings collections can therefore label a section “chamber encounters” (室中機緣). The word names the location and institutional setting, not the student's entrance: “enter the chamber for an interview” (入室) names the entrance, whereas “in the chamber” (室中) names the setting. Nor does the setting itself certify approval or succession. | Object sense confirmed by pickup, transfer, attempted receipt, grasping, color, and instrumental “drive out” syntax (趁). One phrase, clause, line, or saying counted as a unit of speech. Chan records weight this ordinary unit through where it stands and what is done with it, without making every phrase mean the same thing. Linji is asked for “the first phrase” and separately says that a single phrase must contain three mysterious gates, each with three essentials, authority, and function. Later records repeat that a single phrase plainly encompasses the myriad forms. Blue Cliff commentary says that penetrating one phrase penetrates a thousand and ten thousand phrases at once and quotes a line in which one phrase clearly understood surpasses a hundred billion. A verse contrasts three thousand recited scripture sections with “one phrase of Caoxi,” while Layman Pang says that even one phrase is unnecessary in an exchange. Other recurrent positions and qualifications include a silent phrase posed as a question, an “out-of-pattern phrase” demanded after a pause, and a ceremonial house phrase that the speaker asks how to voice. The diminutive “one phrase” (一句子) can be something a master says he has never told anyone. The cited warning “one conforming phrase is a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas” appraises a kind of phrase without defining every instance of the headword that way. The Zen bend is therefore the phrase's deployment as the smallest publicly tested or house-qualified unit that can be raised, withheld, penetrated, ranked, capped, or challenged. First, second, third, final, upward, out-of-pattern, and conforming positions belong to the same countable speech unit unless a longer fixed term has its own entry. | Allowlist count: 15,708 occurrences in 419 texts. Across the Chan corpus the word overwhelmingly marks tested competence—an adept, a real hand, or someone accomplished in the role named beside it. It modifies an adept master (作家宗師), an adept battle-general (作家戰將), and an adept Chan guest (作家禪客); an adepts' meeting (作家相見) names a meeting of people credited with that competence, while the doubled exclamation 'a real hand! | One corpus-wide expert/adept sense is retained after the item-8 family test. Literally (無) (no) + (事) (matter / affair / business): having no matter on hand, nothing that needs doing. Linji Yixuan gives it its sharpest form: (無事是貴人) — the person with nothing to do is the noble person — immediately glossed (但莫造作)，(秖是平常) ('just don't fabricate; only be ordinary'). Linji applies (無事人) even to Buddhas and patriarchs: (佛與祖師是無事人) (Buddhas and patriarchs are people with nothing to do), and glosses it (秖是平常著衣)、(喫飯)、(無事過時) (just ordinarily wearing clothes, eating, passing the time with nothing to do). Huangbo Xiyun, Linji's teacher, states it from the other side: when feelings are exhausted with nothing left to rely on or grasp, that is the (無事人) (情盡都無依執。 | (自然虛而靈寂而妙) ('Deshan said: just have no matter in the mind and no mind in matters, and of itself it is empty and numinous, still and wondrous', B25n0145); the chiasmus (無事於心)，(無心於事) ('no matter in the mind, no mind in matters') recurs across 13 texts. The records also deploy the word inside postures they attack: (無事甲) (the nothing-to-do shell, 163 hits in 92 allowlist texts — 坐在無事甲裏 'sitting inside the nothing-to-do shell', 打在無事甲裏 'knocked into the nothing-to-do shell', 置之無事甲中 'put away in the nothing-to-do shell'; Zhongfeng B25n0145, seven hits in Dahui's record T47n1998A), (無事會) (the nothing-to-do understanding, 46/31) — (切不得作無事會去) ('above all do not take it as the nothing-to-do understanding', J26nB186), (若作平常無事會)，(辜負山僧不少) ('if you take it as an ordinary nothing-to-do understanding, you fail this mountain monk badly', J33nB280), (學者不可作無事會)，(若作無事會)，(則著無事魔) ('a student must not take it as the nothing-to-do understanding; take it so, and the nothing-to-do demon takes hold', J25nB163) — and (無事界) (the nothing-to-do realm, 21/15): (未免墮在無事界裏) ('cannot help falling into the nothing-to-do realm', T47n1997). A (黔南會燈錄) verse separates saying from having: (口說無事易)，(心中無事難) (to say nothing-to-do is easy; nothing-to-do in the mind is hard; X85n1591).

A proper mountain name, "Sumeru" (須彌), attested 4,619 times in 373 allowlisted texts. The full "Mount Sumeru" (須彌山) occurs 1,052 times and the variant transliteration "Sumeru-lu" (須彌盧) 147. Chan records use the mountain's name in questions, comparisons, and statements of size or destruction. One Compendium saying places together "break Sumeru into fine dust" and "take the waters of the four great seas into one hair-pore" (破須彌為微塵，攝四大海水入一毛孔). A Continued Lamp address says, "if the lineage purport is raised, Sumeru must directly be shattered" (舉揚宗旨，須彌直須粉碎). A Dahui lamp witness says, "pick up Sumeru-lu in the palm and swing inside a needle's eye" (拈須彌盧於掌上，向針眼裡打鞦韆). Gulin Qingmao also supplies a local self-definition: "the so-called Mount Sumeru is precisely the move before living beings and buddhas were established" (所謂須彌山者，即是生佛未具已前一著子也). Public exchanges and addresses place a seamless stupa and an unstruck bell on Sumeru's summit, tie Sumeru with a lotus-root filament, and test the claim that a mustard seed contains it. These are the records' stated deployments; Gulin's equation does not replace the proper name throughout the corpus.

In the institutional compound 'the two ranks' or 'the two divisions' (兩序), rank or division (序) names one of the two sides of a Chan community's offices. The Baizhang Regulations labels its sixth chapter 'the chapter on the two divisions' (兩序章), then identifies 'head monks of the western division' (西序頭首) and 'officers of the eastern division' (東序知事). Recorded sayings use 'the two divisions' for the office-holders who request an ascent to the hall, receive thanks, or support the community. Baiyu's record says that the two divisions served mutually as arms and elbows and acted reciprocally as host and guest (兩序交為肘臂、互作主賓).

Zen-allowlist count: 672 hits in 176 texts. Deployment inventory includes blow-verdict, direct instruction, question, spatial reversal, and the compound 'the matter under your heels' (腳跟下事). To slip or misstep (蹉) while passing (過): 'to slip past' or 'to miss it.' The record uses it when someone fails to catch what is directly before him. One recurrent line says, 'by the time you raise an eyebrow, it has already slipped past' (眨上眉毛，早是蹉過). The stock answer 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過) occurs 158 times in 65 texts. Another passage warns not to miss it face-to-face and says that, if one does, one knows only affairs passing before the eyes (切不得當面蹉過；若蹉過，只知事逐眼前過). The near-synonym 'missed it' (錯過) occurs 863 times, including 134 instances of 'missed it face-to-face' (當面錯過). The headword itself occurs 1,340 times in 213 allowlist texts, and the completed form 'let it slip past' (蹉過了) occurs 117 times. In dialogue it can be paired with 'under your heel' (腳跟下), as when a question about why something is under the monk's heel receives the answer 'missed it face-to-face.' | One corpus-wide sense. The dominant collocation is 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過), a recurring answer and verdict; the near-synonym is 'missed it' (錯過).

The records use the same human-role noun individually, collectively, and possessively. Yuanwu calls raising one and understanding three “ordinary tea and rice for the household of patch-robed monks” (衲僧家尋常茶飯), and elsewhere calls activity that ferries beings “the patch-robed monk's own affair” (衲僧家本分事). Eye, gate, conduct, air, household, own portion, and handle compounds do not denote a second kind of monk. Compare monk (僧), master or preceptor (和尚), this old monk (老僧), the household of patch-robed monks (衲僧家), and patched robe (衲衣).

One ritual action is performed by many actors and placed at different points in an encounter. Actor, rank, and narrative consequence do not create different referents. Compare “thereupon struck” (便打), “thereupon applied the staff” (便棒), the hands-folded greeting (問訊), the parting salute (珍重), and the head-to-the-ground bow (頂禮). | The first graph means “then or thereupon” (便), and the second means “strike or hit” (打): “thereupon struck.” It is a stock action formula of encounter dialogue. The framed form “the master thereupon struck” (師便打) occurs more than four thousand times, while the bare form occurs 7,585 times across 360 allowlisted texts. The action is not the master's alone: a monk strikes back in an investigation exchange, another monk explicitly slaps the master with one palm, and an old monk narrates receiving a punch, immediately striking, and striking again when the other hesitates. The formula also appears with an explicit object, as a palm slap, and before the recipient is driven out of the monastery. It stands beside the parallel formulas “thereupon shouted” (便喝) and “thereupon applied the staff” (便棒), and records pair Deshan's staff with Linji's shout. The corpus attaches striking to named masters as a habit—Deshan is said to have loved chasing and beating monks who came to consult—and preserves direct remarks about a blow, including Mazu's “if I did not strike you, all quarters would laugh at me” (我若不打汝諸方笑我也). The action frequently follows a bow or a shout. The Chan deviation is its extraordinary density as public-interview punctuation and response, performed reciprocally by masters and monks. The texts narrate each act and consequence; this entry does not assign the blow an unstated pedagogical meaning. | A stock action-formula performed by many masters and monks across the corpus (師便打 4254× in 271 texts). Occurrences are left unattributed (MasterName null) unless a single master's formal address (示眾) frames one — none of the curated occurrences is such a frame; each is dialogue or a raised/narrated case, so MasterName is null throughout even where the acting (師) is identifiable (Linji, Deshan, Mazu). Cross-ref (便喝) · (便棒) · (棒) · (喝) · (禮拜) · (無位真人).

An emphatic warning governing an action or error: literally 'urgently avoid,' hence 'strictly avoid,' 'take care not to,' or 'beware of.' The object supplied by the record must be translated rather than replaced by a general spiritual warning. Daowu says, 'where knowledge does not reach, strictly avoid speaking of it' (智不到處，切忌道著); Daoqian answers a question about words that display the Way with 'strictly avoid choosing' (切忌揀擇); Tianyin tells the assembly 'strictly avoid conjecturing' (切忌卜度). Other high-seat warnings preserve concrete allusions: 'the sword has long gone; strictly avoid marking the boat' (劍去久矣，切忌刻舟), and 'if you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, beware being branded on the forehead' (不是龍門客，切忌遭點額). Its Chan deployment is a direct warning embedded in interviews and public addresses, not a commentator's private aside.

Literally, “one act” or “single conduct” (一行) plus “complete command” (三昧). In the Chan corpus Huineng's Platform Record supplies the governing definitions and the Zen-specific correction. It defines the term as “at all times, while walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, constantly carrying a straightforward mind” (於一切時中，行住坐臥，常行直心), and again as carrying a straightforward mind without attachment to anything (於一切法上，無有執著). The Record of the Patriarchal Hall gives the parallel: “in every place, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, all is one straightforward mind; this is the site of the way, this is the pure land” (於一切處行住坐臥，皆一直心，即是道場，即是淨土). The Platform Record then identifies and rejects a contrary deployment: people attached to the term say that sitting without moving and suppressing thoughts is “complete command in one act”; the text says that if so, this is the same as insentient things and an obstructing condition (同無情，却是障道因緣). This explicit correction is the entry's central Zen bend: the named “one act” is defined across all four postures and straightforward mind, not reduced to unmoving sitting. A preface to another Platform edition also defines it as “the single aspect of the realm of things” (法界一相) and says that although the many good acts differ, all are made correct in one act (萬善雖殊，皆正於一行).

Literally, 'not yet' or 'not there yet' (未在). Across the Chan corpus it is especially frequent as a master's verdict on a reply, shout, verse, or claimed understanding: Zhaozhou says, 'Not there yet; say more' (未在更道); another exchange records, 'You have got it, but you are still not there yet' (你也得只是未在); and an unnamed elder repeatedly waves a visitor away with, 'Not there yet, not there yet; go for now' (未在未在且去). The same words retain their ordinary temporal force in 'Even if you reached a thousand years, you still would not yet be old' (直至千歲也未在). Thus the corpus deploys one literal phrase both as an evaluative reply and in ordinary statements of something not yet reached or completed. | ' (何謂未在) was found. In the institutional compound 'the two ranks' or 'the two divisions' (兩序), rank or division (序) names one of the two sides of a Chan community's offices. Recorded sayings use 'the two divisions' for the office-holders who request an ascent to the hall, receive thanks, or support the community. Literally, "one-finger Chan." The phrase names Juzhi's recorded use of a raised finger in public interviews. A later record states the visible rule directly: "Whenever someone came, Master Juzhi only extended one finger; he called it one-finger Chan" (俱胝和尚逢人但伸一指頭，喚做一指頭禪). In the transmitted case, Tianlong raises one finger to Juzhi; afterward, whenever students ask, Juzhi raises one finger, and before dying he says, "I obtained Tianlong's one-finger Chan; through my whole life I could not use it up" (吾得天龍一指頭禪，一生用不盡). The record also preserves criticism rather than making the label an unquestioned formula: Xuansha says he would have broken the finger, Caoshan faults Juzhi's taking it up, and Sanshan asks, "What connection does one-finger Chan have? | It cheated that monk and buried him alive his whole life" (一指頭禪有甚交涉？

Literally, 'sit across and cut off.' The compound occurs 3,034 times in 339 allowed texts and takes concrete grammatical objects. Yuanwu answers a monk with 'sit across and cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven' (坐斷天下人舌頭), says that 'emerging and submerging are all sat across and cut off' (頭出頭沒悉皆坐斷), and records a monk's conclusion, 'then one sits across and cuts off the ten directions' (坐斷十方). Blue Cliff commentary says a master's half-phrase 'naturally sits across and cuts off the tongues of everyone under heaven' (自然坐斷天下人舌頭). The Ancestral Guidelines Collection says 'sit across and bar the critical crossing; do not let ordinary or holy pass' (坐斷要津，不通凡聖), and elsewhere, 'sit across and cut off the crown of Vairocana; do not receive Śākyamuni's text' (坐斷毗盧頂，不稟釋迦文). Other frequent objects include past and present, a thousand distinctions, the road's intersection, and the heads of buddhas. The verb is therefore transitive and spatially forceful in the corpus; it is not a term for seated quiet.

To turn or return (回) in reciprocal relation (互): mutual interchange. The corpus provides a compact self-gloss in the lines 'the objects at every gate interchange and do not interchange; turning, they further enter into one another; otherwise each remains in its position' (門門一切境，回互不回互，回而更相涉，不爾依位住). This wording permits both relation and distinct position rather than reducing the term to simple fusion. Caoshan says ordinary feelings and holy views must interchange (直須回互). In Caodong usage upright and crooked (正偏), light and dark (明暗), or guest and host (賓主) can mutually interchange; one later address expands the guest-host deployment as each containing the other and the two exchanging positions without a fixed rank.

A proper name, literally "Mighty-Sound King" (威音王), occurring 487 times in 171 allowlisted texts. The extended form "Mighty-Sound King Buddha" (威音王佛) occurs 80 times. Chan records most often place the name in temporal and spatial formulas: "before Mighty-Sound King" (威音王已前, 181 occurrences), "after Mighty-Sound King" (威音王已後, 33), and "the far side of Mighty-Sound King" (威音王那畔, 17). In the Nanquan-Huangbo exchange, Huangbo says he followed the Way "before Mighty-Sound King"; Nanquan answers, "you are still a descendant of old Master Wang" (猶是王老師兒孫在), using Nanquan's surname Wang in the reply. In the Yongjia record, Xuanze says, "before Mighty-Sound King, it is acceptable; after Mighty-Sound King, awakening by oneself without a teacher is entirely the way of outsiders" (威音王已前即得，威音王已後無師自悟，盡是天然外道). Xuedou records "awakening by oneself without a teacher before Mighty-Sound King" as "the second phrase" (是第二句). A late Sanfeng record supplies an explicit internal gloss: "Mighty-Sound King is outside form and sound, not yet set out in records, without evidence to examine—the highest matter before writing" (威音王者，形聲之外，未有出載，無所考據，文字以前最上事也). This entry reports the proper name and the corpus's formulas without adding another framework.

Literally, 'follow circumstances.' The expression occurs 1,829 times in 308 allowlisted texts. Its subject may be a person, conduct, an event, or a thing's functioning. One paired description is 'follow circumstances, free and unconfined; respond to things and act' (隨緣放曠，應物施為). A biography records the saying, 'In all affairs, follow circumstances; this is a way of ease.' A recurrent exchange asks, 'What is following circumstances as the site of the Way?

Literally, "at the gate or threshold of light and shadow." The phrase occurs 28 times in 22 allowlisted texts. The corpus supplies its architectural contrast directly: people have not recognized "the coarse, shallow business under the gate of light and shadow" and mistake it for "the matter inside the house" (光影門頭戶底麤淺底事，將作屋裏事). Elsewhere students are said to "recognize only the gate of light and shadow as themselves" (惟認光影門頭當作自己), and an address warns, "do not bury yourself at the gate of light and shadow" (切忌向光影門頭自埋沒). The phrase also enters verse as a place not to stop: "do not halt your steps at the gate of light and shadow" (光影門頭休駐足). Hongzhi supplies a notable counter-deployment: "a person who settles the matter at the gate of light and shadow will do" (光影門頭了事底漢即得), then immediately asks how one proceeds before guest and host divide and before an image is formed. Zen thus bends ordinary light, shadow, and doorway language into a recurring label for the visible or reflected threshold that records contrast with the inside of the house, oneself, and the not-yet-formed image.

The first graph names feelings, sentiments, or affective responses; the second names recognizing or discerning cognition. Together they name cognition operating through feeling and recognition. Yuanwu repeatedly pairs it with estimating and reckoning: he asks whether a passage can be estimated through affective cognition (以情識卜度得麼) and calls explanations offered in public addresses affective-cognitive reckoning (情識計較). Xuedou says that even recognizing the lineage at the words still remains dim beyond affective cognition (言下知宗，尚昧情識之表). Across these passages the term is a noun, the base for the verbs estimate, reckon, and distinguish, and the object of the verbs stick to and exhaust. It occurs 475 times in 136 allowlisted files.

A pair made from 'kill' (殺) and 'keep alive or give life' (活): killing and giving life. It appears with other paired Linji-house terms in the list 'killing and giving life, granting and taking, provisional and actual, illuminating and functioning' (殺活縱奪、權實照用). Literally, "not passable even by leaking water": sealed so tight that not even water passes. The phrase occurs 150 times in 76 allowlisted texts. In the records it regularly describes the impassability of the ancestral gate and places associated with Bodhidharma: "before Shaoshi Peak, not even water passes" (少室峰前，水泄不通) and "under the patriarch's gate, not even water passes" (祖師門下，水泄不通). Another makes it one of three eyes: one is watertight and ordinary and initiated cannot be distinguished; one opens the whole earth and the ten directions are unobstructed; one surveys high and low and all kinds look up. As 'wild-fox spirit' (野狐精), the word forms an abusive epithet for a person or view. Masters shout it at interlocutors, and Dahui warns against making a 'wild-fox-spirit interpretation' (野狐精見解). The referent is the person or understanding being denounced, not the animal body in the Baizhang narrative or the case as a textual object.

Literally, “guest-dust”: dust characterized as a visitor rather than the host. Much of the corpus preserves it in the inherited compound “guest-dust troubles” (客塵煩惱), something said to stain, cover, or be unrecognized. The distinct Chan deployment appears in Baizhang Huaihai's recorded classification: “one's own mind is buddha; illuminating function belongs to bodhisattva; mind after mind is the ruler; illuminating function belongs to guest-dust” (自心是佛，照用屬菩薩；心心是主宰，照用屬客塵). Here “guest-dust” is not merely a name for dirt or an outside visitor; Baizhang places it on the “illuminating function” side of a ruler/guest classification and immediately compares it to speaking of water by way of waves (如波說水). The Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings and the Expanded Lamp preserve this wording independently. Elsewhere the Records say a grown child learns explanations and does not know that these are “guest-dust troubles” (不知是客塵煩惱); Dahui speaks of the “stain of guest-dust troubles since beginningless time” (無始時來客塵煩惱之染); and the Admonitions for the Monastic Gate has the compact bodily compound “body-and-mind guest-dust” (身心客塵). The Zen record therefore keeps the inherited dust imagery but also bends it into Baizhang's explicit ruler/function classification.

Literally the body's or person-shaped term (身) formed with "teaching, standard, or law" (法): here, "teaching-body," attested 6,058 times in 376 allowlisted texts. This English target follows the Chan record's own comparisons rather than importing a glossary definition. Qianyan places three word explanations together: a robe displays the teaching and so is a "teaching-robe" (法衣); "a person can enlarge the Way, therefore it is called teaching-body" (人能宏道，故謂之法身); and being everywhere and clear is called the "teaching-eye" (法眼). Other records give deliberately different predicates. Weilin calls it "each person's originally present own nature" (當人本有之自性). Huanglong says, "the teaching-body has no form; responding to things, it manifests form" (法身無相，應物現形), then raises his whisk and calls that the teaching-body before laughing. A Five Lamps exchange answers the question with "a flower in the sky, a heat shimmer" (空華陽焰). The Ancestral Hall Collection answers it by repeating that "all activities are the teaching-body's function" (一切施為，盡是法身用).

Literally 'a true person of no rank' — (位) is rank/office/status (the graded positions of the bureaucracy, or of ranked stages). Linji coins it in his most famous (上堂): 「(赤肉團上有一無位真人)，(常從汝等諸人面門出入)」 — 'on your lump of red flesh there is one true person of no rank, forever going in and out through your face and sense-gates'; those who have not yet witnessed it, 'look! | 頂門上時時顯現，眼睛裏處處…」 — it shows itself on the crown of the head and in the pupils of the eyes). The opening line recurs verbatim across the record — (赤肉團上有一無位真人), 87 hits in 71 allowlist texts — and (如何是無位真人) becomes a standing test-question in its own right (141 hits in 96 texts): the (靈機禪師語錄) answers it "met face to face" (覿面相逢), and when the questioner counters "what is the true person WITH rank? | Exact unsplit count: 1,473 hits in 267 allowlisted texts; true person without rank (無位真人) accounts for 1,259 hits in 250 texts. Without rank/order (無位次) has 91 in 63; originally without rank/order (本無位次) 28 in 25. This Chan rank-language is separated from ordinary lack of institutional position below. Family checked against true person without rank (無位真人), rank/order (位次), with rank (有位), no dependence (無依), red flesh-lump (赤肉團), and rank/position (位).

To be complete, fully endowed, or lacking nothing. The headword occurs 2,264 times in 303 allowlisted texts. Xuansha says, “each person is fully endowed; each person is manifest” (人人具足，人人成現). Another address ranges across monastics and laypeople, women and men, wise and foolish, noble and low, saying all are fully endowed “without the least lacking” (悉皆具足，曾無欠少). Hongzhi pairs “fully endowed from the beginning” (本來具足) with “not a hair's breadth lacking, not a hair's breadth in excess.” A later text warns that merely accepting “fully endowed from the beginning, no need to seek outside” can become empty talk. In the ordination compound “full precepts” (具足戒), the same completeness word modifies the precepts: biographies record receiving or being given the full precepts. Predicate and attributive placement express the same completeness, not different lexical referents. | The former predicate/adjective targets were grammatical uses of the same completeness word and are merged. The Chan deployment includes both lack-nothing formulas and the corpus's criticism of resting on such formulas. The full-precepts compound remains under the precepts gate and should receive longest-match priority when indexed separately. Compare fully endowed from the beginning (本來具足), completely formed (圓成), lack (欠少), full precepts (具足戒), receiving precepts (受戒), and precept (戒).

Literally, 'that bank/side,' hence 'that side,' 'the other side,' or 'beyond.' The allowlisted record has 786 occurrences in 220 texts. The deictic contrast is explicit: questions set 'the matter on that side' (那畔事) against 'the matter on this side' (者邊事), and one exchange says that as soon as words are involved one falls on 'this side' (遮畔) before asking for news from 'that side' (那畔底消息). Its most frequent fixed expansion is 'beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔), which occurs in addresses and verses; other recurrent forms include 'the matter beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔事), 'a person beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔人), and 'a saying from beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔一句). Allowlist counts recorded in the audit: the headword “staff/blow” (棒), 18,109 hits in 415 texts; “one blow” (一棒), 2,954; “thirty blows” (三十棒), 2,766; “twenty blows” (二十棒), 407; “one bout of blows” (一頓棒), 63; “receive a blow” (喫棒), 1,191; and “painful blows” (痛棒), 752. The graphs picture gathering in and mooring. In its dominant Chan deployment, the verb describes trying to approach, fit oneself to, or get a purchase on a saying, encounter, or stated matter. Yuanwu says that once one sets the mind on making an approach, one has already gone astray (擬心湊泊已差池), asks how one could approach when looking neither before the eyes nor within a phrase (且道如何湊泊), and describes Yunmen as leaving no place for one to find an approach (無爾湊泊處). Tianru says that the earlier teachers had no fixed form by which one could approximate and approach them (前輩得之者亦無定法，所以準擬湊泊他不得). A transmission record likewise calls a master's encounters in his room steep and impossible to approach (室中機緣尤為嶮峻不可湊泊). The compound occurs 570 times in 184 allowlisted files; the recurring shapes include “no place to approach,” “unable to approach,” “how can one approach?

Primary person sense. Shide and Hanshan (拾得寒山 / 寒山拾得) and Fenggan (豐干) form the recurring figure family. The ordinary verb is split below because it denotes a different action, not a reading of the person.

The Caodong technical configuration of lord and minister. The term occurs 960 times in 217 allowlisted texts. Caoshan maps the lord to the upright position and the minister to the crooked, then names minister-facing-lord, lord-regarding-minister, and lord-and-minister-in-accord (君為正位。

To possess or be equipped with (具) the eye (眼): to have the eye, meaning to possess genuine discernment. The eye is what distinguishes true from false in the recorded case comments. Recurrent closing invitations include 'let one who possesses the eye discern' (具眼者辨看), 'let one who possesses the eye look and take it up' (具眼者看取), and 'let one who possesses the eye distinguish it' (具眼者辯取); the form 'one who possesses the eye' (具眼者) occurs 363 times in 162 texts. A person may be called 'a patch-robed monk who possesses the eye' (具眼衲僧, 77 occurrences in 54 texts) or 'an adept who possesses the eye' (具眼作家, 4). Related forms are 'possess one eye' (具一隻眼, 381), 'possess the true eye' (具正眼, 52), and 'one who possesses the eye' (具眼底, 70). The headword occurs 1,346 times in 280 allowlist texts.

A repeated descriptive expression for being bare, exposed, and without covering. The term occurs 368 times in 143 allowed texts. Its recurring parallel is 'cleanly naked' (淨裸裸); records expand it with 'without covering' (無蓋覆), 'nothing that can be grasped' (沒可把), and 'fully exposed' (全露). These textual predicates establish what the expression describes without turning it into a condition to seek. The records also qualify it. Yuanwu says that being cleanly naked, cut off from thought, bare, and with nothing to grasp has 'still not left this-side affairs' (猶未離這邊事在). Later collections likewise say that even when one is cleanly naked, bare, and has nothing to grasp, 'there is still something fine remaining' (尚有廉纖), and contrast the relative ease of being bare with the difficulty of being distinctly evident (明歷歷). The corpus has five occurrences of the adverbial extension 'in a bare and uncovered manner' (赤灑灑地).

Literally, "greatly penetrate and greatly awaken": great thorough awakening. The phrase occurs 48 times in 30 allowlisted texts. It names an event or resulting qualification in biographies, appraisals, and questions. One record says that people of great thorough awakening have finished the matter of inquiry and afterward stayed by water and woods until pushed forward to address others (古人大徹大悟，參學事畢，且於水邊林下). A public exchange tests the qualification directly: one master says there is nobody of great thorough awakening in the hall; another asks, "which one is not of great thorough awakening?

The direct Huineng definition, the Fayan public case, Shenhui's reply, and later comments are retained as distinct witnesses. 'Without a place to dwell' (無所住) occurs 370 times in 145 texts; 'not-dwelling as the root' (無住為本) occurs 44 times in 27; 'root of not-dwelling' (無住本) occurs 135 times in 64; and 'not-dwelling mind' (無住心) occurs 38 times in 30. Biographical occurrences where these two graphs form the name Wuzhu were excluded from semantic evidence.

Literally, "the clay ox enters the sea." In the Chan record this impossible animal is repeatedly followed by an explicit report of lost trace or news: Lingyan Yuannri says, "the three-legged donkey leaps into the sky; the clay ox enters the sea without a trace" (三脚驢兒跳上天，泥牛入海無蹤跡), and another verse has "the clay ox enters the sea with no news; the wooden horse neighs into the wind and cannot be pursued back" (泥牛入海無消息，木馬嘶風趁不回). It also appears as an answer: when Baiyun Zhizuo is asked, "what is the eye inside a skull?

The paired roles of guest and host in a face-to-face meeting. The stock verdict 'guest and host stand out distinctly' (賓主歷然) states that the roles are distinct. Fixed forms carry the same pair across the records: Linji's 'guest-host phrase' (賓主句), 'one shout distinguishes guest and host' (一喝分賓主), and Zhaozhou's 'no-guest-no-host story' (無賓主話). Caodong records deploy the pair positionally in 'guest and host exchange places' (賓主互換), pair it with bent and upright (偏正), and expand it into host-within-guest, guest-within-host, host-within-host, and guest-within-guest. Linji's named 'four guest-and-host' (四賓主) is a taxonomy built from this same pair; the added graph 'four' names that lexical object, which has its own entry. It does not give the base pair a second referent.

A fixed compound pairing (棒), the stick/blow associated with Deshan Xuanjian (德山棒), and (喝), the shout associated with Linji Yixuan (臨濟喝) — (德山棒)、(臨濟喝). In the records: 'as soon as a monk enters the gate, Deshan hits, Linji shouts' (德山入門便棒／臨濟入門便喝); after Linji 'came forth, he taught only with stick and shout' (唯以棒喝示徒). The stock phrase is (棒喝交馳) ('blows and shouts flying back and forth'), glossed (令你捫摸不入)、(插足不得) ('leaving you no finger-hold and no foot-hold'). The records also turn the term against its own use: 'call it "stick-and-shout" and you drop into hell like an arrow' (喚作棒喝，入地獄如箭); warnings against 'blind stick and wild shout' and against 'coarse fellows who talk up Linji and do nothing but stick-and-shout' (專事棒喝). A late verse headed (勉謬行棒喝者) ('exhortation to those who wrongly go about with stick-and-shout') states each component's job in so many words — (棒須劈破有無見)，(喝要澄空迷悟情) ('the stick must split apart views of being and non-being; the shout must clear out the passions of delusion and awakening') — and ends by naming the practitioner: (棒頭喝下如親切)，(是則名為棒喝人) ('when at the stick's head and under the shout it is as if intimate, such a one is then named a stick-and-shout person', J39nB447). The corrective deployments continue: (為謬認棒喝者呵斥棒喝) ('for those who wrongly take stick-and-shout he rebukes stick-and-shout', J36nB359), and (至有纔著袈裟便行棒喝者)。

Counted forms: "originally unborn" (本無生), 326; "endurance concerning no arising" (無生法忍), 217; "unborn and unextinguished" (無生無滅), 92. Literally, “an iron hammer without a hole.” The phrase occurs 256 times in 108 allowlisted texts. The missing hole is the missing eye by which a hammer head takes its handle; the records repeatedly deploy the resulting solid object as an image of something with no entry point. It appears in similes—“water cannot wet it and wind cannot enter it, like a holeless iron hammer” (水灑不著，風吹不入，如箇無孔鐵鎚相似)—and as a direct answer to “What thing can heaven not cover and earth not support? | ” Later comments apply the same object-image to answers and exchanges, including “a holeless iron hammer driving in a wedge again” (無孔鐵鎚重下楔). These are uses of the object-image, distinct from passages that directly call people holeless iron hammers.

A doubled imperative: "rest" or "stop" (休去) and "cease" or "settle" (歇去): "rest; cease," attested 123 times in 68 allowlisted texts. Shishuang's recorded sequence expands it: "rest; cease; let one thought last ten thousand years; become cold ashes and a withered tree; become an incense burner in an old shrine; become one strip of white silk; become cold and still" (休去歇去、一念萬年去、寒灰枯木去、古廟香爐去、一條白練去、冷秋秋地去). Yunfeng supplies a contrary sequence beginning "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), and a later speaker refuses both lists. Dahui reports people sitting slack-jawed and calling that "resting and ceasing" (一向嘴盧都地打坐，謂之休去歇去), in an extended criticism. Zhongfeng likewise reports people citing "do not fantasize, put it down, old-shrine incense burner, rest and cease" as evidence, and compares that use to waiting by a stump for a rabbit. Other records retain the literal instruction: a teacher says, "from now on, rest; cease" (自今以往，休去歇去), while Dafang Yin asks, "why not rest and cease? | Counted companions: "one thought for ten thousand years" (一念萬年去), 115; "cold and still" (冷湫湫地去), 48; "old-shrine incense burner" (古廟香爐去), 72; "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), 5. Orthography varies between "cold autumn-like" and "cold and still" in witnesses. The sole late naming formula is excluded because its surrounding sentence applies the words to a different labeled expression, whereas the older imperatives and their recorded criticisms bear the headword directly. | Literally, "cold ashes" (寒灰). The term occurs 215 times in 112 allowlisted texts and can name actual ash that has gone cold: a sick-room verse places cold ash in a stove beside frost on a mat. Chan addresses use that same material image in several recorded formulas. It is commonly paired with "dead wood" (枯木). One discourse states, "one thought for ten thousand years, cold ashes and dead wood—these are all still, sunken dead water" (一念萬年，寒灰枯木，俱是靜沉死水). Earlier transmitted wording lists "go like cold ashes and dead wood" (寒灰枯木去) beside "rest and cease" and "one thought for ten thousand years." The records also say "cold ashes burst into flame" (寒灰發焰), and one seasonal discourse sets "yesterday, cold ashes covered the ground" against "today, spring news fills the whole sky" (昨日匝地寒灰，今朝普天春信). These are literal and image-bearing deployments of the same ash, not different lexical things. The entry reports the contrasts without deciding what the reversal signifies.

Literally the storehouse / treasury (藏) of the eye (眼) of the right teaching (正法) — in the record, the thing the lineage hands down. Its founding story is the World-Honored One on Vulture Peak holding up a flower before the silent assembly; only Mahakasyapa breaks into a smile, and the Buddha says (吾有正法眼藏)，(涅槃妙心)…(付囑摩訶迦葉) ('I have the treasury of the true eye of the teaching, the wondrous mind of nirvana... inherited_lead: Literally, a 'general invitation' or 'summons to all'; in the Chan corpus it is the organized call for the community's shared labor. The term occurs 1,567 times in 282 allowed texts. The monastic regulations define it directly: 'the rule of the general work summons is that upper and lower share the labor equally' (普請之法蓋上下均力也). The same section says that when work requires the assembly's combined strength, the administrators report it, inform the head monk and disciplinarian, and hang the general-summons placard (報眾掛普請牌); at the wooden-fish or drum signal, those not exempted go together to the work site. Literally, 'release' or 'let pass': to permit free movement rather than hold fast. The allowlisted record has 1,034 occurrences in 224 texts. Its recurrent formal counterpart is 'hold fast' (把定) or 'hold in place' (把住): one address says, 'holding fast: dripping water freezes and the rivers stop; releasing: the sun is warm, the wind mild, and the mountains and streams compete in beauty' (把定也，滴水滴凍，江河絕流；放行也，日暖風和，山川競秀), then asks which is good. Literally, "an idle or at-ease person of the Way" (閑道人). Chan usage bends ordinary idleness into a named epithet, most often in the full line "an at-ease person of the Way who has ended study and does nothing contrived" (絕學無為閑道人). Huangbo explains that people of old heard one statement and thereby "ended study" (絕學), and so received this name; he contrasts them with people seeking much knowledge and many explanations. Tianru explicitly lists "the great sea of extinction" (大寂滅海), "the ground of actual principle" (實際理地), and this full epithet as different names for "great rest" (大休). The Mirror Record distinguishes accumulating study, ending study, and then passing beyond both, saying that only on reaching the end of study does one first draw near the Way. Other records deploy the shortened term in verse: the whole world is full of people seeking buddha, but an at-ease person of the Way is hard to find (茫茫盡是覓佛漢，舉世難尋閑道人). The epithet therefore names a Chan roster type through explicit ending-study and great-rest definitions, not a generic loafer.

inherited_lead: 271 raw hits in 111 allowlist texts. The headword is corpus-wide as a quoted and extended Linji classification, not a master-specific sense. Cross-checked the complete four: the Diamond King's jeweled sword (金剛王寶劍), the crouching golden-haired lion (踞地金毛師子; also 踞地師子), probing pole and shadow grass (探竿影草), and a shout not functioning as a shout (一喝不作一喝用).

Family check: compared standalone “as before” (依前) with “ask as before” (依前問), “the words as before” (依前語), “recognize it and it still is not it” (認著依前還不是), and “still sees mountains” (依前見山). These are deployment shapes of the same adverb, not different things; no sense split is warranted.

The paired roles of guest and host in a face-to-face meeting. The stock verdict 'guest and host stand out distinctly' (賓主歷然) states that the roles are distinct. Fixed forms carry the same pair across the records: Linji's 'guest-host phrase' (賓主句), 'one shout distinguishes guest and host' (一喝分賓主), and Zhaozhou's 'no-guest-no-host story' (無賓主話). Caodong records deploy the pair positionally in 'guest and host exchange places' (賓主互換), pair it with bent and upright (偏正), and expand it into host-within-guest, guest-within-host, host-within-host, and guest-within-guest. Linji's named 'four guest-and-host' (四賓主) is a taxonomy built from this same pair; the added graph 'four' names that lexical object, which has its own entry. It does not give the base pair a second referent.

Literally, “like a person drinking water.” In the Chan record the phrase normally continues “knowing cold and warmth oneself” (冷暖自知 / 冷煖自知). Its Zen-specific deployment is as a stock comparison for knowledge that the person concerned reports from his own encounter rather than receives as another person's verbal description. In the Huineng and Huiming encounter, Huiming responds after Huineng's question about his face before his parents were born: “like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself” (如人飲水冷暖自知). Dahui says that at this point it is like drinking water and knowing its temperature oneself, and adds, “unless one has personally verified and personally understood, one can then see it” (除非親證親悟，方可見得). The Record of the Mirror of the School frames a question with “understanding the way and clarifying the school are like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself—how can their manner be spoken?
One corpus-wide sense. The record itself contrasts the arrangements at the gate and courtyard (門庭施設) with the inner hall (堂奧) and the upward road (向上一路).

The heron forms (鷺鶿 and 鷺鷥) are graphic variants within one physical-action family. The direct answer and the verse comparison are different deployments of the same bird-and-snow scene, not further senses.

Literally ‘divine or forecast’ (卜) + ‘measure or estimate’ (度): to calculate and guess, or speculative reckoning. The compound has 702 occurrences in 206 allowlisted texts. Its recurrent coordinations identify its deployment without supplying a separate theory: ‘thinking and conjectural calculation’ (思量卜度) occurs 25 times in 18 texts; ‘reckoning by affective cognition’ (情識卜度) 10 times in 6; ‘reckoning under the root of thought’ (意根下卜度) 47 times in 33; and ‘weighing and conjectural calculation’ (摶量卜度) 7 times in 3. Dahui's record says, in a list, ‘do not reckon under the root of thought; do not give a phrase; do not remain silent for a long time’ (不得向意根下卜度，不得下語，不得良久). His memorial inscription says, ‘Chan, Chan: do not use thinking and conjectural calculation; it does not concern written words and speech’ (禪禪不用思量卜度，非干文字語言). The Blue Cliff Record asks whether the cited matter can be reckoned by affective cognition (以情識卜度得麼), while a Wudeng huiyuan master says not to conjecture inside cognition, adding that this becomes inverted imagining (莫向意識裏卜度，却成妄想顛倒). Another master answers an appraisal with ‘if you conjecture, you lose body and life’ (卜度則喪身失命). Across these uses the word names the act of reaching a guess by mental estimation; the quoted records themselves state their objections to it.

Zen-allowlist count: 563 hits in 216 texts. Family check covered standing in the snow (立雪), Shenguang or Huike (神光／慧可), pacifying the mind (安心), seeking the Way or teaching (求道／求法), nine years facing the wall (面壁九年), and the Second Patriarch (二祖). All refer back to the same bodily act; narrative, epithet, and later question are not different things. Names remain contextual because Huike is a lineage patriarch and belongs on the master roster, not as a separate dictionary figure.

Literally "one" (一) "move, placement, or stroke" (著): "one move," attested 3,121 times in 351 allowlisted texts. The game-like noun appears in recurring Chan compounds: "let one move pass" (放過一著, 617 occurrences), "the final move" (末後一著, 104), "the upward move" (向上一著, 279), "one move ahead" (先一著, 38), and the suffixed "one move" (一著子, 601). A case-comment collection appraises an earlier response as "precisely letting one move pass," then adds "danger" (正是放過一著；險). A lamp address pairs "Linji's vanguard—let one move pass" with "Deshan's later command—set it aside" (臨濟先鋒，放過一著；德山後令，且在一邊). Questions ask, "before living beings and buddhas arose, where did one move fall? | ' (說甚麼向上事). The corpus also attaches 'upward' to named limits: 'the matter upward from buddha' (佛向上事, 149 occurrences) and 'upward from Vairocana' (毘盧向上). It is paired with 'the last word' (末後句) in the statement that one must also know the upward matter and the last word (更須知有向上事末後句始得). Related forms include 'the upward road' (向上一路, 957), 'the upward move' (向上一著, 279), 'the upward aperture' (向上一竅, 270), 'the upward pivot' (向上關捩子, 101), 'the upward person' (向上人, 229), and 'the upward vehicle of the lineage' (向上宗乘, 462). | Wave-plan frequency: 401. Searches covered paired contrast, direct/single formula, word-'no' instruction, sword formula, phrase/move compounds, and public interview. Family check with raise (提起), raise singly (單單提起), the first phrase (第一句), the upward move (向上一著), no (無), and the command (正令) supports one productive verb rather than a fixed category.

Yongjia's Verse on Stopping (奢摩他頌) defines alert as not producing the signs of dull abiding or blank indeterminacy (惺惺謂不生昏住無記等相), and ranks alert-and-still as right, blank-and-still as wrong, still-and-alert as right, and scattered-and-alert as wrong (惺惺寂寂是，無記寂寂非，寂寂惺惺是，亂想惺惺非). Ruiyan's self-calling is reported as dismissed by all quarters as 'playing with spirit-ghosts' (諸方謂其弄精魂); one master reverses the case by saying that the master called Ruiyan, rather than Ruiyan calling the master. inherited_lead: Allowlist count at the depth audit: 35,032 hits in 411 texts. The former entry's two senses—‘a shout’ and ‘to shout/cry out’—were merged because they paraphrased the same vocal event; noun and verb syntax alone did not establish different things. Targeted tests found no allowlisted drinking sense in “drink tea” (喝茶), “drink wine” (喝酒), or “drink water” (喝水). “Cheer” (喝采) and “shout abuse” (喝罵) are separately lexicalized compounds, while “clear the road by shouting” (喝道) supplies the ordinary calling-out baseline. Twelve witnesses preserve definition, master and monk use, simultaneous use, later systematization, explicit appraisal, warning against blind/random shouting, bodily effect, teaching-seat closure, house-device pairing, and ordinary road-clearing use without padding duplicate shouts.

The Zen deviation is institutional and textual: ‘subjective understanding’ (情解) is a recurrent negative label in public-case commentary for understandings generated around quoted sayings. Cross-checking ‘intellectual understanding’ (知解), ‘discriminating feelings’ (識情), and ‘knowledge and views’ (知見) supports this narrower deployment. Apparent nominal and verbal surroundings do not make the headword itself different things.

Eye (目) plus in front or before (前): before the eyes, or what is right in front of someone. The headword occurs 3,984 times in 360 allowlist texts. Its best-known deployment is Jiashan Shanhui's formula: 'before your eyes there is no thing; the meaning is right before your eyes; it is not the thing before your eyes, not what eye and ear reach' (目前無法，意在目前；不是目前法，非耳目之所到). Lamp records place the statement in Jiashan's section, while later compilations raise it with the heading 'Jiashan addressed the assembly, saying' (夾山示眾云). Its clauses recur widely: 'before your eyes there is no thing' (目前無法), 262 occurrences in 120 texts; 'it is not the thing before your eyes' (不是目前法), 222 in 112; and 'not what eye and ear reach' (非耳目之所到), 181 in 95. Other forms point to this location: 'only right before you' (只在目前), 166; 'the Great Way is only right before you, yet what is before you is hard to see' (大道只在目前，要且目前難覩); and 'clearly right before you' (分明在目前), 115. The location can also be emptied in the line 'before your eyes there is no monk-you; here there is no old teacher' (目前無闍黎，此間無老僧), whose first clause occurs 78 times. The word remains a plain locative throughout these deployments; it does not name a state in which to dwell. | One corpus-wide locative sense: 'before the eyes' or 'in front of you.' Jiashan Shanhui (夾山善會) does not give the word a private meaning; he uses its ordinary locative force in the frequently cited formula 'before your eyes there is no thing' (目前無法). The formula receives Jiashan's MasterName only where the text's own heading places it in his record; raised versions remain null.

The named cast iron-ox landmark of Shaanfu. The full headword occurs 1,583 times in 263 allowlisted texts, and the Shaanfu form is repeatedly used as a public answer and animated stage object. One master answers a question about turning around by saying to water the Shaanfu iron ox (陝府灌鐵牛); another address makes it enter western Shu (陝府鐵牛入西蜀). The impossible actions remain predicated of the same named landmark, so watering, traveling, or swallowing do not create separate senses.

The headword occurs 868 times in 243 allowlisted texts. The former physical/figurative targets name the same load-bearing action and are merged. Explicit firewood is rare; responsibility and lineage language dominate. Attested formations include “one who shoulders” (擔荷者), “shoulder successfully” (擔荷得), “shoulder with the whole body” (全身擔荷), “shoulder on one shoulder” (一肩擔荷), “accept and shoulder” (承當擔荷), and “unable to shoulder” (擔荷不起). The reversed form “carry a load” (荷擔) belongs to the family but does not create another referent.

Literally, “turn and look / look at.” The verb retains that visual sense, including an emperor's complaint that a master does not look at him and a monk's looking east and west for an absent teacher. Chan records also make it a recurrent teaching-seat stage direction. At an opening of the hall a master “looked around at the assembly” (顧視大眾) before speaking; elsewhere the look is followed by a shout and questions concerning host and guest. In one encounter the master merely looks, the student comments on the look, and the exchange ends. Some records compress speech and action still further: “then he looked around at the assembly and said, ‘stop! | ’” (乃顧視大眾曰休), or record looking left and right, striking the staff, and leaving the seat (顧視左右，卓拄杖，下座). Thus an ordinary look is bent into an observable public-address action of the teaching seat; the entry does not assign the look an unspoken symbolic message.

Literally, 'raise or present in full.' The expression occurs 1,834 times in 308 allowlisted texts. Chan records contrast it with a half-presentation: one discourse says that seeing no single form is only 'half presented' (半提) and that one must still know a time of full presentation. It regularly modifies a saying or command. Records ask how to speak 'one saying fully presented' (一句全提), pair it with 'the ancestral master's true command' (祖師正令), and call the flower at Vulture Peak and the snow at Shaoshi the separate transmission personally shown and the true command fully presented. Thus the Chan deployment is not merely completeness in the abstract: it is an utterance, command, or teaching-seat presentation brought forward without remainder. The texts also use the fixed compounds 'the true command fully presented' (全提正令) and 'a single saying fully presented' (一句全提).

Zen-allowlist count: 809 hits in 242 texts. Family check covered the elephant king's stride (象王行), backward look or turn (象王回顧／回旋), the lion's roar or vigorous motion (師子吼／奮迅), the fragrant elephant (香象), and Samantabhadra's (普賢) white elephant. The primary Chan image and the Buddhist narrative animal share the same royal-elephant referent, so differing deployments were not split into readings. The narrative white-elephant witness remains listed in SourceTexts but was not curated because it adds outside-story identity rather than defining the Chan bend.

Literally, "the clay ox enters the sea." It also appears as an answer: when Baiyun Zhizuo is asked, "what is the eye inside a skull?
