The corpus does not reduce the word to one theoretical proposition. It asks about the teaching-body, its "function" (法身用), its "side" (法身邊), and "the matter beyond the teaching-body" (法身向上事). The Old Venerables Record even says the teaching-body has "two kinds of illness" (法身兩般病): reaching it while attachment to the standard remains, with one's own view still present and sitting at its side, is the first. Frequent forms include "pure teaching-body" (清淨法身, 487 occurrences), "the teaching-body has no form" (法身無相, 141), "the teaching-body speaks" (法身說法, 27), "the teaching-body's side" (法身邊事, 202), "master of the teaching-body" (法身主, 132), and "the teaching-body's function" (法身用, 23).

Literally “stubborn” or “insensible emptiness.” In Chan records the phrase is predominantly a rejected identification, not a praised condition. Caoshan's house verse commands, “students must first recognize their own house; do not mix the true boundary with stubborn emptiness” (學者先須識自宗，莫將真際雜頑空). Hongzhi likewise warns, “do not recognize stubborn emptiness as oneself” (莫認頑空便為自己). A staff discourse makes the deployment concrete: the ordinary person calls the staff a staff, while the listener who “recognizes a stubborn emptiness” denies that there is a staff (認得箇頑空，撥無拄杖). A later address describes keeping stubborn emptiness at an idle corner, “entirely without openings,” and clinging to being a wooden puppet or a wall (力守頑空，全無孔竅，執為木偶…執為墻壁). A verse draws its own contrast: “do not dwell in stubborn emptiness; do not hide in dead water; directly you must be lively and splashing, like the sun shining at midday” (莫向頑空住，休於死水藏，直須活鱍鱍，如日照當陽). The recurring verbs are recognize, mix with, fall into, cling to, dwell in, and mistake for oneself; the recurrent contrasts are the true boundary, liveliness, things that appear, and the staff that is denied.

inherited_lead: Later commentary preserves a factual and evaluative dispute. The Book of Serenity reports that one critic reproached Nanquan's group for "killing living beings and creating guilt" (殺生造罪), while a defender cited an old text in which Nanquan made only a simulated cutting gesture (以手作虛斫勢). The commentary then evaluates the two critics; this entry records the controversy without choosing between the transmitted narratives or assigning an unstated intention. The traditional spelling of “cat” (貓兒) is a separate searchable entry with the same sense.

A repeated descriptive expression for being bare, exposed, and without covering. The term occurs 368 times in 143 allowed texts. Its recurring parallel is 'cleanly naked' (淨裸裸); records expand it with 'without covering' (無蓋覆), 'nothing that can be grasped' (沒可把), and 'fully exposed' (全露). These textual predicates establish what the expression describes without turning it into a condition to seek. The records also qualify it. Yuanwu says that being cleanly naked, cut off from thought, bare, and with nothing to grasp has 'still not left this-side affairs' (猶未離這邊事在). Later collections likewise say that even when one is cleanly naked, bare, and has nothing to grasp, 'there is still something fine remaining' (尚有廉纖), and contrast the relative ease of being bare with the difficulty of being distinctly evident (明歷歷). The corpus has five occurrences of the adverbial extension 'in a bare and uncovered manner' (赤灑灑地).

Literally, “depend on grass and attach to trees.” Across 128 occurrences in 71 allowlisted texts, Chan masters use the phrase chiefly in the fixed labels “spirits that cling to grass and trees” (依草附木精靈) and “people who cling to grass and trees” (依草附木漢). Its targets are explicit and varied: making a livelihood on circumstances and objects or seeking clever explanations in principle and nature (機境上作活計，理性中求妙解), understanding under a “dead phrase” (死句), and even the stock teaching-seat actions of striking the bench, raising the whisk, blinking, and raising the eyebrows. The phrase therefore shifts from literal plant-dependence to a recurring Chan rebuke for speech, gestures, or understanding that depends on something named in the passage. The record itself supplies “spirit,” “person,” and the criticized dependencies; this entry adds no supernatural account. | The construction modifies both “spirit” (精靈) and “person” (漢). Those are different bearers of the same predicate, not different senses of the headword. No plain botanical referent was established in the sampled Zen deployments.

Exact count: 129 hits in 79 allowlisted texts. The goose-king-selects-milk formula (鵝王擇乳) has 69 hits in 48 texts; not-of-the-duck-kind (素非鴨類) has 55 in 36. One legendary-bird sense. Family checked against selecting milk (擇乳), water and milk (水乳), duck kind (鴨類), choosing the teaching (擇法), and possessing the eye (具眼).

Literally and throughout the sampled corpus, “wherever” or “in every place.” Its Chan value lies chiefly in the predicates whose scope it sets. Linji's record has the fixed line “act as host wherever you are; every place you stand is genuine” (隨處作主，立處皆真). Yuanwu preserves the paired formula “act as host wherever you are; on meeting conditions, they are the source” (隨處作主，遇緣即宗). A teaching-seat address defines the work of a lineage teacher with “wherever he is, he raises the guiding principle; he answers questions according to the occasion” (隨處提綱，應機問答). Other records use the same distributive word in “named wherever [it appears]” (隨處立名), “arise right here and perish wherever” (當處出生，隨處滅盡), and “clear wherever [you are]” (隨處明了). These predicates are distinct; the location word is not. No departure from its ordinary distributive meaning was found, and none is manufactured. | Literally, 'wherever the place, act as host.' The expression occurs 136 times in 85 allowed texts. Linji's record gives its best-known continuation twice: 'act as host wherever you are; every place you stand is genuine' (隨處作主，立處皆真). The first occurrence continues, 'circumstances come and cannot turn you around' (境來回換不得); the second says that whatever comes is not to be received. Later records most often pair the phrase with 'on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source' (遇緣即宗). Yuanwu records variants including 'act as host wherever you are; on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source' (隨處作主，遇緣即宗) and 'act as host wherever you are; on meeting circumstances, immediately act' (隨處作主，遇緣即行). A later collection reverses the order—'the teaching has no fixed form: on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source; the Way does not travel in vain: act as host wherever you are' (法無定相，遇緣即宗；道不虗行，隨處作主)—and another places the phrase beside 'establish the source and set up the purport' (建宗立旨). The records deploy it as a direct imperative, a quoted Linji saying, and a predicate within assembly addresses.

An imagined iron ox used as a comparison, mechanism, or stock figure. Funiu compares his position at Shitou to a mosquito on an iron ox; another saying adds that there is nowhere to put its mouth. Answers to 'What is a clay buddha not crossing water? | The stock clay/gold/wood/true-buddha set is attributed to Zhaozhou in multiple later records. Literally, ‘mutually deceive.’ The phrase occurs 178 times in 97 allowlisted texts. Its most stable teaching formula is ‘only provide the assenting heart, and we certainly will not deceive one another’ (但辦肯心，決不相賺), with graphic variants for ‘provide’ (辦 and 辨) and both ‘certainly’ (決) and ‘necessarily’ (必). Masters use it as an assurance to an audience: ‘trust my words; we certainly will not deceive one another’ and ‘I assure you of this matter; in the end it is not false.’ Elsewhere the same literal verb can state that two sides do deceive each other. The reciprocal participants are supplied by context; these are not different things or separate senses. | Zen bends an ordinary verb of mutual deception into a repeated teaching-seat assurance tied to ‘the assenting heart’ (肯心). The negative formula dominates but does not change the verb’s referent. Family review with ‘conceal from one another’ (相瞞) and ‘deceive’ (誑欺) supports one sense.

Literally, “plant and steady the heels”; in its primary Chan deployment, “establish firm footing.” The phrase occurs 24 times in 18 allowlisted texts, mainly in later instructions, verses, and public exchanges. One instruction says that in traveling on foot and dwelling in the world one must first “establish firm footing, not be stirred by the eight winds” (立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓). A verse places it as a rock amid vast waves; a public exchange receives the direct interjection, “establish firm footing well” (立定腳跟好). The corpus also corrects a rigid use of the phrase: one master says that always establishing firm footing can, upon close examination, be “a one-sided, withered understanding and a dull fellow who does not comprehend adaptation” (偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢). Zen therefore bends bodily footing into a recurrent instruction and appraisal for remaining steady, while preserving a recorded warning that immobility itself can be faulted.

The corpus does not reduce the word to one theoretical proposition. It asks about the teaching-body, its "function" (法身用), its "side" (法身邊), and "the matter beyond the teaching-body" (法身向上事). The Old Venerables Record even says the teaching-body has "two kinds of illness" (法身兩般病): reaching it while attachment to the standard remains, with one's own view still present and sitting at its side, is the first. Frequent forms include "pure teaching-body" (清淨法身, 487 occurrences), "the teaching-body has no form" (法身無相, 141), "the teaching-body speaks" (法身說法, 27), "the teaching-body's side" (法身邊事, 202), "master of the teaching-body" (法身主, 132), and "the teaching-body's function" (法身用, 23).

Literally, "when tiredness comes, then sleep" (困來即眠). Its stable partner is "when hungry, eat" (饑來喫飯), and a recorded exchange supplies the decisive Chan distinction. Asked whether he exerts effort in following the Way, the master says yes and names eating when hungry and sleeping when tired. When the questioner objects that everyone does the same, the master says they differ: while eating, others do not consent simply to eat but make a hundred demands; while sleeping, they do not consent simply to sleep but make a thousand calculations (睡時不肯睡，千般計校). An independent song places the pair after refusing delight in heaven or merit-making and before saying fools laugh while the wise understand. A later Chan mirror names the shortened pair "when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep" (飢來即食、困來即眠) among the predicates of an at-ease person of the Way (閒道人). The words remain ordinary bodily actions; the Chan bend lies in the direct question-and-answer contrast between the master's stated exertion and the same-looking conduct burdened by demands and calculation. | The exact phrase has 12 hits in 10 allowlisted texts. Several files transmit the same master-lawyer exchange; the separate song and later Chan mirror supply independent deployment shapes. Variant first halves are 'when hungry, eat a meal' (饑來喫飯) and 'when hungry, eat' (飢來即食).

Lingyin Wen reverses an expected opposition: in the place of dragging mud and carrying water, a thousand-fathom wall stands; in the place of the thousand-fathom wall, one carries water and drags mud (拖泥帶水處千仞壁立，千仞壁立處帶水拖泥). Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. Chan records cite “Zhuang Zhou dreamed of the butterfly; he is not me; the butterfly dreamed of Zhuang Zhou; I am not him” (莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠), recount that when his wife died he drummed on a basin and sang, and list learning connected with Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the Hundred Schools. The corpus also deploys his name in the recurring sword line “Zhuang Zhou’s sword killed three thousand guests; from then on the road to Peach Spring did not go through” (莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通). A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?

One ritual action is performed by many actors and placed at different points in an encounter. Actor, rank, and narrative consequence do not create different referents. Compare “thereupon struck” (便打), “thereupon applied the staff” (便棒), the hands-folded greeting (問訊), the parting salute (珍重), and the head-to-the-ground bow (頂禮).

A fixed compound pairing (棒), the stick/blow associated with Deshan Xuanjian (德山棒), and (喝), the shout associated with Linji Yixuan (臨濟喝) — (德山棒)、(臨濟喝). In the records: 'as soon as a monk enters the gate, Deshan hits, Linji shouts' (德山入門便棒／臨濟入門便喝); after Linji 'came forth, he taught only with stick and shout' (唯以棒喝示徒). The stock phrase is (棒喝交馳) ('blows and shouts flying back and forth'), glossed (令你捫摸不入)、(插足不得) ('leaving you no finger-hold and no foot-hold'). The records also turn the term against its own use: 'call it "stick-and-shout" and you drop into hell like an arrow' (喚作棒喝，入地獄如箭); warnings against 'blind stick and wild shout' and against 'coarse fellows who talk up Linji and do nothing but stick-and-shout' (專事棒喝). A late verse headed (勉謬行棒喝者) ('exhortation to those who wrongly go about with stick-and-shout') states each component's job in so many words — (棒須劈破有無見)，(喝要澄空迷悟情) ('the stick must split apart views of being and non-being; the shout must clear out the passions of delusion and awakening') — and ends by naming the practitioner: (棒頭喝下如親切)，(是則名為棒喝人) ('when at the stick's head and under the shout it is as if intimate, such a one is then named a stick-and-shout person', J39nB447). The corrective deployments continue: (為謬認棒喝者呵斥棒喝) ('for those who wrongly take stick-and-shout he rebukes stick-and-shout', J36nB359), and (至有纔著袈裟便行棒喝者)。 | One corpus-wide sense. The two-graph compound is used jointly across the corpus; the master-specific attributions belong to its components (棒) (Deshan) and (喝) (Linji), not to the compound itself — hence a single corpus-wide sense here rather than split master senses. Broad attestation (232 allowlist files, 992 occurrences by tag-stripped grep; an earlier figure of ~487 was the 德山棒 count, corrected here). Attested collocations (allowlist grep): (棒喝交馳) 185 hits in 110 texts; (一棒一喝) 112 in 61; (棒頭喝下) 55 in 36; (棒喝齊施) 33 in 19; (棒喝交加) 9 in 8. The named components: (德山棒) 490 hits in 173 texts, (臨濟喝) 442 in 155.

Literally "existing in oneself" or "being at one's own disposal" (自在): "free and at ease," "unconstrained," or adverbially "freely," attested 4,537 times in 388 allowlisted texts. A record closes an address with "everyone drink tea in the hall, free and at ease" (堂中喫茶，自由自在). Another says, "only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired" (卷舒自在，應用無虧). A later compilation uses the result phrase "obtain great freedom" (獲大自在), while Zhe'an Fan says "unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time" (一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患). Dahui says, "then one enters birth and death and obtains great freedom" (出生入死得大自在). Other records say one can be freely at ease at every time and place, pair freedom in birth and death with freedom in coming and going, and explicitly test whether freedom at death matches ordinary freedom amid encountered objects. The word thus appears as adjective, adverb, result noun, and reduplicated "free and at ease" (自由自在), without requiring a further religious abstraction. | Counted constructions: "free and at ease" (自由自在), 185; "free and unobstructed" (自在無礙), 50; "obtain great freedom" (得大自在), 258; "not at ease" (不自在), 134. The compound personal/title name "Contemplating Freely" (觀自在, 278) and personal names such as Yun Zizai are proper-name uses and are not merged into this adjectival sense.

Literally, “plant and steady the heels”; in its primary Chan deployment, “establish firm footing.” The phrase occurs 24 times in 18 allowlisted texts, mainly in later instructions, verses, and public exchanges. One instruction says that in traveling on foot and dwelling in the world one must first “establish firm footing, not be stirred by the eight winds” (立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓). A verse places it as a rock amid vast waves; a public exchange receives the direct interjection, “establish firm footing well” (立定腳跟好). The corpus also corrects a rigid use of the phrase: one master says that always establishing firm footing can, upon close examination, be “a one-sided, withered understanding and a dull fellow who does not comprehend adaptation” (偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢). Zen therefore bends bodily footing into a recurrent instruction and appraisal for remaining steady, while preserving a recorded warning that immobility itself can be faulted. | The same four graphs also describe a literal bodily stance. Wuyi Yuanlai compares possessing the eye of inquiry to a skilled archer who “plants his heels firmly, then takes up the bow and sets the arrow, and only then can hit the target” (立定腳跟，然後拈弓架箭，始能中的). Here the phrase names what the archer physically does before shooting, not a second reading of figurative steadiness.

The concrete institutional action: ascend the teaching hall or take its high seat. Linji’s record pairs the request that he “take the seat” (升座) with “the master ascended the hall” (師上堂). The resulting address is a different thing and belongs to the primary sense. | The paired “take the seat” construction (升座) is the clearest non-heading anchor for the physical action.

” (如何是衲僧), one teacher answers, “investigating, seeking, and visiting the Way” (參尋訪道). Another exchange asks for “the patch-robed monk's own affair” (衲僧分上事) and answers, “when you want to walk, walk; when you want to sit, sit” (要行即行，要坐即坐). The corpus also asks directly about “the patch-robed monk's eye” (衲僧眼) and “the patch-robed monk's place of conduct” (衲僧行履處). It speaks institutionally of what can be used “under the patch-robed monk's gate” (衲僧門下), and appraises an assembly as lacking anyone with “the air of a patch-robed monk” (衲僧氣息). The Chan deviation lies in this public standard: the robe-word names the person expected to answer within the encounter record, while the compounds test that person's eye, conduct, handle, own affair, and house. These are attested compound deployments, not claims about an inner state.

Literally the gate and courtyard (門庭) at the front of a house; in the records, the frontage and distinctive approach of a teaching house. It is used for establishing a house in the forms 'set up a gate and courtyard' (立門庭, 79 occurrences), 'each set up a gate and courtyard' (各立門庭, 20), and 'establish a gate and courtyard' (建立門庭, 25). The common compound 'arrangements at the gate and courtyard' (門庭施設) occurs 180 times in 92 texts. The texts themselves set these outer arrangements against the inner hall and the upward road: one passage says that this is still an affair at the edge of Shouchang's gate-and-courtyard arrangements and that the honored upward road is separately distinguished (此猶是壽昌門庭施設邊事，須知向上一路尊貴自別); another says that this is still a small wonder among the gate-and-courtyard arrangements and has no connection at all with a patch-robed monk's own share (此猶是門庭施設小不思議，衲僧分中了無交涉). A house's demanding style is described as 'high and steep at the gate and courtyard' (門庭高峻, 34 occurrences) or 'solitary and steep at the gate and courtyard' (門庭孤峻, 44). The headword occurs 1,462 times in 291 allowlist texts. | One corpus-wide sense. The record itself contrasts the arrangements at the gate and courtyard (門庭施設) with the inner hall (堂奧) and the upward road (向上一路).

Literally, 'raise or present in full.' The expression occurs 1,834 times in 308 allowlisted texts. Chan records contrast it with a half-presentation: one discourse says that seeing no single form is only 'half presented' (半提) and that one must still know a time of full presentation. It regularly modifies a saying or command. Records ask how to speak 'one saying fully presented' (一句全提), pair it with 'the ancestral master's true command' (祖師正令), and call the flower at Vulture Peak and the snow at Shaoshi the separate transmission personally shown and the true command fully presented. Thus the Chan deployment is not merely completeness in the abstract: it is an utterance, command, or teaching-seat presentation brought forward without remainder. The texts also use the fixed compounds 'the true command fully presented' (全提正令) and 'a single saying fully presented' (一句全提).

Literally, 'turn the light around and shine back': 'turn around' (迴), 'light' (光), 'return' (返), and 'shine or illuminate' (照). This written form occurs 50 times in 35 allowed texts; the common variant 'turn the light around and shine back' (回光返照) occurs 168 times in 88 texts, and the reversed order 'shine back and turn the light' (返照回光) occurs 16 times. The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp gives the literal instruction, 'turn the light around and shine back; look: what are body and mind?

Literally "empty" or "vacant" (虛) "space" (空): "empty space," also the open sky, attested 5,943 times in 279 allowlisted texts. Chan records use it as a location, comparison, and grammatical object. Productive forms include "in empty space" (虛空中, 90 occurrences), "inside empty space" (虛空裏, 136), and "like empty space" (如虛空, 364). They also record impossible or emphatic actions: "empty space shattered" (虛空粉碎, 167), "break empty space" (打破虛空, 85), and "empty space burst apart" (虛空迸裂). Zhongfeng says of an incense offering, "empty space cannot contain it; the great earth cannot support it" (虛空包不住，大地載不起). Zhe'an Fan says that if one understands at a stated point, "empty space can be measured" (虛空可量). A memorial narrative describes one who raised his head and suddenly forgot confusion and awakening, "lucid like empty space, impossible to approach or lodge in" (如虛空玲瓏不可湊泊). The corpus also says "empty space has no inside or outside" (虛空無內外, 9), while a formal address says that the Chan lineage's defining feature "fills empty space, with nowhere to evade it" (充塞虛空，無處回避). These are literal comparisons and recorded predicates; no single further sense is imposed on all 5,943 occurrences.

Literally, rolling or buoyant (騰騰) and letting the course of things run (任運): "rolling along, letting things run." The exact order occurs 79 times in 58 allowlisted texts; the reversed form "letting things run, rolling along" (任運騰騰) occurs 140 times in 94 texts. In the Anquan lyric transmitted by the Collection of the Patriarchal Hall, eating gruel in the morning and another meal at midday leads directly to, "today, letting things run, rolling along; tomorrow, rolling along, letting things run," followed by "inside, clearly knowing it all, only feigning foolishness and binding up dullness" (今日任運騰騰，明日騰騰任運，心中了了總知，只沒佯癡縛鈍). Yuanwu places it after "thoroughly ordinary" (徹底平常). Gaofeng twice repeats both orders together; one passage describes a person who has no household property to return to and nothing named Chan to study, life-and-death to escape, or extinction to certify, and who spends the whole day "rolling along, letting things run; letting things run, rolling along." Feiyin uses the doubled reversible formula for walking, standing, sitting, lying, dressing, and eating, and elsewhere pairs it with "free and easy" and "cleanly fallen away" (灑灑落落). Chan thus bends an ordinary adverbial expression into a rhythmic, reversible stock description attached to meals, ordinary activity, and appraisals of a person; the texts do not reduce it to a named procedure.

Another address turns the term against fixation: "when the mind dwells in the unborn, the unborn itself is birth and death," then raises the staff and says, "this is not the unborn" (心住，無生即生死；拈拄杖，云：這箇不是無生). In a raised case, being recognized earns banishment "into the country of the unborn," which is immediately rejected as dead water that holds no dragon. The record also joins the term to Chan action in "endurance of the unborn beneath the staff" (棒下無生忍). These constructions state or work directly on no birth or arising; the entry does not replace them with a broader framework.

The normal Chan use is a title for the person who teaches and presides over a monastic community. It follows a personal name in lineage headings, as in “Master Bodhidharma” (菩提達摩和尚), and opens biographies such as “Master Puhua of Zhenzhou, who ...” (鎮州普化和尚者). A student can state that he comes from Master An of Songshan, while lamp records quote an authority with “Master Wuzu Fayan said” (五祖演和尚曰). The title also marks institutional and public relations. The “master at the head of the hall” (堂頭和尚) is asked to address the assembled community; another monk asks the master to “speak the teaching for the assembly” (請和尚為眾說法). Direct address changes English capitalization and syntax but not the referent. Huike says, “I only beg you, Master, to show compassion” (惟願和尚慈悲); a monk asks the Cloth-Bag Monk, “Master, what are you doing here?

Literally ‘the lion's roar.’ In the Chan record it names forceful speech or teaching and is repeatedly opposed to the cry of a jackal. One record supplies an explicit definition: ‘teaching with something gained is the jackal's cry; teaching with nothing gained is called the lion's roar’ (說法有所得，斯則野干鳴；說法無所得，是名師子吼). The phrase is not merely an appraisal applied by compilers: masters order monks to ‘try making a lion's roar,’ monks claim it, and it becomes a public-interview challenge. Guishan says that Shishuang's speaking of Chan is ‘like a lion's roar, frightening the foxes, wolves, and jackals to death.’ In another exchange a monk asks what happens on meeting a lion's roar; the master answers ‘let the jackal cry as it likes,’ after which the monk shouts. Thus an animal sound is bent into a name, test, and verdict for speech in the teaching encounter; the texts themselves establish the lion/jackal contrast without requiring an imported symbolic reading.

Literally, holding up (拈) a flower (華) and faintly smiling (微笑): "holding up the flower and smiling." The exact traditional-flower form occurs 36 times in 26 allowlisted texts; the common-flower graph variant "holding up the flower and smiling" (拈花微笑) occurs 163 times in 102. In the Chan Buddha's defining lineage scene, the World-Honored One holds up a flower before the assembly at Vulture Peak; the multitude is at a loss, while Kashyapa breaks into a smile. The recorded Buddha then entrusts Kashyapa with "the treasury of the true teaching eye, the wondrous mind of extinction, the subtle gate of the real mark without a mark, not established in written words, transmitted separately outside teachings" (正法眼藏、涅槃玅心、實相無相微玅法門，不立文字，教外別傳). Later masters repeatedly quote and challenge the scene. Yue Lin says that at precisely the moment the Buddha holds up the flower and Kashyapa smiles, both deserve thirty blows. Dongshan Shouchu says people know only the flower and smile but do not know the World-Honored One. Yulin calls it the single transmission of the treasury of the true teaching eye, then says it has made clear-eyed people laugh ever since. Zen thus defines its Buddha chiefly through this public action, Kashyapa's visible response, the assembly's failure to respond, and the announced entrustment; the later critical comments are part of the same Zen deployment, not outside hagiography.

Literally, “great function appears before one”: “great” (大), “functioning or use” (用), and “appears before one or is manifest” (現前). The phrase occurs 447 times in 170 allowlisted texts. It is frequently followed by “does not retain rules” (不存軌則); the unpunctuated five-character continuation occurs 21 times in 12 texts. The records deploy the headword as an assertion, a question, and a line in an address. In an early collected discourse, the statement “great function appearing is the unequalled body of the teaching” (大用現前即是無等等法身) directly equates it with another named expression. Asked, “When great function appears and does not retain rules, what then?

Literally, 'inside a ghost cave.' The phrase occurs 309 times in 122 allowed texts. The corpus repeatedly extends it as 'making a living inside a ghost cave' (鬼窟裏作活計, 164 occurrences), 'sitting inside a ghost cave' (鬼窟裏坐, 17), and 'inside a ghost cave beneath the black mountain' (黑山下鬼窟裏, 15). Dahui warns, 'take special care not to reckon inside a ghost cave' (切忌向鬼窟裏卜度), and elsewhere describes remaining motionless inside a ghost cave below the black mountain. Yuanwu writes that activity based on conscious calculation is 'making a living inside a ghost cave' and repeats the wording after 'as soon as you calculate' (纔作計較). Yunmen's record sets up a conditional choice: if the monk cannot answer, he is 'sitting inside a ghost cave.' These are the corpus's own spatial and verbal extensions of the image; the texts do not supply a separate object-definition for the cave.

(生) birth + (死) death + (事) matter/affair + (大) great: "life and death is the great matter." In the corpus it is overwhelmingly a fixed four-graph line, and in 84 places across 56 allowlist texts it stands in the paired form "life and death is the great matter; impermanence is swift" (生死事大，無常迅速); (無常迅速) itself occurs 160 times, 76 of them outside the pair. One text names the pair for what it is — "...two ready-made phrases" (生死事大，無常迅速，兩句現話, J28nB208). The attested deployment range is observable and wide: (i) as the reason for leaving home or seeking a teacher — (念生死事大) (19×) and (為生死事大) (39×), as in (念生死事大)，(奮志尋師) and (念生死事大)，(乃薙染完具) (X82n1571); (ii) as a plea addressed to a master — "...I beg the master to save me" (問生死事大請師相救, 古尊宿語錄); (iii) as an inscription — the (續燈正統) biography of (雲棲蓮池袾宏大師) records "at seventeen... he kept writing the four graphs (生死事大) on his desk" (年十七，補邑庠，每書生死事大四字於案頭, X84n1583), and (弘覺忞禪師北遊集) records of the emperor's lodging that (堂門書)「(生死事大)」 ("the hall door bore ", J26nB180); (iv) as the opening of a (上堂) sermon — (上堂)：「(大眾)！ | (又是九月半也)，(生死事大)，(無常迅速) (J32nB273); (v) as a raised (示眾) with a directive — (天如和尚示眾云)：『(生死事大)。

Zen-allowlist count: 617 hits in 174 texts. Searches covered the golden-body reversal, monastery erection, palace manifestation/covering, medicine case, later qualification, and ordinary botanical use. Family check with the sixteen-foot golden body (丈六金身), monastery (梵剎), jeweled halls and jade palaces (瓊樓玉殿), medicine (藥), and mustard seed (芥子) supports one concrete blade deployed in distinct comparisons, not separate referents; no split.

Literally, 'one who does or makes': a doer of a craft. Across the Chan corpus the word overwhelmingly marks tested competence—an adept, a real hand, or someone accomplished in the role named beside it. It modifies an adept master (作家宗師), an adept battle-general (作家戰將), and an adept Chan guest (作家禪客); an adepts' meeting (作家相見) names a meeting of people credited with that competence, while the doubled exclamation 'a real hand! | One corpus-wide expert/adept sense is retained after the item-8 family test. The poet phrase occurs in seven allowlisted files, but all seven transmit the same Dayu Zhi encounter; no productive reversed or related poet family was found. Expert poet (作家詩客), adept master (作家宗師), adept battle-general (作家戰將), and adept Chan guest (作家禪客) are applications of one accomplished-person meaning, not different things. Allowlist count: 2,744 hits in 331 texts. Productive families include adepts' meeting (作家相見), 117; an adept's means (作家手段), 34; doubled praise (作家作家), 22; adept fellow (作家漢), 14; adept eye (作家眼), 10; and adept forge (作家爐韛), 4. The modern default 'author/writer' is unsupported.

To slip or misstep (蹉) while passing (過): 'to slip past' or 'to miss it.' The record uses it when someone fails to catch what is directly before him. One recurrent line says, 'by the time you raise an eyebrow, it has already slipped past' (眨上眉毛，早是蹉過). The stock answer 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過) occurs 158 times in 65 texts. Another passage warns not to miss it face-to-face and says that, if one does, one knows only affairs passing before the eyes (切不得當面蹉過；若蹉過，只知事逐眼前過). The near-synonym 'missed it' (錯過) occurs 863 times, including 134 instances of 'missed it face-to-face' (當面錯過). The headword itself occurs 1,340 times in 213 allowlist texts, and the completed form 'let it slip past' (蹉過了) occurs 117 times. In dialogue it can be paired with 'under your heel' (腳跟下), as when a question about why something is under the monk's heel receives the answer 'missed it face-to-face.' | One corpus-wide sense. The dominant collocation is 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過), a recurring answer and verdict; the near-synonym is 'missed it' (錯過). | The close variant “to miss it directly face-to-face” (當面蹉過) occurs 158 times in 65 files. “To miss it right before one” (覿面錯過) occurs 12 times in 11 files, and “to miss it before the eyes” (眼前錯過) occurs three times in three files. The entry translates the observable spatial and verbal shape; it does not supply an object where the text leaves that object unstated.

Literally, the first graph names gruel and the second cooked rice or a rice meal. The corpus uses the pair as physical food: a verse says that mountain-field gruel and rice smell fragrant, and a discourse observes that after three days without being fed gruel and rice a person cannot move, but can move after eating some. Another address enumerates eating gruel and eating rice beside relieving oneself, walking, sitting, and sleeping as the listener's own fundamental matter. The rebuke “puffing gruel-and-rice breath” (鼓粥飯氣) is a food-derived fixed compound; it depends on consumed food but does not turn the literal food pair into the institutional schedule above. | Literal food predicates include eating, being fed, smelling fragrant, and having enough gruel and rice. The gruel-and-rice breath phrase (粥飯氣) and the gruel-and-rice monk (粥飯僧) are longer compounds and remain separate lexical articles or families. Their existence does not collapse physical food into the communal meal system.

Literally, worn-out or torn straw sandals. Straw sandals are the footwear of travel on foot between teachers, and the fixed phrase “wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) records that travel. The compound is also spoken as an answer and a comparison. Huangbo says, “the patriarchs' dark purport is worn-out straw sandals; it would be best to go barefoot and not put them on” (祖師玄旨是破草鞋，寧可赤脚不著最好). Another master answers “what is the Way? | The allowlisted concordance has 418 matches in 147 texts. The retained set covers the direct comparison to the patriarchs' dark purport, a direct Way question, a buddha question, the travel-on-foot institutional collocation, and the barefoot consequence. Family revalidation against “straw sandals” (草鞋), “travel on foot” (行脚), and “wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) confirms one object sense. ‘Wear out sandals’ is a verb phrase involving that object, not a second thing. | Footwear woven from grass or straw. In Chan records the sandals belong especially to going on foot between teachers: “to wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) and “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years” (更買草鞋行脚三十年) make the ordinary shoe part of the institutional life of itinerant inquiry. The object also enters named encounters: Deshan turns his back on the hall, puts on his sandals, and leaves; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head after Nanquan recounts cutting the cat. Huangbo calls “the patriarchs' dark purport” (祖師玄旨) “worn-out straw sandals” (破草鞋) and says bare feet would be better. The corpus records these concrete actions and comparisons without supplying a symbolic gloss for the sandals.

Allowlist count: 32 hits in 26 texts. One copying-action sense. Family checked against following another's heels (隨人腳跟轉), stamped from a printing block (印板上打來), released from a mold (模子裏脫出), and copying a model (依樣).

Literally, “great rest and great cessation.” The phrase occurs 93 times in 57 allowlisted texts. Chan records repeatedly call it a “secure field” or “field of great ease” (安穩之場; 大安樂田地), something one “reaches” or “personally arrives at” rather than an ordinary pause from activity. Yuanwu places it after “a great dead man has already lost his breath” and says, “upon reaching one’s own ground, great rest and great cessation” (到本分地上大休大歇). Xueyan immediately refuses to make that field an endpoint: “if you wish to head directly for the field of great rest, great cessation, and great ease, there is a great living road ahead” (前頭大有活路在). A later master criticizes descendants who bite onto Linji’s four shouts and take that for the field of great rest and cessation, calling the identification “a sheep’s substance in a tiger’s hide” (羊質虎皮). The Chan deviation is therefore an explicitly named field of arrival that remains subject to public correction; the entry reports those predicates without defining an inner state.

It is paired with 'the last word' (末後句) in the statement that one must also know the upward matter and the last word (更須知有向上事末後句始得). Related forms include 'the upward road' (向上一路, 957), 'the upward move' (向上一著, 279), 'the upward aperture' (向上一竅, 270), 'the upward pivot' (向上關捩子, 101), 'the upward person' (向上人, 229), and 'the upward vehicle of the lineage' (向上宗乘, 462). | A corpus-wide term, with 1,363 hits in 222 allowlist texts. The full dialogue—whether there is an upward matter, yes, then what it is—recurs across houses. The word 'upward' (向上) is relative to whatever the text has just named, as shown by 'the matter beyond Buddha' (佛向上事) and 'beyond Vairocana' (毘盧向上).

A proper mountain name, "Sumeru" (須彌), attested 4,619 times in 373 allowlisted texts. The full "Mount Sumeru" (須彌山) occurs 1,052 times and the variant transliteration "Sumeru-lu" (須彌盧) 147. Chan records use the mountain's name in questions, comparisons, and statements of size or destruction. One Compendium saying places together "break Sumeru into fine dust" and "take the waters of the four great seas into one hair-pore" (破須彌為微塵，攝四大海水入一毛孔). A Continued Lamp address says, "if the lineage purport is raised, Sumeru must directly be shattered" (舉揚宗旨，須彌直須粉碎). A Dahui lamp witness says, "pick up Sumeru-lu in the palm and swing inside a needle's eye" (拈須彌盧於掌上，向針眼裡打鞦韆). Gulin Qingmao also supplies a local self-definition: "the so-called Mount Sumeru is precisely the move before living beings and buddhas were established" (所謂須彌山者，即是生佛未具已前一著子也). Public exchanges and addresses place a seamless stupa and an unstruck bell on Sumeru's summit, tie Sumeru with a lotus-root filament, and test the claim that a mustard seed contains it. These are the records' stated deployments; Gulin's equation does not replace the proper name throughout the corpus.

Literally, the "gate and court" established for teaching or transformation. Chan records use it for the organized framework of explanations and responsive teaching, then explicitly place it below what questioners call the matter beyond or above it. One monk says, "one question and one answer still fall within the teaching establishment's gate and court" (一問一答猶落建化門庭) and asks how to raise the first principle. A sermon supplies a direct apposition: even a shout said to contain all these features "is still the teaching establishment's gate and court—responsive expedients—called a small resting place, not yet the treasure-site" (猶是建化門庭隨機方便，謂之小歇場，未至寶所). Another says that even holding the seal, raising the banner, and moving freely still falls within it and "is not yet the monk's essential road" (未為衲僧徑要一路). The Chan-specific use is evaluative and institutional: masters name their own question-and-answer and explanatory apparatus as a constructed teaching precinct, commonly in a contrast the texts themselves draw with what is "beyond or above" (向上) or the monk's essential road.

A repeated descriptive expression for being bare, exposed, and without covering. The term occurs 368 times in 143 allowed texts. Its recurring parallel is 'cleanly naked' (淨裸裸); records expand it with 'without covering' (無蓋覆), 'nothing that can be grasped' (沒可把), and 'fully exposed' (全露). These textual predicates establish what the expression describes without turning it into a condition to seek. The records also qualify it. Yuanwu says that being cleanly naked, cut off from thought, bare, and with nothing to grasp has 'still not left this-side affairs' (猶未離這邊事在). Later collections likewise say that even when one is cleanly naked, bare, and has nothing to grasp, 'there is still something fine remaining' (尚有廉纖), and contrast the relative ease of being bare with the difficulty of being distinctly evident (明歷歷). The corpus has five occurrences of the adverbial extension 'in a bare and uncovered manner' (赤灑灑地).

Further collocations include “turn and shift step” (轉身移步), “no road to turn” (轉身無路), and “turn, then…” (轉身便). Later records use “turning phrase” (轉身句) as a label in stylized exchanges, while Zhongfeng criticizes stock phrases called by that name. Compare road to turn (轉身一路), turning phrase (轉身句), place to turn (轉身處), and shifting step (移步).

Literally, “stir a thought and at once deviate.” The phrase's Zen-specific deployment is a compact verdict and answer, frequently paired with “form an intention and at once err” (擬心即差), but the corpus explicitly refuses to turn its negative wording into mere mental stillness. Huangbo says, “it is just this; stir a thought and at once deviate” (當體便是，動念即乖), then compares what he has described to measureless space. Linji pairs “form an intention and at once err” with the headword and immediately continues with the person who understands not being apart from what is before the eyes (不離目前). Shimen Cizhao quotes the pair and adds: “not intending and not moving, one is doing business in dead water” (不擬不動，正在死水裏作活計). Huanglong Huinan gives the parallel correction: “not intending and not moving is no different from wood and earth; a traveling monk must obtain a turning phrase” (不擬不動，土木無殊，行脚人須得轉身一句). In direct questions, Tianyin answers “What is the body of things?

” A student says that he no longer doubts “the tongues of the old masters everywhere” (天下老和尚舌頭), and his teacher immediately asks him to state what he understands. In the Linji succession account Huangbo predicts that Linji will “sit across and cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven” (坐斷天下人舌頭); the same countable verdict recurs widely without narrating bodily injury. The concrete organ is thus the corpus's recurring word for what is tested, trusted, shortened, or cut off in public speech.

Zen bends an ordinary verb of mutual deception into a repeated teaching-seat assurance tied to ‘the assenting heart’ (肯心). The negative formula dominates but does not change the verb’s referent. Family review with ‘conceal from one another’ (相瞞) and ‘deceive’ (誑欺) supports one sense.

Literally “turn” (轉) the “body or self” (身): to turn oneself around, attested 2,135 times in 327 allowlisted texts. The action can be direct bodily narration: Magu turns intending to sit and is struck, while another master turns and immediately walks away. Chan records also build a productive family from the same turning action. Yuanwu defines a “place to turn oneself” by “speak at the place without words; go at the place where going cannot be done” (無言處言得，行不得處行得，謂之轉身處). Hongzhi says one must know a road to turn; another record directly asks what that road is and answers, “you travel in the wild grass; I again enter the deep village” (汝行荒草裏，我又入深村). Compare road to turn (轉身一路), turning phrase (轉身句), place to turn (轉身處), and shifting step (移步).

inherited_lead: Literally, "outside mind, no thing stands." The phrase occurs 199 times in 100 allowlisted texts. Here the graph translated as "thing" or "what is established" (法) is contextual: in the recurring pair "this thing is mind; outside mind no thing stands; this mind is the thing; outside it no mind stands" (此法即心，心外無法；此心即法，法外無心), it names what could be set up as a thing apart, not an untranslated religious loanword. Shao's frequently quoted verse places the phrase beside visible landscape: "the summit of Tongxuan is not the human world; outside mind no thing stands; blue mountains fill the eyes" (通玄峰頂，不是人間；心外無法，滿目青山). A later master quotes that verse and says it has been "broken into two pieces" (打成兩橛). Another hall address strikes the Chan seat and asks: "mind has not arisen—where could the things be established?

Literally (無) (no) + (事) (matter / affair / business): having no matter on hand, nothing that needs doing. Linji Yixuan gives it its sharpest form: (無事是貴人) — the person with nothing to do is the noble person — immediately glossed (但莫造作)，(秖是平常) ('just don't fabricate; only be ordinary'). Linji applies (無事人) even to Buddhas and patriarchs: (佛與祖師是無事人) (Buddhas and patriarchs are people with nothing to do), and glosses it (秖是平常著衣)、(喫飯)、(無事過時) (just ordinarily wearing clothes, eating, passing the time with nothing to do). Huangbo Xiyun, Linji's teacher, states it from the other side: when feelings are exhausted with nothing left to rely on or grasp, that is the (無事人) (情盡都無依執。 | Held identically across teacher and disciple in the Hongzhou line — Huangbo (傳心法要) and Linji (臨濟語錄) — two independent witnesses of the same sense. Linji supplies the stock formula (無事是貴人) and (無事人); kept as one corpus-wide sense because the meaning does not differ between masters. Zen-scoped grep (tag-stripped, 2026-07-11): (無事) 3453 hits in 373 allowlist texts; (無事人) 253/109; the exact formula (無事是貴人) 6 hits in 6 texts (T47n1985, C077n1710, X78n1553, X79n1557, J23nB134, J34nB301) — it circulates beyond Linji's own record. The criticized-posture collocations quoted in the explanation count (無事甲) 163/92, (無事會) 46/31, (無事界) 21/15.

The headword has 1,076 hits in 257 allowlisted texts. The corpus-wide animal remains one referent across ox-herding, a posthumous buffalo declaration, teasing, public questions, and case allusions. Nanquan's lines are retained as especially important deployments, but neither the person who knows-there-is (知有底人) nor going among the different kinds (異類中行) provides a corpus definition that changes the buffalo into a second thing. The floating Da'an/Nanquan attribution of the ox-herding line is preserved in its occurrence note rather than used to manufacture a master-specific sense.

Counted constructions: "free and at ease" (自由自在), 185; "free and unobstructed" (自在無礙), 50; "obtain great freedom" (得大自在), 258; "not at ease" (不自在), 134. The compound personal/title name "Contemplating Freely" (觀自在, 278) and personal names such as Yun Zizai are proper-name uses and are not merged into this adjectival sense.

Literally, “every mote and every land”: the repeated nouns make the phrase distributive. Across 205 occurrences in 116 allowlisted texts, Chan masters pair it with “each thing and each particular” (物物頭頭), say that every mote and land “fully displays” (全彰), and place it in public addresses as the range of an action or disclosure. One address says, “every mote and every land once manifested awe-inspiring light; each thing and each particular fully displayed the true eye” (塵塵剎剎，曾現威光。 | 物物頭頭，全彰正眼). Another gives the compact parallel, “each thing and each particular—the whole body; every mote and every land—the great function” (物物頭頭全身，塵塵剎剎大用). The phrase is also made a test: “if you understand, every mote and every land; if you do not, a kick to the head” (若也會得，塵塵剎剎；若也不會，當頭一蹋). The corpus thus bends a cosmological distributive into recurring teaching-seat language for an all-pervading range; this entry makes no claim beyond those deployments.

Literally, “recognize the servant as the master/gentleman.” The corpus records 143 occurrences in 91 allowlisted texts. Masters use the household reversal as an adverse appraisal in public exchanges and comments. It is repeatedly coupled with “point to a deer as a horse” (指鹿為馬). One address applies both verdicts even to the old advice “seek only from yourself, do not look elsewhere” (但向己求，莫從他覓); another identifies “taking the one capable of seeing and hearing as real” (認著一箇能見能聞……執以為真) as precisely mistaking servant for master. Elsewhere a student is allowed to bow but warned, “you must not mistake the servant for the master” (不得認奴作郎), while later case commentary applies the same verdict to Deshan. The ordinary status reversal becomes a portable Chan verdict on a proposed identification; which identification receives it is supplied by each passage.

Zen-allowlist count: 563 hits in 216 texts. Family check covered standing in the snow (立雪), Shenguang or Huike (神光／慧可), pacifying the mind (安心), seeking the Way or teaching (求道／求法), nine years facing the wall (面壁九年), and the Second Patriarch (二祖). All refer back to the same bodily act; narrative, epithet, and later question are not different things. Names remain contextual because Huike is a lineage patriarch and belongs on the master roster, not as a separate dictionary figure.

On a battlefield, 'defeat' (敗) is a rout and 'breach' (闕) is a gap. In Chinese Chan records the compound is a recurrent verdict of failure on an exchange, statement, answer, or speaker. The allowlisted corpus has 594 hits in 193 texts. It records the constructions 'incur a failure' (納敗闕, 130 hits in 80 texts), 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕, 129 hits in 85 texts), and 'the place of the failure' (敗闕處, 39 hits in 28 texts). In one direct exchange a monk asks, 'What failure do I have? | The word carries a military register: 'rout' (敗) plus 'breach' (闕) becomes a verdict that an exchange has failed, as in 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕) and 'incur a failure' (納敗闕). All seven required definition formulas were searched; none produced a lexical definition. The entry therefore foregrounds the direct 'what failure?

Literally, 'one who does or makes': a doer of a craft. Across the Chan corpus the word overwhelmingly marks tested competence—an adept, a real hand, or someone accomplished in the role named beside it. It modifies an adept master (作家宗師), an adept battle-general (作家戰將), and an adept Chan guest (作家禪客); an adepts' meeting (作家相見) names a meeting of people credited with that competence, while the doubled exclamation 'a real hand! | One corpus-wide expert/adept sense is retained after the item-8 family test. The poet phrase occurs in seven allowlisted files, but all seven transmit the same Dayu Zhi encounter; no productive reversed or related poet family was found. Expert poet (作家詩客), adept master (作家宗師), adept battle-general (作家戰將), and adept Chan guest (作家禪客) are applications of one accomplished-person meaning, not different things. Allowlist count: 2,744 hits in 331 texts. Productive families include adepts' meeting (作家相見), 117; an adept's means (作家手段), 34; doubled praise (作家作家), 22; adept fellow (作家漢), 14; adept eye (作家眼), 10; and adept forge (作家爐韛), 4. The modern default 'author/writer' is unsupported.

Literally "hand over, entrust" (付) the "teaching" (法): "entrust the teaching," attested 608 times in 143 allowlisted texts. Lamp records use it for a named predecessor handing the teaching to a successor: "after the buddha's extinction, the teaching was entrusted to Kasyapa and mind was transmitted by mind" (佛滅後付法於迦葉，以心傳心). Narrative closure frequently says "after the patriarch had entrusted the teaching" (祖付法已), followed by his departure or death. The compound "verse on entrusting the teaching" (付法偈) names verses spoken or recorded at that handover.

“Occasion” keeps the range of the graph “occasion/capacity” (機) without importing a mystical faculty. The heading, question-and-discrimination phrase, direct answer, and “eye” collocation all require an interpersonal responsive sense. Compare “meet the occasion” (當機), “occasion of encounter” (機緣), “question-and-answer” (問答), and “responsive engagement” (應酬); none is simply synonymous.

Literally "single, sole" (單) and "transmit" (傳): "transmit singly," attested 692 times in 211 allowlisted texts. Zhongfeng says Bodhidharma's coming west is "called single transmission and direct pointing" and "at first had no twists and turns" (謂之單傳直指，初無委曲). In another address he gives a direct local definition: "the four holy and six ordinary [classes] are each originally complete; this is called single transmission," then asks, "what is transmitted? | " (各各本來具足謂單傳，傳箇甚麼). Frequent compounds are "single transmission and direct pointing" (單傳直指), "single transmission of the mind-seal" (單傳心印), and "single transmission outside the teachings" (教外單傳).

Literally, "ten oxen." As a Chan title and label, it denotes Liangshan Kuoan's ordered set of ox-herding verses and the pictures made from them. A collection titles the work "Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses" (梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌); another record says, "our school has the account of herding the ox, and Liangshan has the verses on the Ten Oxen" (我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌). The sequence begins with named sections including "seeking the ox" (尋牛) and "seeing the tracks" (見跡). The corpus also records direct criticism of its later handling: Baichi calls Liangshan's verses "compassionate, talk that descends into the weeds" (慈悲之故，落草之談), says later people "made a wrong move and then painted these Ten-Ox forms" (錯下手腳，更畫此十牛樣子), and urges burning them. In an encounter, a teacher interrupts a monk asked to recite the verses and asks, "Where is the ox?

Literally, "brows intertwined with one another." The phrase occurs 129 times in 80 allowlisted texts. The records use the bodily image for persons brought into exceptionally close conjunction: one master says that for five or six years he has had his brows intertwined with the assembly, yet in fact they have had "no traffic in rice or water" (五六年來雖則與諸人眉毛廝結，其實水米無交). Another requires "brows intertwined, sharing life and sharing death" (眉毛廝結，同生同死). It also appears as an answer in a public interview: asked for the phrase for opening the retreat, the master replies, "brows intertwined" (眉毛廝結). Elsewhere a hall address sets saying and silence against each other: "if one speaks, heaven and earth are far apart; if one does not speak, brows are intertwined" (說即天地懸殊，不說即眉毛廝結). The Chan use turns a physical impossibility into a compact, repeatable encounter phrase; the accompanying clauses establish proximity or conjunction but do not authorize this entry to decide what speakers intend by it.

Literally, 'link the lamps.' Outside the book title, records use the phrase for succession from one Chan teacher or generation to another. A history of Drum Mountain says that from the founding of Xingsheng, 'the linked lamps were unbroken for more than seventy generations' (聯燈不絕，七十餘代), and later describes 'those who linked the lamps and continued the flame for more than seventy generations' (聯燈續焰者七十餘代). Memorial words say, 'continue the flame, link the lamp—the Way is not alone' (續燄聯燈道不孤); another memorial says two teachers later 'linked lamps, each in a different region' (聯燈各一方). An ancestral-hall address speaks of 'one portrait, in succession linking the lamp far away' (一㡧次第聯燈遠). The lamp image is defined in the same record: the Chan houses' transmission through successive generations is compared to a lamp because it breaks darkness and shows things, and because its illumination can be continued without end. | The corpus contains 104 occurrences of the graphs in 28 allowed texts, but 77 occurrences in 13 texts belong to the proper title 'Linked-Lamp Essentials' (聯燈會要). This primary sense records the free verb/noun phrase in temple histories, memorials, and ancestral-hall addresses. Its recurring partner is 'continue the flame' (續燄／續焰).

A doubled imperative: "rest" or "stop" (休去) and "cease" or "settle" (歇去): "rest; cease," attested 123 times in 68 allowlisted texts. Shishuang's recorded sequence expands it: "rest; cease; let one thought last ten thousand years; become cold ashes and a withered tree; become an incense burner in an old shrine; become one strip of white silk; become cold and still" (休去歇去、一念萬年去、寒灰枯木去、古廟香爐去、一條白練去、冷秋秋地去). Yunfeng supplies a contrary sequence beginning "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), and a later speaker refuses both lists. Dahui reports people sitting slack-jawed and calling that "resting and ceasing" (一向嘴盧都地打坐，謂之休去歇去), in an extended criticism. Zhongfeng likewise reports people citing "do not fantasize, put it down, old-shrine incense burner, rest and cease" as evidence, and compares that use to waiting by a stump for a rabbit. Other records retain the literal instruction: a teacher says, "from now on, rest; cease" (自今以往，休去歇去), while Dafang Yin asks, "why not rest and cease? | Counted companions: "one thought for ten thousand years" (一念萬年去), 115; "cold and still" (冷湫湫地去), 48; "old-shrine incense burner" (古廟香爐去), 72; "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), 5. Orthography varies between "cold autumn-like" and "cold and still" in witnesses. The sole late naming formula is excluded because its surrounding sentence applies the words to a different labeled expression, whereas the older imperatives and their recorded criticisms bear the headword directly.

Literally ‘whole or complete’ (全) + ‘trigger, pivot, or dynamic’ (機): the whole dynamic or full pivotal function. The compound has 843 occurrences in 224 allowlisted texts. It is especially visible in ‘the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用), with 115 occurrences in 60 texts. Yuanwu says this ‘whole dynamic and great function is manifest wherever one touches’ (全機大用觸處見成); elsewhere his record says ‘as the grass bends and the wind moves, the whole dynamic alone is exposed’ (草偃風行全機獨露), then asks what one says without relying on any thing or phrase. ‘The whole dynamic alone exposed’ (全機獨露) occurs 21 times in 19 texts; ‘the whole dynamic thoroughly freed’ (全機透脫) occurs 5 times in 5; and ‘the whole dynamic alone functioning’ (全機獨用) occurs twice in 2. The Blue Cliff Record uses it both in the rubric ‘the whole dynamic is displayed everywhere’ (全機隨處齊彰) and in its comment that several actions are all ‘places of the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用處). A lamp-record master also uses the compound predicatively: ‘if I deploy the whole dynamic, where will you search? | " and receives a blow across the back for each. The corpus coordinates "great function" with "great capacity" (大機大用, 276 occurrences), and "great function" with "the whole capacity" (全機大用, 115). It also records the explicit contrast "you people have obtained only the great body, not great function" (汝等諸人只得大體不得大用). These are named formulas, questions, pairings, and contrasts in the record; the entry makes no claim about a metaphysical entity behind them. | No distinct referent emerged from 'great function' (大用), 'great function manifests before you' (大用現前), 'great capacity and great function' (大機大用), 'the whole capacity and great function' (全機大用), and the 'great body/great function' (大體/大用) comparison. 'Use' and 'function' are alternate English readings of the same attested thing, not separate senses.

The paired graphs mean to wander or roam at ease. In a lamp narrative, Tianhuang tells Longtan, “roam at ease according to your nature and range freely following conditions; exhaust the ordinary mind, with no other superior understanding” (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). An Ancestral Hall narrative describes someone “delighting in clouds and waters, roaming at ease whether going or staying” (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Productive forms include “roam at ease and be unbound” (逍遙自在), “range freely and roam at ease” (放曠逍遙), and “roam at ease according to one's nature” (任性逍遙).

Tianyin Yuanxiu (天隱圓修) gives it as an instruction: '(十二時中須教打成一片)，(自無不辦之理)' ('throughout the twelve periods of the day you must have it pounded into one piece; then of itself there is nothing that cannot be accomplished'). The variant (打作一片) ('struck into one piece'; 6× in 6 files) carries the same sense — Yulin Tongxiu, in his (工夫說) ('Discourse on Work'): '(所謂行住坐臥動靜閒忙打作一片)' ('what is called walking, standing, sitting, lying, motion and stillness, leisure and busyness struck into one piece'). (打成一片) occurs 311× in 139 allowlist files. The texts assign the word no gloss beyond its literal sense, and neither does this entry. The Blue Cliff Record gives an explicit equivalence: being on 'the one-color side' (一色邊) is 'also called being pounded into one piece' (亦謂之打成一片). Zhongfeng Mingben's Miscellaneous Record supplies a correction to a different equation: if one knows it as 'a silver mountain and iron wall' (銀山鐵壁), 'it cannot be called pounded into one piece' (不可謂之打成一片). These are the texts' own equivalence and rejection; the entry does not reconcile them beyond reporting both.

Both graphs name bearing a load: to shoulder or carry it. One exact verse names physical firewood carried on one shoulder until the carrying pole breaks. Far more often the Chan corpus leaves the load unstated or names responsibility, succession, inheritance, or teaching. Productive forms include “shoulder it successfully” (擔荷得), “shoulder with the whole body” (全身擔荷), and “shoulder it on one shoulder” (一肩擔荷). Yuanwu lists “accept successfully, shoulder successfully, head toward successfully, carry out successfully” (承當得，擔荷得，趣向得，行履得). Jiufeng Daoqian says, “knowing to accept and shoulder it inwardly is inner succession” (知向裏許承當擔荷，是為內紹), then says one must see “the person with no accepting and the person with no shouldering” before reaching “one color” (須見無承當底人，無擔荷底人，始得同一色). The same load-bearing verb therefore spans physical cargo and the corpus's dominant responsibility and lineage deployments. Literal and figurative loads do not make the act of shouldering two lexical things.

Literally "one" (一) "move, placement, or stroke" (著): "one move," attested 3,121 times in 351 allowlisted texts. The game-like noun appears in recurring Chan compounds: "let one move pass" (放過一著, 617 occurrences), "the final move" (末後一著, 104), "the upward move" (向上一著, 279), "one move ahead" (先一著, 38), and the suffixed "one move" (一著子, 601). A case-comment collection appraises an earlier response as "precisely letting one move pass," then adds "danger" (正是放過一著；險). A lamp address pairs "Linji's vanguard—let one move pass" with "Deshan's later command—set it aside" (臨濟先鋒，放過一著；德山後令，且在一邊). Questions ask, "before living beings and buddhas arose, where did one move fall? | " and receives, "break through and come meet me" (末後一著始到牢關，如何是牢關；打破來，與汝相見). Literally, a wall stands upright for a thousand fathoms. The corpus uses the whole clause as a predicate or appraisal of a statement, a person, a house style, or a position in an encounter. Nanyuan opens an address with “on the red flesh-lump, a thousand-fathom wall stands” (赤肉團上壁立千仞); a monk repeats the line back, overturns the Chan seat after Nanyuan confirms it, and is struck when he hesitates. A Dongshan record places “sometimes mingling with mud and mixing with water” beside “sometimes standing like a thousand-fathom wall” (有時和泥合水，有時壁立千仞), then says Dongshan is found in neither location. Yuanwu likewise sets “standing like a thousand-fathom wall” against “dragging through mud and water, ash-covered head and dirt-covered face,” and elsewhere writes that in the ash-covered, dirt-covered place one stands like a thousand-fathom wall, while in the thousand-fathom-wall place one is dirt-covered and ash-covered. A commentary classifies three turning phrases as respectively “standing like a thousand-fathom wall,” “sailing a boat on dry land,” and “host and guest interchanging” (一句壁立千仞，一句陸地行船，一句賓主交參). Langya appraises Nanyuan's line with the single word “dangerous” (險). The exact four-character phrase occurs 434 times in 113 allowlisted files.

proposing_entries: 函蓋乾坤、截斷眾流、東山水上行
inherited_lead: The components mean “box or case” (函), “lid or cover” (蓋), and “heaven and earth,” literally qian and kun, the first two trigrams of the Book of Changes (乾坤): "a lid fitting the box, heaven and earth." The corpus attests (函蓋) as a box and its lid that correspond — the collocation (函蓋相稱) / (函蓋相應) recurs (e.g. B25n0144 著函，函蓋相稱故, "[the lid] on the box, because box and lid correspond"), and (乾坤) is the standard pairing for the whole cosmos. The phrase is the FIRST of the (雲門三句) (Yunmen's three phrases), paired with (截斷眾流) and (隨波逐浪). Its attested history in the corpus: Yunmen (雲門文偃) delivers it in his own (廣錄) as a (示眾) — (函蓋乾坤目機銖兩)。 | The three-phrase set (雲門三句) = (函蓋乾坤) · (截斷眾流) · (隨波逐浪). Structural facts (describe-only): (1) the phrase originates in Yunmen's own (示眾) as one line of the triad (函蓋乾坤)、(目機銖兩)、(不涉萬緣) (春緣 in T47n1988); the numbered (三句) framing and the phrase-name (函蓋乾坤句) are the systematization of his heir (德山緣密), recorded in (人天眼目) and the lamp/(語錄) texts. (2) ORTHOGRAPHIC VARIANT: the water-radical form (涵蓋乾坤) occurs once in the allowlist (J40nB472), there in a different phrase (有時芥子藏身，有時涵蓋乾坤), not the (雲門三句) context. Do not cross-attribute the retold cases: Yunmen's own (示眾) (T47n1988) vs. the compiler-systematized exposition (人天眼目) vs. later (上堂) that merely raise the three (五燈會元 昔日雲門有三句). | As a fixed technical term, (截斷眾流句) (139 hits / 69 files) is the middle of the (雲門三句) (Yunmen's three phrases; the set-name itself 76 hits / 44 files): (函蓋乾坤句) (covering heaven and earth) · (截斷眾流句) (cutting off the myriad streams) · (隨波逐浪句) (following the waves). (人天眼目) gives the corpus's own account of the set's origin — (師示眾云)。

Literally, "ten oxen." As a Chan title and label, it denotes Liangshan Kuoan's ordered set of ox-herding verses and the pictures made from them. A collection titles the work "Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses" (梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌); another record says, "our school has the account of herding the ox, and Liangshan has the verses on the Ten Oxen" (我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌). The sequence begins with named sections including "seeking the ox" (尋牛) and "seeing the tracks" (見跡). The corpus also records direct criticism of its later handling: Baichi calls Liangshan's verses "compassionate, talk that descends into the weeds" (慈悲之故，落草之談), says later people "made a wrong move and then painted these Ten-Ox forms" (錯下手腳，更畫此十牛樣子), and urges burning them. In an encounter, a teacher interrupts a monk asked to recite the verses and asks, "Where is the ox?

In running prose, sequence or order (序) names an ordered progression. The Jingde-era lamp record says that beginning students did not know the sequence (初心後學未知次序). Konggu Daocheng's record says that matters for someone newly entering have an order (初進工夫，一一皆有次序) and names taking refuge and requesting instruction first (皈依請益為先). These witnesses state order directly; they do not turn the graph into a technical Chan category. | This sense is represented through the transparent compound 'sequence/order' (次序). It is kept separate from the bibliographic preface and the institutional rank/division senses.

To be complete, fully endowed, or lacking nothing. The headword occurs 2,264 times in 303 allowlisted texts. Xuansha says, “each person is fully endowed; each person is manifest” (人人具足，人人成現). Another address ranges across monastics and laypeople, women and men, wise and foolish, noble and low, saying all are fully endowed “without the least lacking” (悉皆具足，曾無欠少). Hongzhi pairs “fully endowed from the beginning” (本來具足) with “not a hair's breadth lacking, not a hair's breadth in excess.” A later text warns that merely accepting “fully endowed from the beginning, no need to seek outside” can become empty talk. In the ordination compound “full precepts” (具足戒), the same completeness word modifies the precepts: biographies record receiving or being given the full precepts. Predicate and attributive placement express the same completeness, not different lexical referents. | The former predicate/adjective targets were grammatical uses of the same completeness word and are merged. The Chan deployment includes both lack-nothing formulas and the corpus's criticism of resting on such formulas. The full-precepts compound remains under the precepts gate and should receive longest-match priority when indexed separately. Compare fully endowed from the beginning (本來具足), completely formed (圓成), lack (欠少), full precepts (具足戒), receiving precepts (受戒), and precept (戒).

Dahui uses the word self-deprecatingly when he says, 'I have not read Guo Xiang's explanation or the various commentators' explanations; I only rely on my own fabrication to explain your silence' (我也不曾看郭象解并諸家注解，只據我杜撰說破爾這默然). The stock rebuke 'fabricated elder' (杜撰長老) occurs 68 times in 40 texts, often in the fuller comparison 'fabricated elders are like hemp and millet'—that is, extremely numerous (杜撰長老如麻似粟). 'Fabricated Chan fellow' (杜撰禪和) likewise appears as a verdict on a respondent, while 'fabricated conjectural talk' (杜撰臆說) names speech. These are grammatical deployments of one shared judgment; the texts do not establish a distinct sense from the proper name Du Mo, whose 18 hits refer to a person or to being silent.

Literally, “awaken through-and-through.” The term appears 142 times in 71 allowlisted texts, both as a verb in encounter and biographical retrospectives and as a noun-like condition in instruction and contrast. Wuyi Yuanlai supplies the clearest corpus definition: there are two awakenings, “interpretive awakening obtained from written words and speech” and “thorough awakening obtained by investigating on one’s own part”; he adds, “interpretive awakening is like hearing someone describe a thing; thorough awakening is like seeing the thing with one’s own eyes” (解悟者如聞人說物，徹悟者如親眼見物). Other records say not to stop if one has not thoroughly awakened, describe the World-honored One seeing the morning star and thoroughly awakening, and contrast the many who thoroughly awaken with the equally many who misunderstand. Thus the Chan record bends an ordinary intensive verb into a named contrast with “interpretive awakening” (解悟), while also using it in lineage biographies; the direct contrast, not an imported theory of enlightenment, controls the gloss. | Verbal and noun-like grammar denotes the same event/state and does not warrant a split. The related term “interpretive awakening” (解悟) is a text-drawn contrast, not an annotator’s ranking.

渠今正是我，我今不是渠。 | The quotation has one corpus-wide identity despite its origin with Dongshan; later masters preserve, question, and criticize it without establishing a different master-specific referent. The paired line “I am now not him” (我今不是渠) is required context, not a second sense.

Literally a cake drawn or painted rather than edible. Chan records make it a stock verdict by completing the image: “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” (畫餅不可充飢／不充飢). In the Xiangyan case, after he cannot answer Guishan's question and searches all the writings he has read for a reply, he sighs, “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” (畫餅不可充饑); the record then has him burn those writings. Dahui's verse pairs it with another ineffective likeness: “how could a shimmering mirage ever stop thirst? | #0g deviation: Chan turns an ordinary painted object into a recurrent verdict applied not only to textual learning but also to Chan-sounding discourse, staff work, and shouting. This entry reports the stated inability to feed; it does not infer a hidden spiritual effect. Headword count: 88 hits in 63 texts. Exact forms: “painted cake cannot fill hunger” (畫餅不可充飢) 8/8; “painted cake does not fill hunger” (畫餅不充飢) 2/2; the deliberately contradictory “fill hunger with a painted cake” (畫餅充飢) 4/4. The variant graph for “hungry” (饑) occurs widely beside the headword's form (飢).

(本來) from the root / origin, originally + (無) there is no + (一物) one thing: "from the origin, not one thing." The line is the third of (慧能)'s verse in the received (宗寶) (六祖大師法寶壇經): (菩提本無樹)，(明鏡亦非臺)；(本來無一物)，(何處惹塵埃) (the text writes his name 惠能). The corpus shows the line is a feature of the LATER Platform-Sutra text: the Dunhuang (壇經) (T48n2007) gives the same verse with the third line "the buddha-nature is ever pure" (佛性常清淨，何處有塵埃), without (本來無一物). Across the lamp records the couplet varies — (何處惹塵埃) (法寶壇經); (何處有塵埃) (祖堂集, which carries the verse twice, with first lines 菩提本無樹 and 身非菩提樹); and (本來無一物何假拂塵埃) with first line (菩提本非樹) (傳燈玉英集). Zen-scoped the phrase occurs 214 hits / 106 texts; the contracted (本無一物) 34 / 30. Attested deployment beyond the verse: (洞山良价) issues a verdict on the line — asked why (神秀)'s (時時勤拂拭) verse did not win the robe, (洞山答曰)：「(直道本來無一物)，(也未得衣缽在)。

Zen-allowlist count: 809 hits in 242 texts. Family check covered the elephant king's stride (象王行), backward look or turn (象王回顧／回旋), the lion's roar or vigorous motion (師子吼／奮迅), the fragrant elephant (香象), and Samantabhadra's (普賢) white elephant. The primary Chan image and the Buddhist narrative animal share the same royal-elephant referent, so differing deployments were not split into readings. The narrative white-elephant witness remains listed in SourceTexts but was not curated because it adds outside-story identity rather than defining the Chan bend.

The graphs name a mustard seed. The allowlisted corpus has 442 hits in 146 texts. Its small size supplies the comparison ‘mustard-seed-sized’ (芥子許, 67 hits in 50 texts), as when a teacher speaks of a doubt as small as a mustard seed. The corpus also repeatedly pairs the seed with Mount Sumeru in both directions: ‘Sumeru contains a mustard seed’ (須彌納芥子, 46 hits in 30 texts) and ‘a mustard seed contains Sumeru’ (芥子納須彌, 59 hits in 44 texts). In the Guizong encounter, Li Bo accepts the first statement but asks whether the second is false; Guizong asks where Li Bo’s ten thousand books are held in a body the size of a coconut. In another exchange, the two directions receive the one-word answers ‘easy’ and ‘difficult.’ A later address records mountains, earth, trees, monastics, laypeople, sages, and ordinary people placed inside a mustard seed without the seed becoming narrow. These are the corpus’s recorded scale constructions; the entry does not turn them into a symbolic meaning for the seed.

The paired graphs mean to wander or roam at ease. In a lamp narrative, Tianhuang tells Longtan, “roam at ease according to your nature and range freely following conditions; exhaust the ordinary mind, with no other superior understanding” (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). An Ancestral Hall narrative describes someone “delighting in clouds and waters, roaming at ease whether going or staying” (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Productive forms include “roam at ease and be unbound” (逍遙自在), “range freely and roam at ease” (放曠逍遙), and “roam at ease according to one's nature” (任性逍遙).

A question about the student's place to emerge receives 'Xuefeng was originally a man from Lingnan' (雪峰元是嶺南人), using the graphs' ordinary sense of geographic origin inside the same question form. The corpus also has 66 occurrences of 'the one route of emergence' (出身一路), 61 of 'have a place to emerge' (有出身處), and 13 of 'have no place to emerge' (無出身處).

Related narrative formulas show the same productive construction: “awakened at the words” (言下契悟), 41 hits in 28 texts; “suddenly awakened at the words” (言下頓悟), 65 in 40; “at the words, suddenly greatly awakened” (言下豁然大悟), 10 in 9; “thoroughly penetrated at the words” (言下大徹), 34 in 31; and “had an insight at the words” (言下有省), 215 in 89. These are related formulas, not alternate spellings of the four-character headword.

Transmission wording places "true form, markless" (實相無相, 103) between "the subtle mind of extinction" and "subtle correct teaching." The corpus further records Mazu asking how to accord with "markless complete command" (無相三昧). The former concrete/abstract split was a literal-versus-extended reading of the same raising action and is merged. Compare whisk (拂子), sitting cloth (坐具), upright raising (豎起), raised saying (話頭), investigated saying (所參話), and lifting or citing (舉起). No fixed spiritual force is assigned to raising either kind of object.

It is consequently used as a qualification for a monk or person addressed in the hall: "you people must have blood under the skin" (汝諸人須是皮下有血始得), and "if he has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood" (他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯).
