The first graph means “buddha” (佛), and the second means “nature” (性): 'buddha-nature.' The term reaches the Chan record as a sutra line the masters quote and put in play — (一切眾生皆有佛性) ('all sentient beings have buddha-nature'): Yanguan Qi'an preaches the line straight to his assembly, and it stands inside the stock phrase (見性成佛) ('see the nature, become buddha'). The corpus also records the term against social rank: told a 'Lingnan barbarian has no Buddha-nature,' Huineng answers (人則有南北)，(佛性無南北) ('people may be north or south, but Buddha-nature is neither north nor south'). The record's most-repeated instruction bearing the term is given as a scripture quotation in Baizhang's mouth at Guishan's awakening over the stirred ember (五燈會元, 溈山靈祐 chapter): (經云)。 | ') recurs 334x/123 (counting 有佛性也無). The same corpus-wide headword is also deployed in Zhaozhou's dog case. A monk quotes the statement 'all sentient beings have buddha-nature' (一切眾生皆有佛性) and asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has buddha-nature. Zhaozhou answers, 'no' (無). Pressed—'from the buddhas down to ants everything has it; why not a dog?

Exact count: 129 hits in 79 allowlisted texts. The goose-king-selects-milk formula (鵝王擇乳) has 69 hits in 48 texts; not-of-the-duck-kind (素非鴨類) has 55 in 36. One legendary-bird sense. Family checked against selecting milk (擇乳), water and milk (水乳), duck kind (鴨類), choosing the teaching (擇法), and possessing the eye (具眼).

Literally (拈) 'to pick up / hold up (between the fingers)' + (古) 'the old [ones]', i.e. (古則) / (公案), old cases: 'picking up the old cases.' It names a commentarial genre and a standard section of a master's record — a master takes up (舉) a recorded old case and adds a prose remark (his 拈, typically marked 師拈云). The corpus enumerates it inside a family of old-case commentary forms — X67n1307: (古來有拈古)、(頌古)、(徵古)、(代古)、(別古) ('from of old there have been niangu, songgu [verse], zhenggu [interrogating], daigu [substituting], biegu [alternating]') — and it is standardly paired with, and distinct from, (頌古) ('versifying the old cases,' verse comment): a master's record files (拈古) and (頌古) as separate juan (T47n1997, 圓悟佛果禪師語錄, runs 拈古上/中/下 then 頌古; B25n0145, 中峰廣錄, 卷第三拈古頌古). Whole anthologies collect them (X66n1296 宗門拈古彙集, 'Collected Niangu of the [Chan] School'), and a further commentary layer (評唱) can be built on a master's (拈古) — Wansong Xingxiu's (評唱) on Tiantong (Hongzhi) Zhengjue's (拈古) is the (請益錄) (X67n1307). As an act it is countable (B27n0152: 呈拈古十餘則, 'presented a dozen niangu') and attached to a master's name (B27n0152: 余閱雪竇拈古, 'I read Xuedou's niangu'). The same act of taking up cases for comment is also called (拈提) (354 hits / 142 files): (拈提公案如雪竇老真可謂與古人心心相契) ('in taking up cases, old Xuedou can truly be said to be mind-to-mind with the ancients') and (者個公案叢林中少有拈提者) ('few in the monasteries have taken this case up'), both B27n0152. | Genre term, corpus-wide; no master bends the meaning, so a single sense. (拈古) itself: 517 hits / 155 files; the pair (拈古頌古) in direct sequence: 65 / 57 (all counts over the 462-file allowlist, XML tags/notes/rdg stripped, whitespace collapsed, punctuation retained). Distinguish from (a) the live hall verb (拈) 'to pick up / hold up' a topic or object (拈云 4412× / 236 files, 師拈云 1170× / 92 files in the allowlist), of which picking up an OLD case is the specialised case; and (b) (頌古), its verse counterpart. Also called (拈提) (354× / 142 files; quotes in the Explanation). Sibling genres in the same enumeration are attested in the allowlist: (頌古) (1075× / 264 files), (代古) (64× / 35), (別古) (36× / 23), (徵古) (17× / 9). All curated occurrences are labels, titles, TOC/section heads, or the act of composing/reading niangu, so MasterName is null (the genre is not spoken by one master in these lines).

Allowlist counts recorded in the audit: the headword “staff/blow” (棒), 18,109 hits in 415 texts; “one blow” (一棒), 2,954; “thirty blows” (三十棒), 2,766; “twenty blows” (二十棒), 407; “one bout of blows” (一頓棒), 63; “receive a blow” (喫棒), 1,191; and “painful blows” (痛棒), 752. The object-versus-blow split is preserved and strengthened: six object witnesses and seven act witnesses, with every sense independently anchored. Attribution remains cautious because several formulas circulate in raised cases and later compilations, and witnesses differ over which Deshan bears the thirty-blows formula.

Literally, 'fall into emptiness,' but in these records the observable warning is against falling into a blank nothing. The term occurs 325 times in 128 allowed texts; the expanded form 'fall into blank annihilation' (落空亡) occurs 63 times in 37 texts. Dahui reports people who hear 'a teaching in which nothing is obtained' (無所得法) and become afraid that they will fall into blankness; he answers by asking whether the very one who fears falling into blankness is empty. A lamp dialogue answers the charge that Chan teachers mostly fall into blankness by saying that letters and other things arise from wisdom and that, when 'great function appears before one' (大用現前), there can be no falling into blankness. Another exchange dismantles the spatial wording itself: asked whether 'originally there is nothing' falls into blankness, the reply asks, 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?

Allowlist count: 15,708 occurrences in 419 texts. Family checks covered “first phrase” (第一句), “second phrase” (第二句), “third phrase” (第三句), “final phrase” (末後一句) and its shorter form (末後句), “upward phrase” (向上一句), “out-of-pattern phrase” (出格一句), the diminutive “one phrase” (一句子), “one conforming phrase” (一句合頭語), “under one phrase” (一句下), “a thousand and ten thousand phrases” (千句萬句), and the general “phrase” entry (句). Item-8 review found position and qualification families, not different objects: verse line, spoken phrase, quoted saying, and section-qualified phrase remain countable utterance units in the harvested passages. Twelve exact-headword witnesses replace the former thin set; two former KWICs that contained only the shorter “final phrase” form (末後句), rather than the exact headword “one phrase” (一句), were removed. No occurrence is retained merely to support an interpretive meaning for an unspecified phrase.

Literally, “when hunger comes, eat rice.” Zen records turn this ordinary act into a compact answer, appraisal, and recurring line, most often paired with “when tired, sleep” (困來眠／困來打睡). Lingzhao answers her family's hard/easy exchange, “neither hard nor easy: when hungry, eat rice; when tired, sleep” (也不難，也不易，飢來喫飯，困來睡). Yuanwu places the line directly after “understand that ordinary mind is the Way” (了取平常心是道，饑來喫飯困來眠). One Dongshan teacher says he does not know how to discuss Chan or speak of the Way and “only, when hungry, eats rice; when tired, sleeps” (祇是饑來喫飯，困來打睡). Dazhu Huihai's recorded exchange supplies the crucial contrast: asked whether everyone does the same, he says no, because “when they eat, they refuse simply to eat and make a hundred demands; when they sleep, they refuse simply to sleep and make ten thousand calculations” (他喫飯時不肯喫飯，百種須索；睡時不肯睡，萬般計較). Other records caution that merely repeating the line as if already finished may still be “not yet” (未在), and one later speaker calls it only “one flavor of the ordinary” and not yet the monk's further matter. The entry therefore records both its elevated interview use and the corpus's own refusal to make parroting it sufficient.

Literally, "one-finger Chan." The phrase names Juzhi's recorded use of a raised finger in public interviews. A later record states the visible rule directly: "Whenever someone came, Master Juzhi only extended one finger; he called it one-finger Chan" (俱胝和尚逢人但伸一指頭，喚做一指頭禪). In the transmitted case, Tianlong raises one finger to Juzhi; afterward, whenever students ask, Juzhi raises one finger, and before dying he says, "I obtained Tianlong's one-finger Chan; through my whole life I could not use it up" (吾得天龍一指頭禪，一生用不盡). The record also preserves criticism rather than making the label an unquestioned formula: Xuansha says he would have broken the finger, Caoshan faults Juzhi's taking it up, and Sanshan asks, "What connection does one-finger Chan have?

Literally, a buddha image made of clay or mud. The term occurs 200 times in 92 allowed texts. Literally, a 'patched-robed person': 'patched robe' (衲) plus the person-noun (子). Literally, 'solitary brightness.' The term occurs 243 times in 112 allowed texts. The three graphs form an established phonetic borrowing, rendered here as 'complete command'; the Chan corpus determines its usable content through named compounds and direct definitions. The term occurs 4,852 times in 382 allowed texts. Huineng defines 'complete command of the single conduct' as 'at every place, while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, always carry one straight mind' (一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，常行一直心是也). It also says beings remain within 'complete command of the nature of the teaching' while dressing, eating, speaking, responding, using the six sense-roots, and carrying out every action (法性三昧中著衣喫飯言談祇對六根運用一切施為). Xuansha says that buddhas are people's 'self-receiving complete command' and that walking, standing, sitting, and lying down have never not been it; when asked what that complete command is, he replies, 'What use are so many modes of complete command?

Literally, "the Han hound chases the clod." The phrase occurs 64 times in 46 allowlisted texts. A Blue Cliff Record comment gives the named allusion: the hound of the Han family was a swift dog, capable of tracking the cunning hare of Zhongshan; the monk in Dongshan's cold-and-heat exchange is compared to that hound running up the steps after a reflected moon and finding no moon there. Across the corpus the compact phrase is repeatedly contrasted with "the lion bites the person" (師子咬人，韓獹逐塊): one address says, "you must have the lion bite the person; do not imitate the Han hound chasing the clod" (直須師子咬人，莫學韓獹逐塊). Literally “a dead snake,” attested 335 times in 135 allowlisted texts. The literal alternate 'pure regulations' is retained, but 'monastic code' states the observable corpus function in English. Generic references to Baizhang's monastic code (百丈清規) belong here when a passage says Baizhang made it, a community observes it, or its commands operate. The technical name of the Caodong house's signature scheme, created by Dongshan Liangjie and systematized by Caoshan Benji. 'Five' configurations arrange two terms — the upright or straight (正) and the crooked or bent (偏) — as: crooked within the upright (正中偏), upright within the crooked (偏中正), coming from within the upright (正中來), arriving from both together (兼中至 / 偏中至), attained in both together (兼中到). The same five are recast as ruler and minister (君臣, the 君臣五位); Dongshan also taught parallel fivefold sets — the five ranks of merit/achievement (功勳五位) and the five ranks of princes (王子五位) — and Caoshan's 'five ranks facing the guest' (五位對賓) works them into interview form ('I come from the crooked position, please receive me into the upright'). Across the corpus the term functions as the emblem of the Caodong house, almost always named in one breath with its Linji-house counterpart, the three mysteries (and three essentials) (臨濟三玄（三要）) — 'Dongshan's five ranks / Linji's three mysteries' (洞山五位／臨濟三玄), 'not Linji's three mysteries, not Caodong's five ranks' (不是臨濟三玄不是曹洞五位) — so that 'the Five Ranks' effectively names the Caodong house the way 'three mysteries' names the Linji house. The scheme is defined inside the house's own records. Both graphs name bearing a load: to shoulder or carry it. One exact verse names physical firewood carried on one shoulder until the carrying pole breaks. Far more often the Chan corpus leaves the load unstated or names responsibility, succession, inheritance, or teaching. Productive forms include “shoulder it successfully” (擔荷得), “shoulder with the whole body” (全身擔荷), and “shoulder it on one shoulder” (一肩擔荷). Yuanwu lists “accept successfully, shoulder successfully, head toward successfully, carry out successfully” (承當得，擔荷得，趣向得，行履得). Jiufeng Daoqian says, “knowing to accept and shoulder it inwardly is inner succession” (知向裏許承當擔荷，是為內紹), then says one must see “the person with no accepting and the person with no shouldering” before reaching “one color” (須見無承當底人，無擔荷底人，始得同一色). The same load-bearing verb therefore spans physical cargo and the corpus's dominant responsibility and lineage deployments. Literal and figurative loads do not make the act of shouldering two lexical things.

Zen bends a domestic act of arson into a named case continually reopened in public comment and questioning. The label names the whole encounter, not only the final fire. The usual graph for ‘hermitage’ (庵) and its witness variant (菴) spell the same word. Cross-checking ‘a withered tree leans against a cold cliff’ (枯木倚寒巖) and ‘through the three winter months there is no warmth’ (三冬無暖氣) confirms the quoted hermitage-dweller's response without turning that response into a second sense of the case title.

Literally “to bite and chew” (咬嚼), the term is attested 209 times in 109 allowlisted texts. Chan records extend the bodily action to sayings and public cases: one teacher tells beginners to “chew over a ready-made sentence that cannot be knocked down” and repeats “chew it over, chew it over” (咬嚼來、咬嚼去); the same record says Wujin spent his whole life unable to chew through “the bowl-carrying public case” (托缽公案). Other comments use the resistance of food as an explicit comparison: a saying can be “unable to be chewed through” (咬嚼不破), while Donglin offers only “wooden-slat soup and iron-nail rice—chew as you will” (木札羹、鉄釘飯，任汝咬嚼). The record also issues the opposite verdict, “strictly avoid chewing” (切忌咬嚼), after the answer “a thousand-year peach pit.”

A proper name, literally "Mighty-Sound King" (威音王), occurring 487 times in 171 allowlisted texts. The extended form "Mighty-Sound King Buddha" (威音王佛) occurs 80 times. Chan records most often place the name in temporal and spatial formulas: "before Mighty-Sound King" (威音王已前, 181 occurrences), "after Mighty-Sound King" (威音王已後, 33), and "the far side of Mighty-Sound King" (威音王那畔, 17). In the Nanquan-Huangbo exchange, Huangbo says he followed the Way "before Mighty-Sound King"; Nanquan answers, "you are still a descendant of old Master Wang" (猶是王老師兒孫在), using Nanquan's surname Wang in the reply. In the Yongjia record, Xuanze says, "before Mighty-Sound King, it is acceptable; after Mighty-Sound King, awakening by oneself without a teacher is entirely the way of outsiders" (威音王已前即得，威音王已後無師自悟，盡是天然外道). Xuedou records "awakening by oneself without a teacher before Mighty-Sound King" as "the second phrase" (是第二句). A late Sanfeng record supplies an explicit internal gloss: "Mighty-Sound King is outside form and sound, not yet set out in records, without evidence to examine—the highest matter before writing" (威音王者，形聲之外，未有出載，無所考據，文字以前最上事也). This entry reports the proper name and the corpus's formulas without adding another framework.

Literally "enter the room" (入室); in the primary Chan institutional deployment, enter a master's chamber for a private question, examination, or report: "enter the chamber for an interview." The headword occurs 2,365 times in 313 allowlisted texts across both senses. Productive interview forms include "entered the chamber and asked" (入室問, 31), "entered the chamber and presented his understanding" (入室陳解, 3), "chamber-entering disciples" (入室弟子, 44), and "during a chamber interview" (入室次, 204). Huqiu Shaolong enters and is questioned by Yuanwu. Another biography records a student entering to present his understanding, followed by the teacher asking how he understands. Tianyi Yihuai is tested during a chamber interview. A lineage notice counts 139 "chamber-entering disciples" and says each became a lineage master in one region. A later case describes Ciming placing a sword, sandals, and a basin in the chamber and saying "look, look" whenever someone entered; those who hesitated by the sword were shouted out. The term names the institutional setting, access, and status; it does not by itself guarantee approval, succession, or a particular result.

Literally, 'solitary brightness.' The term occurs 243 times in 112 allowed texts. A sharp vocal cry: a shout. In Chan records it is a public-interview action available to both sides, not a sound reserved to masters. A master may shout at an arriving monk, a monk may shout and be struck, and the two head monks of Linji's halls shout simultaneously; Linji says host and guest are distinctly present in that encounter. Linji's record gives four explicit comparisons: a shout like the Diamond-King Treasure Sword, like a golden-haired lion crouching on the ground, like a probing pole and shadowing grass, and a shout not used as a shout. When the monk hesitates over them, Linji shouts. The Eye of Humans and Gods later states that a shout distinguishing host and guest has host and guest within it and that a shout carrying illumination and function has both within it. The public interview also judges rather than automatically ratifies a shout: after answering a question on the great purport with a shout, Linji asks whether it was a good shout, and the exchange continues through fault and repeated offense. Another instruction expressly tells the assembly not to shout blindly or shout at random. A recorded shout can have an immediate bodily effect—after Mazu's shout, Baizhang is said to have been deaf for three days—but the corpus does not assign that effect or any one result to every shout. The act also closes teaching-seat speech in the stage direction “shouted once and left the seat,” and lists of house devices pair Linji's shout with Deshan's staff. The ordinary baseline remains audible in the Puhua episode, where an officer cries out to clear the road and Puhua also cries out while making a wrestling gesture. These are all the same vocal act in different institutions and sentence positions. The longer compounds “cheer” (喝采), “shout abuse” (喝罵), and “clear the road by shouting” (喝道) must be translated as compounds; no allowlisted drinking use was established. | Allowlist count at the depth audit: 35,032 hits in 411 texts. High-frequency families include “one shout” (一喝), “shout once” (喝一喝), “the master then shouted” (師便喝), “the monk then shouted” (僧便喝), “four shouts” (四喝), “a shout not used as a shout” (一喝不作一喝用), and “staff and shout” (棒喝). Literally a “good knowing acquaintance,” this corpus-wide person label names a good teacher, guide, or good friend. The term occurs 2,832 times in 311 allowlisted texts. Dahui directly says, “those called good teachers guide all beings and cause them to see nature” (夫稱善知識者，引導一切眾生，令見佛性), then describes observing people's capacities and giving teaching as medicine matches illness. Another narrative has a student say, “a great good teacher is hard to encounter even across ages; now that I have met one, why begrudge body or life? | Dahui's role definition and Fohai's materially different answer are both retained, preventing an exclusively institutional or human-office definition. In the compound (音律), (律) denotes regulated sound, meter, or tonal pattern rather than a monastic code. A Chan verse says that an old tune is not reducible to musical regulation before turning to the South Mountain turtle-nosed snake; two major lamp compilations preserve that deployment. Literally, "on" or "upon" (上) the "lump of red flesh" (赤肉團): "on the lump of red flesh," attested 316 times in 144 allowlisted texts. Its most frequent named deployment quotes Linji: "on the lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, constantly going in and out through the face-gate of each of you; those who have not verified this, look, look" (赤肉團上有一無位真人，常在汝諸人面門出入，未證據者看看). In the institutional compound 'the two ranks' or 'the two divisions' (兩序), rank or division (序) names one of the two sides of a Chan community's offices. The Baizhang Regulations labels its sixth chapter 'the chapter on the two divisions' (兩序章), then identifies 'head monks of the western division' (西序頭首) and 'officers of the eastern division' (東序知事). Recorded sayings use 'the two divisions' for the office-holders who request an ascent to the hall, receive thanks, or support the community. Baiyu's record says that the two divisions served mutually as arms and elbows and acted reciprocally as host and guest (兩序交為肘臂、互作主賓).

A paired expression: ordinary feelings (凡情) and holy views (聖見). Caoshan's recorded statement supplies its defining deployment: ordinary feelings and holy views are the golden lock on the dark road and must turn back and forth (凡情聖見是金鎖玄路，直須回互). Later records preserve that statement, ask how the required interchange is accomplished without falling into one of Caoshan's three fallings (三種墮, 'three fallings'), say that the activity produced by ordinary feelings and holy views both ceases (凡情聖見所作俱息), or say that the two mutually interchange (凡情聖見共相回互). Another recorded address says there is no need to pick them away before naming cold as cold everywhere and heat as heat everywhere. These uses describe what the texts do with the pair without recasting it as a generic abstraction.

The corpus supplies several relations—distinct, intermingling, unconcerned, and together—without reducing them to one abstract theory.

#0g deviation: the compound is a Chan roster-word for an explicitly rejected blank, inert, object-denying identification. It is not defined here by meanings outside these recorded commands and contrasts; its sense comes from the record's commands, predicates, and contrasts. Headword count: 91 hits in 62 texts. The Zen deviation is the stable use of the dead animal as something said, quoted, held, discarded, or made alive in public teaching exchanges. The texts retain the concrete snake throughout; these are deployments of one image, not separate referents requiring a sense split. The family check found “live snake” (活蛇), “dead snake’s head” (死蛇頭), “handle a dead snake” (弄死蛇), and “make a dead snake live” (死蛇弄得活); all preserve the same object/action contrast.

Literally, "the road" or "course" (道) of "language and words" (言語) is "cut off" (斷): "the road of language is cut off," attested 171 times in 71 allowlisted texts. It is most often paired with "the place of mental activity is extinguished" (心行處滅, 128 occurrences); the unpunctuated full pair occurs 12 times and the punctuated pair 17 times. The Trust in Mind verse places it in "trust in mind is not two; not two is trust in mind; the road of language is cut off; it is not past, future, or present" (信心不二，不二信心，言語道斷，非去來今). A lamp record gives an explicit correction: closing the eyes and seeing nothing in the dark is not what is called "the road of language is cut off" (不是閉目藏睛、暗覩無所見喚作言語道斷). A later address first quotes "it cannot be known by wisdom and cannot be recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished," then answers, "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and mental activity is not extinguished" (亦可以智知，亦可以識識，言語道斷，心行不滅). Hongzhi asks directly, "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then? | Dahui quotes a correspondent who says that looking at a saying leaves "the road of language cut off and the place of mental activity extinguished, with no words to say and no principle to advance" (看此話，直得言語道斷心行處滅，無言可說，無理可伸); the following context is Dahui's reply to that report, so the quoted claim is not assigned to him. The exact collocation "close the eyes and hide the pupils" (閉目藏睛) occurs 29 times, but the lamp record explicitly rejects it as the definition here.

The same bare graph can name a physical buddha image rather than a person or title. The Record of the Chan Gate's Forged Reflections lists the twenty-fifth case as “Danxia burns a buddha” (丹霞燒佛). The corpus has 115 exact occurrences in 35 allowlisted files. Definition searches found a direct 'gradual refinement is...' formula in the Record of Refining Mind and explicit fourfold enumerations in the Chan Source preface and Record of the Mirror of the School. The term is frequently paired with sudden realization (頓悟漸修) and contrasted with sudden refinement (頓修). | All at once or sudden (頓), plus to awaken (悟): to awaken all at once. The Platform Record gives the line that one's own nature awakens of itself, sudden awakening and sudden refining, with no gradual steps (自性自悟，頓悟頓修，亦無漸次). Its standing contrast is gradual (漸). A lamp record explains 'Southern sudden, Northern gradual' (南頓北漸) as a difference in how people are led to awaken, not as original north and south labels within Chan (開導發悟有頓漸之異，故曰南頓北漸，非禪宗本有南北之號也). In encounter narratives it appears in the formula 'awakened all at once at the words' (言下頓悟), where a recorded statement immediately precedes the awakening. Later Chinese Chan records pair sudden and gradual across awakening and refining. The Record of the Source-Mirror gives four propositions: gradual refining and sudden awakening, sudden awakening and gradual refining, gradual refining and gradual awakening, and sudden awakening and sudden refining (漸修頓悟 / 頓悟漸修 / 漸修漸悟 / 頓悟頓修). Another pairing states that principle must be awakened to all at once while affairs are removed gradually (理須頓悟，事在漸除). A Chinese Chan succession chart defines the term by saying that turning from delusion to awakening is sudden and turning an ordinary person into a sage is sudden awakening (從迷而悟即頓，轉凡成聖即頓悟也), then describes beginningless confusion that takes the four elements as the body and deluded thinking as the mind. Dazhu Huihai's book title also preserves the term: Treatise on the Essential Gate of Entering the Way by Sudden Awakening (頓悟入道要門論). The allowlist count is 878 hits in 183 texts; 'awakened all at once at the words' (言下頓悟) occurs 57 times, 'sudden awakening and gradual refining' (頓悟漸修) 14, and 'sudden awakening and sudden refining' (頓悟頓修) 13. | A corpus-wide Chinese Chan term described through the sudden and gradual contrast (頓 / 漸). The entry distinguishes awakening all at once (頓悟) from refining all at once (頓修): the recorded phrase 'sudden awakening and gradual refining' (頓悟漸修) deliberately separates them. The evidence is limited to Chinese Chan texts and Chinese Chan discussions preserved in the allowlist.

In the institutional compound 'the two ranks' or 'the two divisions' (兩序), rank or division (序) names one of the two sides of a Chan community's offices. The Baizhang Regulations labels its sixth chapter 'the chapter on the two divisions' (兩序章), then identifies 'head monks of the western division' (西序頭首) and 'officers of the eastern division' (東序知事). Recorded sayings use 'the two divisions' for the office-holders who request an ascent to the hall, receive thanks, or support the community. Baiyu's record says that the two divisions served mutually as arms and elbows and acted reciprocally as host and guest (兩序交為肘臂、互作主賓).

Literally "dead water" (死水), attested 535 times in 180 allowlisted texts. The dominant fixed saying is "dead water does not conceal a dragon" (死水不藏龍, 80 occurrences). In Liangshan Yuanguan's exchange, that answer is immediately contrasted with "a dragon in living water" (活水龍), described as "raising swells without making waves" (興波不作浪). Yuanwu's Blue Cliff Record comment likewise contrasts using a place of living water with making one's livelihood in dead water (不向活水處用，自去死水裏作活計). Ying'an's recorded informal address places "dead water" in a text-drawn list with "a sweat-shirt stuck to the flesh," "a deep pit of release," "ink," and "clarity" (貼肉汗衫、解脫深坑、死水、墨汁、明白). Xueyan Zuqin explicitly calls one described condition "dead water soaking a stone, with never any share of waking or movement" (死水浸石頭，永無醒動底分子). Thus the corpus uses the phrase as a noun, in a proverb, in direct contrast with living water, and in critical appraisals; the entry reports those wordings without supplying an unstated significance. | The graph pair also has an ordinary literal use for water without current. Literally, “guest-dust”: dust characterized as a visitor rather than the host. Much of the corpus preserves it in the inherited compound “guest-dust troubles” (客塵煩惱), something said to stain, cover, or be unrecognized. The distinct Chan deployment appears in Baizhang Huaihai's recorded classification: “one's own mind is buddha; illuminating function belongs to bodhisattva; mind after mind is the ruler; illuminating function belongs to guest-dust” (自心是佛，照用屬菩薩；心心是主宰，照用屬客塵). Here “guest-dust” is not merely a name for dirt or an outside visitor; Baizhang places it on the “illuminating function” side of a ruler/guest classification and immediately compares it to speaking of water by way of waves (如波說水). The Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings and the Expanded Lamp preserve this wording independently. Elsewhere the Records say a grown child learns explanations and does not know that these are “guest-dust troubles” (不知是客塵煩惱); Dahui speaks of the “stain of guest-dust troubles since beginningless time” (無始時來客塵煩惱之染); and the Admonitions for the Monastic Gate has the compact bodily compound “body-and-mind guest-dust” (身心客塵). The Zen record therefore keeps the inherited dust imagery but also bends it into Baizhang's explicit ruler/function classification.

Literally the body's or person-shaped term (身) formed with "teaching, standard, or law" (法): here, "teaching-body," attested 6,058 times in 376 allowlisted texts. This English target follows the Chan record's own comparisons rather than importing a glossary definition. Qianyan places three word explanations together: a robe displays the teaching and so is a "teaching-robe" (法衣); "a person can enlarge the Way, therefore it is called teaching-body" (人能宏道，故謂之法身); and being everywhere and clear is called the "teaching-eye" (法眼). Other records give deliberately different predicates. Weilin calls it "each person's originally present own nature" (當人本有之自性). Huanglong says, "the teaching-body has no form; responding to things, it manifests form" (法身無相，應物現形), then raises his whisk and calls that the teaching-body before laughing. A Five Lamps exchange answers the question with "a flower in the sky, a heat shimmer" (空華陽焰). The Ancestral Hall Collection answers it by repeating that "all activities are the teaching-body's function" (一切施為，盡是法身用). | The corpus does not reduce the word to one theoretical proposition. It asks about the teaching-body, its "function" (法身用), its "side" (法身邊), and "the matter beyond the teaching-body" (法身向上事). The Old Venerables Record even says the teaching-body has "two kinds of illness" (法身兩般病): reaching it while attachment to the standard remains, with one's own view still present and sitting at its side, is the first. Literally, "the road" or "course" (道) of "language and words" (言語) is "cut off" (斷): "the road of language is cut off," attested 171 times in 71 allowlisted texts. It is most often paired with "the place of mental activity is extinguished" (心行處滅, 128 occurrences); the unpunctuated full pair occurs 12 times and the punctuated pair 17 times. The Trust in Mind verse places it in "trust in mind is not two; not two is trust in mind; the road of language is cut off; it is not past, future, or present" (信心不二，不二信心，言語道斷，非去來今). A later address first quotes "it cannot be known by wisdom and cannot be recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished," then answers, "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and mental activity is not extinguished" (亦可以智知，亦可以識識，言語道斷，心行不滅). Literally, a straight or straightforward mind. The term occurs 163 times in 89 allowed texts. The corpus supplies two compact definitions: 'straight mind means without bends or twists' (直心者，無委曲故), and 'straight mind is the site of the Way because it has no falseness' (直心是道場，無虛假故). The Platform Record repeats 'straight mind is the site; straight mind is the clean land' (直心是道場，直心是淨土), then contrasts inwardly acting crookedly while verbally speaking straight with actually carrying out straight mind. Its positive clause is 'only carry out straight mind; regarding all things, have no grasping' (但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著). Another address expands the pattern into four coordinated expressions: 'straight mind is the site; straight speech is the subtle teaching; straight conduct is subtle conduct; straight verification is the subtle result' (直心是道場，直說是妙法，直行是妙行，直證是妙果). The common collocation 'straight mind and straight conduct' (直心直行) occurs 22 times in 16 texts. One record describes it by the absence of self-versus-other, right-versus-wrong, falseness, and crookedness; another uses 'straight mind, straight conduct, original color, original share' (直心直行，本色本分) to characterize a master's meetings with people.

Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?

Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" (擔雪填井): the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it" (拈來便用), to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger" (談玄說妙，畫餅充饑), and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle" (證龜成鱉). Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball (捏雪成團). Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing (吹網欲滿) and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific deployment is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.

Literally to issue into brightness: to bring something to light or make it clear. The term occurs 1,304 times in 250 allowlisted texts. Chan biographies repeatedly say that someone brings “the great matter,” “the mind-ground,” or “the essentials of mind” to light. The technical name of the Caodong house's signature scheme, created by Dongshan Liangjie and systematized by Caoshan Benji. 'Five' configurations arrange two terms — the upright or straight (正) and the crooked or bent (偏) — as: crooked within the upright (正中偏), upright within the crooked (偏中正), coming from within the upright (正中來), arriving from both together (兼中至 / 偏中至), attained in both together (兼中到). The same five are recast as ruler and minister (君臣, the 君臣五位); Dongshan also taught parallel fivefold sets — the five ranks of merit/achievement (功勳五位) and the five ranks of princes (王子五位) — and Caoshan's 'five ranks facing the guest' (五位對賓) works them into interview form ('I come from the crooked position, please receive me into the upright'). Across the corpus the term functions as the emblem of the Caodong house, almost always named in one breath with its Linji-house counterpart, the three mysteries (and three essentials) (臨濟三玄（三要）) — 'Dongshan's five ranks / Linji's three mysteries' (洞山五位／臨濟三玄), 'not Linji's three mysteries, not Caodong's five ranks' (不是臨濟三玄不是曹洞五位) — so that 'the Five Ranks' effectively names the Caodong house the way 'three mysteries' names the Linji house. The scheme is defined inside the house's own records. Dongshan's record has him compose the verses: 'The master composed the verses on the five ranks of ruler and minister: Crooked within the upright — the third watch, early in the night, before the moon shines; no wonder that meeting they do not recognize each other, dimly still harboring the old days' estrangement' (師。 | 君臣道合是兼帶語) (T47n1987A, the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Caoshan Yuanzheng of Fuzhou (撫州曹山元證禪師語錄); the 'ruler = the upright position' (君為正位) mapping recurs 11 times, incl. T47n1987B and the Eye of Humans and Gods 人天眼目 T48n2006). The Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目) also glosses each fivefold set: 'the five ranks of merit clarify the stages of effort in study, up to the stage beyond effort; the five ranks of ruler and minister clarify the conditioned and the unconditioned; the five ranks of princes clarify that inward succession is originally complete of itself, while outward succession has an end and a beginning; roughly, the Caodong house style is nothing beyond substance/function, upright/crooked, host/guest, to clarify the road going beyond' (功勳五位者。

In a separate literal and contrastive classification, the compound denotes a monk characterized as consuming the community's gruel and rice without the activity set against it. An official asks whether Weishan's assembly consists of “monks who eat gruel and rice” or “monks who investigate Chan” (喫粥飯僧 / 參禪僧); Weishan rejects both offered categories. Xiangyan says that he will cease studying the buddha teaching and become such a monk, sparing his mind the labor. Later records reuse the same eat-versus-study contrast. Here the headword classifies a monk by meal consumption, not by the non-abbatial institutional identity in the primary sense.

Literally, "meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch" (逢祖殺祖). Linji's surviving record places it inside a five-member roster: "meet buddha, kill buddha; meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; meet an arhat, kill the arhat; meet parents, kill parents; meet kin, kill kin" (逢佛殺佛、逢祖殺祖、逢羅漢殺羅漢、逢父母殺父母、逢親眷殺親眷). This is the Chan bend: the honored religious and familial titles become the grammatical objects of the same repeated verb, and later masters preserve, question, and redeploy that severe roster. A successor record explicitly asks why a good teacher would want to kill people after quoting the three religious members, without supplying a prose gloss. Later uses attach the phrase to a sharp sword, place it opposite "carry the infant and encourage the child" (提攜赤子，撫獎嬰兒) in a contrast about grandmotherly kindness, or quote it in a New Year's address before comments on lineage descent. The records use killing language literally in the formula but do not record bodily killings in these deployments; this entry adds no symbolic object behind the named roster.

(2) The Nanquan (南泉普願)–Zhaozhou (趙州從諗) dialogue: (趙州問南泉)。

To address or instruct the assembled community publicly. The term occurs 12,002 times in 399 allowlisted texts and is a standard discourse heading beside the formal hall address (上堂) and small convocation (小參): a master “addresses the assembly, saying” (示眾云/曰), sometimes after ascending the seat. The corpus groups the formal hall address (上堂) and address to the assembly (示眾) as public formats and compares a small convocation with an address to the assembly. It can be delivered in writing as a verse after the assembly answers a question. The format also includes final instructions (臨終示眾), as when Luopu begins by asking the assembly about one matter. Chan turns “show to the assembly” into a recurring name for the master’s public verbal address; it is not a private exchange.

Literally, “stir a thought and at once deviate.” The phrase's Zen-specific deployment is a compact verdict and answer, frequently paired with “form an intention and at once err” (擬心即差), but the corpus explicitly refuses to turn its negative wording into mere mental stillness. Huangbo says, “it is just this; stir a thought and at once deviate” (當體便是，動念即乖), then compares what he has described to measureless space. Linji pairs “form an intention and at once err” with the headword and immediately continues with the person who understands not being apart from what is before the eyes (不離目前). Shimen Cizhao quotes the pair and adds: “not intending and not moving, one is doing business in dead water” (不擬不動，正在死水裏作活計). Huanglong Huinan gives the parallel correction: “not intending and not moving is no different from wood and earth; a traveling monk must obtain a turning phrase” (不擬不動，土木無殊，行脚人須得轉身一句). Literally (拈) 'to pick up / hold up (between the fingers)' + (古) 'the old [ones]', i.e. (古則) / (公案), old cases: 'picking up the old cases.' It names a commentarial genre and a standard section of a master's record — a master takes up (舉) a recorded old case and adds a prose remark (his 拈, typically marked 師拈云). The corpus enumerates it inside a family of old-case commentary forms — X67n1307: (古來有拈古)、(頌古)、(徵古)、(代古)、(別古) ('from of old there have been niangu, songgu [verse], zhenggu [interrogating], daigu [substituting], biegu [alternating]') — and it is standardly paired with, and distinct from, (頌古) ('versifying the old cases,' verse comment): a master's record files (拈古) and (頌古) as separate juan (T47n1997, 圓悟佛果禪師語錄, runs 拈古上/中/下 then 頌古; B25n0145, 中峰廣錄, 卷第三拈古頌古). Whole anthologies collect them (X66n1296 宗門拈古彙集, 'Collected Niangu of the [Chan] School'), and a further commentary layer (評唱) can be built on a master's (拈古) — Wansong Xingxiu's (評唱) on Tiantong (Hongzhi) Zhengjue's (拈古) is the (請益錄) (X67n1307). As an act it is countable (B27n0152: 呈拈古十餘則, 'presented a dozen niangu') and attached to a master's name (B27n0152: 余閱雪竇拈古, 'I read Xuedou's niangu'). The same act of taking up cases for comment is also called (拈提) (354 hits / 142 files): (拈提公案如雪竇老真可謂與古人心心相契) ('in taking up cases, old Xuedou can truly be said to be mind-to-mind with the ancients') and (者個公案叢林中少有拈提者) ('few in the monasteries have taken this case up'), both B27n0152. | Genre term, corpus-wide; no master bends the meaning, so a single sense. Literally, open (開) the mouth (口) and immediately or already (即) be wrong (錯): "open your mouth and you are already wrong." The phrase occurs 43 times in 34 allowlisted texts; the variant "open your mouth and it is then wrong" (開口便錯) occurs 13 times in 10. Its early defining exchange has a monk ask Dabe to speak apart from removing the upper and taking away the lower. Dabe answers, "when I open my mouth I am already wrong" (我開口即錯). The monk calls him truly his teacher; Dabe replies, "today I died in the disciple's hands" (今日向弟子手裏死), so the record shows the verdict catching the speaker's own utterance. Later masters make it a portable paired formula: Po'an says, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; aim the mind and you immediately miss" (開口即錯，擬心即差). Other records pair it with "move a thought and immediately go against" (動念即乖). Wuzhun states the closed-mouth counterpart, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; close your mouth and you are already lost," then asks how communication is possible apart from opening and not opening (開口即錯，閉口即喪，不開不合，十萬八千). The phrase also becomes an encounter instruction: Baishan tells a monk, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; move a thought and immediately go against; leave these two roads and speak quickly!

inherited_lead: The three graphs form an established phonetic borrowing, rendered here as 'complete command'; the Chan corpus determines its usable content through named compounds and direct definitions. The term occurs 4,852 times in 382 allowed texts. Huineng defines 'complete command of the single conduct' as 'at every place, while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, always carry one straight mind' (一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，常行一直心是也). The same address rejects the claim that 'not raising thought while constantly sitting unmoving is complete command of the single conduct' (常坐不動，妄不起心，即是一行三昧), saying that this understanding is like the insentient and blocks the Way. Mazu's record says that thought after thought becoming still is called 'complete command of the ocean seal,' which 'takes in all things as a hundred thousand different streams return together to the great sea' (喚作海印三昧攝一切法如百千異流同歸大海). It also says beings remain within 'complete command of the nature of the teaching' while dressing, eating, speaking, responding, using the six sense-roots, and carrying out every action (法性三昧中著衣喫飯言談祇對六根運用一切施為). Xuansha says that buddhas are people's 'self-receiving complete command' and that walking, standing, sitting, and lying down have never not been it; when asked what that complete command is, he replies, 'What use are so many modes of complete command?

Literally, the "gate and court" established for teaching or transformation. Chan records use it for the organized framework of explanations and responsive teaching, then explicitly place it below what questioners call the matter beyond or above it. One monk says, "one question and one answer still fall within the teaching establishment's gate and court" (一問一答猶落建化門庭) and asks how to raise the first principle. A sermon supplies a direct apposition: even a shout said to contain all these features "is still the teaching establishment's gate and court—responsive expedients—called a small resting place, not yet the treasure-site" (猶是建化門庭隨機方便，謂之小歇場，未至寶所). Another says that even holding the seal, raising the banner, and moving freely still falls within it and "is not yet the monk's essential road" (未為衲僧徑要一路). The Chan-specific use is evaluative and institutional: masters name their own question-and-answer and explanatory apparatus as a constructed teaching precinct, commonly in a contrast the texts themselves draw with what is "beyond or above" (向上) or the monk's essential road.

The corpus contains five occurrences of 'the teaching has no sudden and gradual' (法無頓漸). | All at once or sudden (頓), plus to awaken (悟): to awaken all at once. The Platform Record gives the line that one's own nature awakens of itself, sudden awakening and sudden refining, with no gradual steps (自性自悟，頓悟頓修，亦無漸次). Its standing contrast is gradual (漸). A lamp record explains 'Southern sudden, Northern gradual' (南頓北漸) as a difference in how people are led to awaken, not as original north and south labels within Chan (開導發悟有頓漸之異，故曰南頓北漸，非禪宗本有南北之號也). In encounter narratives it appears in the formula 'awakened all at once at the words' (言下頓悟), where a recorded statement immediately precedes the awakening. Later Chinese Chan records pair sudden and gradual across awakening and refining. The Record of the Source-Mirror gives four propositions: gradual refining and sudden awakening, sudden awakening and gradual refining, gradual refining and gradual awakening, and sudden awakening and sudden refining (漸修頓悟 / 頓悟漸修 / 漸修漸悟 / 頓悟頓修). Another pairing states that principle must be awakened to all at once while affairs are removed gradually (理須頓悟，事在漸除). A Chinese Chan succession chart defines the term by saying that turning from delusion to awakening is sudden and turning an ordinary person into a sage is sudden awakening (從迷而悟即頓，轉凡成聖即頓悟也), then describes beginningless confusion that takes the four elements as the body and deluded thinking as the mind. Dazhu Huihai's book title also preserves the term: Treatise on the Essential Gate of Entering the Way by Sudden Awakening (頓悟入道要門論). The allowlist count is 878 hits in 183 texts; 'awakened all at once at the words' (言下頓悟) occurs 57 times, 'sudden awakening and gradual refining' (頓悟漸修) 14, and 'sudden awakening and sudden refining' (頓悟頓修) 13. | A corpus-wide Chinese Chan term described through the sudden and gradual contrast (頓 / 漸). The entry distinguishes awakening all at once (頓悟) from refining all at once (頓修): the recorded phrase 'sudden awakening and gradual refining' (頓悟漸修) deliberately separates them. The evidence is limited to Chinese Chan texts and Chinese Chan discussions preserved in the allowlist.

Literally, not (不) one inch of thread (寸絲) hanging or attached (掛): "not a thread hanging." This graph form occurs 59 times in 43 allowlisted texts; the variant with the simplified hanging graph (寸絲不挂) occurs 97 times in 57 texts, and the reversal "not hanging one thread" (不掛寸絲) occurs 14 times in 14 texts. Chan records make the clothing image into a repeatedly tested claim. When Xuanji answers Xuefeng's weaving question, "not a thread hanging," Xuefeng calls after him that the corner of his robe is dragging; Xuanji turns his head and Xuefeng strikes him, saying, "a fine 'not a thread hanging'!

Literally, a wooden man or wooden figure. The term occurs 940 times in 231 allowlisted texts. Chan verse and teaching-seat speech repeatedly make the inert figure perform human acts: it beckons, speaks, sings, dances, claps a board in the clouds, embroiders a flowered cap at midnight, and converses with the stone woman. One exchange says, 'The wooden man always replies; one with nature cannot speak.' The most stable family pairing is wooden man and stone woman (木人石女), and the pair are made to speak, gesture, sew, sing, or dance. This is where the corpus bends the ordinary object: the impossible acting figure is a stock Chan poetic speaker and actor. The entry records that deployment without assigning a hidden referent to it.

Literally, a straight or straightforward mind. The term occurs 163 times in 89 allowed texts. The corpus supplies two compact definitions: 'straight mind means without bends or twists' (直心者，無委曲故), and 'straight mind is the site of the Way because it has no falseness' (直心是道場，無虛假故). The Platform Record repeats 'straight mind is the site; straight mind is the clean land' (直心是道場，直心是淨土), then contrasts inwardly acting crookedly while verbally speaking straight with actually carrying out straight mind. Its positive clause is 'only carry out straight mind; regarding all things, have no grasping' (但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著). Another address expands the pattern into four coordinated expressions: 'straight mind is the site; straight speech is the subtle teaching; straight conduct is subtle conduct; straight verification is the subtle result' (直心是道場，直說是妙法，直行是妙行，直證是妙果). The common collocation 'straight mind and straight conduct' (直心直行) occurs 22 times in 16 texts. One record describes it by the absence of self-versus-other, right-versus-wrong, falseness, and crookedness; another uses 'straight mind, straight conduct, original color, original share' (直心直行，本色本分) to characterize a master's meetings with people.

Literally, open (開) the mouth (口) and immediately or already (即) be wrong (錯): "open your mouth and you are already wrong." The phrase occurs 43 times in 34 allowlisted texts; the variant "open your mouth and it is then wrong" (開口便錯) occurs 13 times in 10. Its early defining exchange has a monk ask Dabe to speak apart from removing the upper and taking away the lower. Dabe answers, "when I open my mouth I am already wrong" (我開口即錯). The monk calls him truly his teacher; Dabe replies, "today I died in the disciple's hands" (今日向弟子手裏死), so the record shows the verdict catching the speaker's own utterance. Later masters make it a portable paired formula: Po'an says, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; aim the mind and you immediately miss" (開口即錯，擬心即差). Other records pair it with "move a thought and immediately go against" (動念即乖). Wuzhun states the closed-mouth counterpart, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; close your mouth and you are already lost," then asks how communication is possible apart from opening and not opening (開口即錯，閉口即喪，不開不合，十萬八千). The phrase also becomes an encounter instruction: Baishan tells a monk, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; move a thought and immediately go against; leave these two roads and speak quickly!

Knowing (知) joined to interpreting or explaining (解): intellectual understanding, or knowing reached through explanation. The corpus overwhelmingly uses the term as a rebuke or warning. Its flagship form is 'a follower of the intellectual-understanding lineage' (知解宗徒, 35 occurrences), a label applied to Shenhui and Guifeng Zongmi: even Shenhui and Guifeng were rejected as followers of intellectual understanding (神會、圭峰尚斥為知解宗徒). In an origin case, a student names the matter 'Buddha-nature at the original source' (本源佛性), and the master says that even if this fellow later founds a place, he will become only a follower of intellectual understanding (此子已後設有把茅蓋頭，只成得箇知解宗徒). Another passage puts a whole list of teaching styles under the same verdict (此等見解盡屬知解宗徒). The common gate-entry warning 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) occurs 80 times. Its continuation says that when intellectual understanding does not arise, one is like the king's sword, killing or giving life according to the occasion (知解既不生，如王寶劍，殺活臨時). Other records say people are deceived by intellectual understanding and conjecture (多被知解卜度瞞過), or that the matter is not an affair on the side of intellectual understanding (不是知解邊事). The headword occurs 1,044 times in 215 allowlist texts. This entry reports the corpus's repeated pejorative deployment without turning it into a general theory of mind. The Huangbo record extends the term through a food-and-digestion comparison stated by the text: after calling the students' condition 'food not digested' (食不消), it says, 'what is called intellectual understanding not digested is all poison' (所謂知解不消。

The phrase occurs more than one thousand times across more than two hundred allowlisted texts. The Deshan–Yantou case recurs across independent records, while the bare challenge and death or memorial uses have their own spread. The former “last word” and “master's last word at death” targets described a general phrase and a contextual subtype of that same phrase; they are merged. Compare the way up and beyond (向上一路), upward dynamic (向上機), last locked barrier (末後牢關), turning phrase (轉身句), late master's last word (先師末後句), memorial morning (忌晨), and dying seated or standing (坐脫立亡).

The close variant “to miss it directly face-to-face” (當面蹉過) occurs 158 times in 65 files. “To miss it right before one” (覿面錯過) occurs 12 times in 11 files, and “to miss it before the eyes” (眼前錯過) occurs three times in three files. The entry translates the observable spatial and verbal shape; it does not supply an object where the text leaves that object unstated.
The fixed physical-description phrase broad forehead and full cheeks (廣額豐頤) has 2 hits in 2 allowlisted texts. Both are anchored; neither passage concerns the butcher.

The Zen deviation is the invoked figure's deployment as a recurring public-interview question and as a designation applied to a raised teaching-seat implement. “The thousand hands and eyes” (千手眼), “Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes” (大悲千手眼), and “the hundred-thousand hands and eyes” (百千手眼) retain one figure/image across noun phrase, question, verse, and demonstration, so no split is warranted.

Event phrase, attributive person-label, and poetic heading all retain the same cold-ash image. They do not name different things. The family comparison with “dead ashes” (死灰), “cold ashes” (寒灰), and “a withered tree flowers” (枯木開花) supports the contrast visible in the passages but not an imported psychological explanation.

Literally, "ten oxen." As a Chan title and label, it denotes Liangshan Kuoan's ordered set of ox-herding verses and the pictures made from them. A collection titles the work "Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses" (梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌); another record says, "our school has the account of herding the ox, and Liangshan has the verses on the Ten Oxen" (我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌). The sequence begins with named sections including "seeking the ox" (尋牛) and "seeing the tracks" (見跡). The corpus also records direct criticism of its later handling: Baichi calls Liangshan's verses "compassionate, talk that descends into the weeds" (慈悲之故，落草之談), says later people "made a wrong move and then painted these Ten-Ox forms" (錯下手腳，更畫此十牛樣子), and urges burning them. In an encounter, a teacher interrupts a monk asked to recite the verses and asks, "Where is the ox?

181 occurrences in 103 allowlisted texts. Nominal compounds such as "an eye for testing people" (驗人眼) and "a barrier for testing people" (驗人關) retain the same testing act and do not require a separate sense.

Literally "without" (無) "marks, appearance, or form" (相): "without marks" or "markless," attested within 2,588 total occurrences across 324 allowlisted texts. Huineng's Platform Record gives a direct definition: "markless means being among marks while apart from marks" (無相者，於相而離相). It also says the teaching establishes "marklessness as its body" (無相為體, 11 occurrences). A later small assembly quotes that three-part formula and asks why marklessness is not also made the source. In a Compendium encounter, a monk asks, "what is without marks?

Allowlist count: 99 hits in 42 texts. One speech-category sense. The texts' contrary appraisals do not create separate referents. Family checked against dead phrase (死句), live phrase (活句), live saying (活語), dead teaching (死法), and dead words and dead sayings (死言死語).

The pair also names the objects as passed evidence of succession. The corpus records ‘transmit the robe and bowl’ (傳衣鉢, 31 hits in 26 texts), ‘entrust the robe and bowl’ (付衣鉢, 10 hits in 8 texts), and one exact occurrence of ‘robe and bowl transmitted in succession’ (衣鉢相傳). The Dayu Ridge account explicitly calls the robe ‘a token of trust.’ Later addresses say that Huangmei’s robe and bowl were entrusted to Lu, while another asks which robe and bowl Lu actually transmitted. The question is recorded as a question rather than resolved here into an object different from the material robe and bowl.

The headword has 1,075 hits in 264 allowlisted texts. Headings, numbered sets, anthologies, prefaces, and composition predicates establish one concrete Chan literary genre. The former result/act targets were grammatical views of the same verse and could not be distinguished as different referents from the targets alone. Compare picking up old cases (拈古), old cases (古則), public cases (公案), and appraisal-commentary (評唱).

In ordination accounts the same title names the person from whom someone receives the precepts, a different office from the teaching master. Biographical sequences distinguish the roles explicitly: one nun "first shaved her head at Wanyuan Cloister, investigated under Guixi Zhuang, then received the precepts from Preceptor Baochi, and finally heard the teaching from Old Man Yi'an" (初披剃於萬緣寺，參學於桂谿莊，繼受戒於寶池和尚，終聞法於易菴老人). Another record separates "listening to the teaching under Teacher Buye" from "receiving the precepts from Preceptor Yulin" (聽教於不夜天師、受戒於玉林和尚). The office is also named directly: a woman asks "Preceptor Ruo'an of Louze to serve as the preceptor from whom she received the precepts" (乞漏澤箬菴和尚為得戒師), while incense verses honor a "preceptor from whom the precepts were received" (得戒和尚) alongside the distinct tonsure teachers. This is a precept-family deployment of the title: it identifies the human conferrer in an ordination relation, not merely a respectful reading of the teaching-master sense. | Do not infer this sense from every occurrence of “precept/Master Jie” (戒和尚). In early lamp records that sequence often means “Master Jie,” where Jie is a personal name, especially Wuzu Jie. The verified line “arrived at Master Wuzu Jie” (到五祖戒和尚處) is a teacher-name use, not ordination. Assign the preceptor sense only when receiving or conferring precepts, the explicit title “preceptor from whom the precepts were received” (得戒和尚), or an equivalent role statement supplies the relation.

Unsplit string: 136 hits in 72 allowlisted texts, substantially including proper names and places. Purple Fungus Song (紫芝歌) has 20 hits in 18 texts; Four Hoaryheads of Mount Shang (商山四皓) 9 in 8; gather purple fungus (採紫芝) 1 in 1. Zizhi-named lineage figures belong on the roster, while Purple-Fungus Hermitage (紫芝菴) and Purple-Fungus Crag (紫芝巖) are place compounds; they are excluded from the lexical sense rather than blurred into it.

The paired graphs mean to wander or roam at ease. In a lamp narrative, Tianhuang tells Longtan, “roam at ease according to your nature and range freely following conditions; exhaust the ordinary mind, with no other superior understanding” (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). An Ancestral Hall narrative describes someone “delighting in clouds and waters, roaming at ease whether going or staying” (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Productive forms include “roam at ease and be unbound” (逍遙自在), “range freely and roam at ease” (放曠逍遙), and “roam at ease according to one's nature” (任性逍遙).

The graphs name a robe and an alms bowl. The allowlisted corpus has 513 hits in 115 texts, including records in which the objects are thrown onto a rock, lifted, carried, guarded, inventoried, or burned with a person’s other implements. Monastic regulations also name a ‘robe-and-bowl attendant’ (衣鉢侍者, 9 hits in 3 texts), who receives the seal in one installation procedure. In the Caoqi record, this attendant raises the robe associated with the object that could not be lifted at Dayu Ridge. These passages keep the material objects and their custodial office visible even where the same pair also marks succession.

In its primary Zen-loaded use, Handan names the imitator in the stock verdict “Handan learns the Tang gait” (邯鄲學唐步), attested 43 times in 31 allowlisted files; the shorter “learn the Handan gait” (邯鄲學步) occurs eight times in seven. Jingqing applies the verdict when a monk walks away after being asked how he understands Zhaozhou’s “drink tea”; Xuedou then asks, “this monk is not a Handan man—why does he learn the Tang gait?

Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" (擔雪填井): the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it" (拈來便用), to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger" (談玄說妙，畫餅充饑), and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle" (證龜成鱉). Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball (捏雪成團). Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing (吹網欲滿) and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific deployment is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.

Literally, polishing or grinding (磨) a tile or brick (磚) to make (作) a mirror (鏡): "polishing a tile to make a mirror." This graph form occurs 43 times in 37 allowlisted texts. Graphic variants include "polishing a tile to make a mirror" (磨甎作鏡, 19 hits in 13 texts) and the form with another tile graph (磨塼作鏡, 5 in 5); "polishing a tile into a mirror" (磨磚成鏡) occurs 8 times in 5. In the defining encounter, Mazu Daoyi is sitting Chan to become a buddha. Nan'yue Huairang polishes a tile; asked why, he says he is making a mirror. Mazu says, "how could polishing a tile make a mirror?

The headword clusters with "pass through the final locked barrier" (透末後牢關, 7 occurrences), "break free through the final locked barrier" (透脫末後牢關), and the shorter "final checkpoint" (末後一關, 8). The related line "only with the final sentence does one first reach the locked barrier" (末後一句始到牢關, 54) explains the compound's final-position force without itself containing the exact four-graph headword.

Bian He is the pre-Chan jade-bearer whom the corpus invokes through the uncut-jade story. The name occurs 78 times in 47 allowlisted texts. The Book of Serenity retells the defining event: Bian He found an uncut stone in a valley of Mount Jing, offered it to King Li of Chu, was told it was stone, and had one foot cut off. Chan interviews compress the story into answers such as “white jade without flaw; Bian He has his foot cut off” (白玉無瑕，卞和刖足). A student explicitly adopts the role by saying, “I bring the uncut jade to the master and ask the master to carve and polish it”; when the master refuses it as beam material, the student says, “then Bian He has nowhere to emerge” (卞和無出身處). Yuanwu’s verse names the repeated offering and its cost: “laughable, Bian He presents the jade three times; even if honored, both feet are cut off” (卞和三獻玉，縱榮刖却一雙足). Another verse draws its own comparison: “Mount Jing’s fine jade—why discern it?

Literally, "brows intertwined with one another." The phrase occurs 129 times in 80 allowlisted texts. The records use the bodily image for persons brought into exceptionally close conjunction: one master says that for five or six years he has had his brows intertwined with the assembly, yet in fact they have had "no traffic in rice or water" (五六年來雖則與諸人眉毛廝結，其實水米無交). Another requires "brows intertwined, sharing life and sharing death" (眉毛廝結，同生同死). It also appears as an answer in a public interview: asked for the phrase for opening the retreat, the master replies, "brows intertwined" (眉毛廝結). Elsewhere a hall address sets saying and silence against each other: "if one speaks, heaven and earth are far apart; if one does not speak, brows are intertwined" (說即天地懸殊，不說即眉毛廝結). The Chan use turns a physical impossibility into a compact, repeatable encounter phrase; the accompanying clauses establish proximity or conjunction but do not authorize this entry to decide what speakers intend by it.

Literally, “take the road and return home.” The Zen bend is visible in the corpus's repeated reversals and pairings: the phrase is a stock Chan verdict for a person's handling of what is already under discussion, yet the records deny that its homeward journey is an ordinary change of location. One record says that even if someone speaks of “turning back with mastery and taking the road home,” it is “a thousand miles and ten thousand miles” away (回途得妙，就路還家，便是千里萬里). Another sets “take the road and return home” against “leave home and take the road” (離家就路), then says that leaving does not move an inch and returning has no bodily image. Wuyi Yuanlai explicitly pairs it with “turn around and return to the father” (轉身歸父). Shiyu Mingfang applies the phrase three times to actual travel stages—leaving Jinze by boat, passing Jiaxing and Chongde, and reaching Fojih monastery—so the literal journey remains available inside the stock expression. Juelang Sheng calls “responding to the occasion and benefiting beings; taking the road and returning home” (因機利物，就路還家) the staff-bearer's ordinary occupation, alongside “meeting conditions and acting as host” (遇緣作主) as his own-house style. The corpus therefore bends a homeward-road idiom into a recurring Chan appraisal while also recording literal journeys and explicit counter-journeys.

A doubled imperative: "rest" or "stop" (休去) and "cease" or "settle" (歇去): "rest; cease," attested 123 times in 68 allowlisted texts. Shishuang's recorded sequence expands it: "rest; cease; let one thought last ten thousand years; become cold ashes and a withered tree; become an incense burner in an old shrine; become one strip of white silk; become cold and still" (休去歇去、一念萬年去、寒灰枯木去、古廟香爐去、一條白練去、冷秋秋地去). Yunfeng supplies a contrary sequence beginning "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), and a later speaker refuses both lists. Dahui reports people sitting slack-jawed and calling that "resting and ceasing" (一向嘴盧都地打坐，謂之休去歇去), in an extended criticism. Zhongfeng likewise reports people citing "do not fantasize, put it down, old-shrine incense burner, rest and cease" as evidence, and compares that use to waiting by a stump for a rabbit. Other records retain the literal instruction: a teacher says, "from now on, rest; cease" (自今以往，休去歇去), while Dafang Yin asks, "why not rest and cease? | Counted companions: "one thought for ten thousand years" (一念萬年去), 115; "cold and still" (冷湫湫地去), 48; "old-shrine incense burner" (古廟香爐去), 72; "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), 5. Orthography varies between "cold autumn-like" and "cold and still" in witnesses. The sole late naming formula is excluded because its surrounding sentence applies the words to a different labeled expression, whereas the older imperatives and their recorded criticisms bear the headword directly.

All at once or sudden (頓), plus to awaken (悟): to awaken all at once. The Platform Record gives the line that one's own nature awakens of itself, sudden awakening and sudden refining, with no gradual steps (自性自悟，頓悟頓修，亦無漸次). Its standing contrast is gradual (漸). A lamp record explains 'Southern sudden, Northern gradual' (南頓北漸) as a difference in how people are led to awaken, not as original north and south labels within Chan (開導發悟有頓漸之異，故曰南頓北漸，非禪宗本有南北之號也). In encounter narratives it appears in the formula 'awakened all at once at the words' (言下頓悟), where a recorded statement immediately precedes the awakening. Later Chinese Chan records pair sudden and gradual across awakening and refining. The Record of the Source-Mirror gives four propositions: gradual refining and sudden awakening, sudden awakening and gradual refining, gradual refining and gradual awakening, and sudden awakening and sudden refining (漸修頓悟 / 頓悟漸修 / 漸修漸悟 / 頓悟頓修). Another pairing states that principle must be awakened to all at once while affairs are removed gradually (理須頓悟，事在漸除). A Chinese Chan succession chart defines the term by saying that turning from delusion to awakening is sudden and turning an ordinary person into a sage is sudden awakening (從迷而悟即頓，轉凡成聖即頓悟也), then describes beginningless confusion that takes the four elements as the body and deluded thinking as the mind. Dazhu Huihai's book title also preserves the term: Treatise on the Essential Gate of Entering the Way by Sudden Awakening (頓悟入道要門論). The allowlist count is 878 hits in 183 texts; 'awakened all at once at the words' (言下頓悟) occurs 57 times, 'sudden awakening and gradual refining' (頓悟漸修) 14, and 'sudden awakening and sudden refining' (頓悟頓修) 13.

A sharp vocal cry: a shout. In Chan records it is a public-interview action available to both sides, not a sound reserved to masters. A master may shout at an arriving monk, a monk may shout and be struck, and the two head monks of Linji's halls shout simultaneously; Linji says host and guest are distinctly present in that encounter. Linji's record gives four explicit comparisons: a shout like the Diamond-King Treasure Sword, like a golden-haired lion crouching on the ground, like a probing pole and shadowing grass, and a shout not used as a shout. When the monk hesitates over them, Linji shouts. The Eye of Humans and Gods later states that a shout distinguishing host and guest has host and guest within it and that a shout carrying illumination and function has both within it. The public interview also judges rather than automatically ratifies a shout: after answering a question on the great purport with a shout, Linji asks whether it was a good shout, and the exchange continues through fault and repeated offense. Another instruction expressly tells the assembly not to shout blindly or shout at random. A recorded shout can have an immediate bodily effect—after Mazu's shout, Baizhang is said to have been deaf for three days—but the corpus does not assign that effect or any one result to every shout. The act also closes teaching-seat speech in the stage direction “shouted once and left the seat,” and lists of house devices pair Linji's shout with Deshan's staff. The ordinary baseline remains audible in the Puhua episode, where an officer cries out to clear the road and Puhua also cries out while making a wrestling gesture. These are all the same vocal act in different institutions and sentence positions. The longer compounds “cheer” (喝采), “shout abuse” (喝罵), and “clear the road by shouting” (喝道) must be translated as compounds; no allowlisted drinking use was established. | Allowlist count at the depth audit: 35,032 hits in 411 texts. High-frequency families include “one shout” (一喝), “shout once” (喝一喝), “the master then shouted” (師便喝), “the monk then shouted” (僧便喝), “four shouts” (四喝), “a shout not used as a shout” (一喝不作一喝用), and “staff and shout” (棒喝). The former entry's two senses—‘a shout’ and ‘to shout/cry out’—were merged because they paraphrased the same vocal event; noun and verb syntax alone did not establish different things. Targeted tests found no allowlisted drinking sense in “drink tea” (喝茶), “drink wine” (喝酒), or “drink water” (喝水). “Cheer” (喝采) and “shout abuse” (喝罵) are separately lexicalized compounds, while “clear the road by shouting” (喝道) supplies the ordinary calling-out baseline. Twelve witnesses preserve definition, master and monk use, simultaneous use, later systematization, explicit appraisal, warning against blind/random shouting, bodily effect, teaching-seat closure, house-device pairing, and ordinary road-clearing use without padding duplicate shouts.

(菩提煩惱坐斷兩頭)' ('hell and heaven pounded into one piece; awakening and affliction — both ends cut off'; Zhongfeng Mingben). Tianyin Yuanxiu (天隱圓修) gives it as an instruction: '(十二時中須教打成一片)，(自無不辦之理)' ('throughout the twelve periods of the day you must have it pounded into one piece; then of itself there is nothing that cannot be accomplished'). The variant (打作一片) ('struck into one piece'; 6× in 6 files) carries the same sense — Yulin Tongxiu, in his (工夫說) ('Discourse on Work'): '(所謂行住坐臥動靜閒忙打作一片)' ('what is called walking, standing, sitting, lying, motion and stillness, leisure and busyness struck into one piece'). (打成一片) occurs 311× in 139 allowlist files. The texts assign the word no gloss beyond its literal sense, and neither does this entry. The Blue Cliff Record gives an explicit equivalence: being on 'the one-color side' (一色邊) is 'also called being pounded into one piece' (亦謂之打成一片). Zhongfeng Mingben's Miscellaneous Record supplies a correction to a different equation: if one knows it as 'a silver mountain and iron wall' (銀山鐵壁), 'it cannot be called pounded into one piece' (不可謂之打成一片). These are the texts' own equivalence and rejection; the entry does not reconcile them beyond reporting both. | (乆乆綿密自然打成一片)' ('the moment such a mind arises it is already interrupted; long, long and closely continuous, it of itself becomes pounded into one piece'; B25n0145); '(古人道我數十年打成一片又云我數十年尚有走作)' ('an ancient said, "for decades I pounded it into one piece," and also said, "after decades I still have running-off"'; Yulin Tongxiu 玉林通琇, B27n0152), and Yongquan Jingxin's (湧泉景欣) '(我四十年在裏許)，(尚有走作)' ('forty years I have been in here, and still there is running-off') raised in (三宜盂禪師語錄) (the recorded sayings of Sanyi Yu, J27nB189). Reaching it is dated in decades (四十年 'forty years' / 數十年 'several decades'). The pairs said to be pounded into one piece vary by passage — (動靜) ('motion and stillness'), (生滅) ('arising and perishing'), (內外) (內心外境, 'inner mind and outer objects'), (情境) ('subject and object'), (聖凡) ('holy and ordinary'), (佛法世法) ('Buddha's teaching and worldly affairs'), (地獄天堂) ('hell and heaven') / (菩提煩惱) ('awakening and affliction') — but the frame — long continuity, then the paired terms spoken of as one piece — is constant across houses. Variant graph (打作一片) ('struck into one piece'; 6×) is the same term; do not treat as separate. Attested across Zhongfeng Mingben (中峰明本) (his extensive record 中峰廣錄, B25n0145), Tianyin Yuanxiu (天隱圓修) (his recorded sayings 天隱語錄, J25nB171), Yulin Tongxiu (玉林通琇) (his recorded sayings 玉琳國師語錄, B27n0152), plus Wei'an Deran (唯菴德然) (J25nB154) and Ruibai Mingxue (瑞白明雪) (J26nB188), the last two off-roster so left unattributed.

Literally, “guest-dust”: dust characterized as a visitor rather than the host. Much of the corpus preserves it in the inherited compound “guest-dust troubles” (客塵煩惱), something said to stain, cover, or be unrecognized. The distinct Chan deployment appears in Baizhang Huaihai's recorded classification: “one's own mind is buddha; illuminating function belongs to bodhisattva; mind after mind is the ruler; illuminating function belongs to guest-dust” (自心是佛，照用屬菩薩；心心是主宰，照用屬客塵). Here “guest-dust” is not merely a name for dirt or an outside visitor; Baizhang places it on the “illuminating function” side of a ruler/guest classification and immediately compares it to speaking of water by way of waves (如波說水). The Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings and the Expanded Lamp preserve this wording independently. Elsewhere the Records say a grown child learns explanations and does not know that these are “guest-dust troubles” (不知是客塵煩惱); Dahui speaks of the “stain of guest-dust troubles since beginningless time” (無始時來客塵煩惱之染); and the Admonitions for the Monastic Gate has the compact bodily compound “body-and-mind guest-dust” (身心客塵). The Zen record therefore keeps the inherited dust imagery but also bends it into Baizhang's explicit ruler/function classification.

Literally, 'the bucket-bottom comes off' or 'the bottom drops out of the bucket.' The phrase occurs 109 times in 75 allowed texts. Its comparison form 'like the bucket-bottom falls out' (如桶底脫) occurs 38 times, including 26 exact endings in 'resembling the bucket-bottom falling out' (桶底脫相似). Xuefeng reports that after Deshan struck him, 'at that time I was as if the bucket-bottom had fallen out' (我當時如桶底脫相似); Yantou immediately challenges what Xuefeng brought in through the gate. Yuanwu uses the same comparison after 'under one phrase' (一言之下) and elsewhere joins the literal image to 'the mechanisms are exhausted' (桶底脫機關盡). The phrase is also recorded as a direct answer: asked 'What is buddha?

Literally, the "gate and court" established for teaching or transformation. Chan records use it for the organized framework of explanations and responsive teaching, then explicitly place it below what questioners call the matter beyond or above it. One monk says, "one question and one answer still fall within the teaching establishment's gate and court" (一問一答猶落建化門庭) and asks how to raise the first principle. A sermon supplies a direct apposition: even a shout said to contain all these features "is still the teaching establishment's gate and court—responsive expedients—called a small resting place, not yet the treasure-site" (猶是建化門庭隨機方便，謂之小歇場，未至寶所). Another says that even holding the seal, raising the banner, and moving freely still falls within it and "is not yet the monk's essential road" (未為衲僧徑要一路). The Chan-specific use is evaluative and institutional: masters name their own question-and-answer and explanatory apparatus as a constructed teaching precinct, commonly in a contrast the texts themselves draw with what is "beyond or above" (向上) or the monk's essential road.

Literally ‘to deceive people.’ The phrase is accusation, warning, and public-interview vocabulary throughout the Chan record. Yunmen asks for ‘a saying that does not deceive people’ (不瞞人底句), then supplies ‘do not say this is the one that deceives people.’ Miyun writes the maxim ‘deceiving people is no good affair; a good affair does not deceive people’ (瞞人不好事，好事不瞞人). Yet the record also refuses a simple division between deceptive speakers and innocent words. The Blue Cliff Record asks whether the patriarchs and buddhas have an intention to deceive, answers by comparing them to rivers and lakes that have no intention to obstruct, and says that when people cannot pass through, the patriarchs and buddhas consequently ‘become deceivers of people.’ Other records pair deceiving people with deceiving oneself and distinguish being able to do one but not the other. Chan thus bends ordinary deception into a recurrent test of sayings, teachers, hearers, and self-deception while retaining the literal verb; the entry does not decide who intends deception where the text expressly denies such intention.
