As part of the stable labels 'Baizhang's wild fox' (百丈野狐), 'the wild-fox story' (野狐話), and 'the wild-fox public case' (野狐公案), the word names the public case attached to Baizhang. Masters raise, debate, and versify this case. Its recorded hinge is the contrast between 'does not fall under cause and effect' (不落因果) and 'is not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果). This is a named lexical object, not the animal body inside its narrative and not a person rebuked as a wild-fox spirit.

Literally, 'solitary brightness.' The term occurs 243 times in 112 allowed texts. Its most frequent expansion is 'solitary brightness, distinct and distinct' (孤明歷歷), with 42 occurrences in 35 texts; another recurring form is 'solitary brightness shining alone' (孤明獨照). Literally, 'main cord and ancestral line' (綱宗): the main cord of a net (綱) joined to the ancestral line or school (宗). In Chan records it names the organizing framework by which a lineage's inherited sayings and distinctions are arranged and identified. The preface to the Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目) places 'the key outlines of the five houses' (五宗綱要) beside 'the terms of the lineage framework' (綱宗語句), including the names and decisive details that an abbot is expected to know. Other texts specify 'the Linji lineage framework' (臨濟綱宗), 'the Dongshan lineage framework' (洞上綱宗), and 'the Caodong lineage framework' (曹洞綱宗), showing that the compound can be qualified by a named house. A record quoting Yantou says, 'Only recognize the lineage framework; originally there is no actual thing' (但識綱宗本無實法), and another version gives, 'For the great governing lineage framework, first one must recognize the phrase' (大統綱宗先須識句). The term also occurs with verbs such as establish, uphold, display, grasp, and restore, and with enumerated house vocabulary such as Linji's 'three mysteries and three essentials' (三玄三要). | ' (何謂綱宗 and 如何是綱宗) did not produce a simple dictionary-style self-definition. The strongest structural evidence is instead the corpus's explicit pairing of 'five-house key outlines' (五宗綱要) with 'lineage-framework terms' (綱宗語句), Yantou's two quoted formulas, and the named-house collocations. This is a corpus-wide category; a Linji or Caodong collocation does not create a master-specific sense.

Allowlist count: 870 hits in 134 texts. Noun and verb constructions denote the same general-address event; the two former targets could not distinguish different referents without their explanations and are merged. The general-address placard (普說牌) names the placard for this genre, not another sense. General address remains distinct from ascending the hall (上堂), small gathering (小參), addressing the assembly (示眾), question-and-answer (問答), and taking up the whisk (秉拂).

Literally ‘five houses,’ this is a corpus label for a five-part grouping of Chan lines and their recorded styles of address. The allowlisted corpus has 376 hits in 128 texts, including ‘five-house lineages’ (五家宗派, 54 hits in 41 texts), ‘purports of the five houses’ (五家宗旨, 115 hits in 58 texts), and ‘records of the five houses’ (五家語錄, 12 hits in 4 texts). One preface supplies an exact enumeration: Guiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan. The same preface says that differing encounter language came to form five houses without deliberate division. Zhongfeng gives two direct definitions: ‘What are called the five houses are five in their people, not five in their way,’ and ‘What are now called the five houses arise from Nanyue and Qingyuan; below those two branches the stream reached these five people.’ A recension preface likewise begins with the Nanyue and Qingyuan branches and says that five lineages later divided from them. The corpus also has four occurrences in four texts of the expanded label ‘five houses and seven lineages’ (五家七宗), including Yuanwu’s critical comment that people divided them and established separate gateways. Accordingly, this entry reports each text’s label or enumeration and does not impose one later sectarian table on every occurrence.

Literally “a dead snake,” attested 335 times in 135 allowlisted texts. The Chan record repeatedly makes the carcass an image for words or material that lie inert until someone can handle them: one record calls faultless but fixed talk “a dead snake across the main road” (死蛇當大路), while Hongzhi pairs “make a dead snake live” (死蛇弄得活) with turning a spirited horse around. The recurring warning “on meeting a dead snake on the road, do not kill it; carry it home in a bottomless basket” (路逢死蛇莫打殺，無底籃子盛將歸) circulates as a quoted line, question, and comment. Other records rebuke clinging to a fixed formulation as “gripping the dead snake’s head” (把死蛇頭) and tell the listener to steer with the wind instead. | The Zen deviation is the stable use of the dead animal as something said, quoted, held, discarded, or made alive in public teaching exchanges. The texts retain the concrete snake throughout; these are deployments of one image, not separate referents requiring a sense split. The family check found “live snake” (活蛇), “dead snake’s head” (死蛇頭), “handle a dead snake” (弄死蛇), and “make a dead snake live” (死蛇弄得活); all preserve the same object/action contrast.

These are text-drawn criticisms of named actions; they do not supply a single imported category for the headword.

Literally, "steam sand to make cooked rice." The phrase occurs 12 times in nine allowlisted texts. The records state the failure inside the comparison. One says that seeking outside and blind refining are "like steaming sand to make rice: in the end the matter is not accomplished" (如蒸砂作飯，終不成事). Another asks whether steaming sand to make rice could cure the sore of hunger (譬如蒸砂作飯，豈療飢瘡). The phrase is paired with other impossible operations: "steaming sand to make rice, climbing a tree to seek fish" (蒸砂作飯，緣木求魚), and "striking ice to seek fire, steaming sand to make rice" (敲冰覓火、蒸砂作飯). It also appears in public interview: a monk says, "talking mystery and speaking subtlety is painted cakes filling hunger; raising the old and discussing the present is steaming sand to make rice. Apart from these two roads, how is a message passed?
